Around midnight a traveller sees a will-o'-the-wisp coming towards him, which he baptises out of pity and fear. So many other will-o'-the-wisps come up that only in the morning does he see the last little light float away.
50019: At night a man is lifted up by invisible hands, carried through the air and set down on the ground somewhere. He says he is glad he was not carried through hedge and bush, because then he would have had to go straight ahead the whole way and would not have got off without bruises, scratches and torn clothes.
50021: A farmer sends his farmhand to the priest for advice about unexplained things that are happening, such as pots of beer falling over and cattle being untied. During the journey a carriage drives over the farmhand's head, the trip takes much longer, and the priest knows all about everything. He says the farmer's wife is to blame and predicts that she will soon die. At the moment the wife dies all the elder trees move, although everything is still. After that there are no more problems. When the farmer has the floor broken open, toads come out. The children's fingers have grown together.
50023: Night-time encounters with black cats are dangerous: if you kick or strike at cats, more appear. A cat answers a man's question and later comes to a gathering of young people.
50024: Every night at twelve o'clock the glowing ball falls down on the spot where a murder was committed.
50025: One evening a man ends up among a group of cats holding a feast, who give him a cup that he must drink up. He pretends to and speaks God's name, whereupon the cats disappear. The man takes the cup with him, but no one comes to claim it. Years later the goldsmith to whom he wants to sell the cup discovers initials on it, and it becomes known who the owner is. After the man's story it becomes clear why the woman never asked for her cup back.
50026: The quality of a brewer's beer declines after his marriage. One evening he discovers a pack of black cats on the brewing kettle and throws a bucket of boiling water over them, whereupon they run off burned. In the morning his wife lies dead in bed, covered in burns.
50027: Someone who strikes a cat sitting on a barrier is told to do it again. Whoever strikes the cat a second time will find several cats appearing that maul the person. Most people do not dare; others who have heard the story avoid the place.
50031: A hunter's shot misses a large hare, but at once the hunter is surrounded by hundreds of hares that escort him as he flees home.
50033: Poachers see riders dressed as gendarmes racing across the heath, who turn into a four-wheeled carriage drawn by two horses, which, as they come closer, turns into a dog cart that vanishes without a trace.
50034: At midnight a man gets a box on the ear because he is in the way of a funeral procession that must pass.
50035: A young man sees a man on a large horse pass by so fast that it looks like a flock of birds flying through the air, while the ground shakes with the thud of hooves.
50036: The black cat that a man has taken home and locks up at night under a wooden box in a closed room has disappeared the next morning without any signs of a break-in.
50037: A man is lifted up by an invisible hand and thrown from the road onto the ice. Although he is not afraid, from then on he no longer ventures onto the sunken road at that hour.
50038: Friends unwittingly end up one evening in a churchyard surrounded by a stone rampart without an exit. They climb over the rampart, whereupon two of the men decide not to go any further. The third calls them cowards and says that even if the devil comes he will go on. On the way he is accompanied to his village by a dog with glowing eyes.
50039: A carter tries to knock away two black cats hanging on the horse's collar, whereupon more cats appear that circle the cart dancing on their hind legs and holding each other with their front paws. The horse can barely move forward. On the same road a man also sees at night something white that grows as big as a horse, picks him up and flies over the road.
50042: A man who moves a boundary post is punished by God after his death. At night he haunts the spot of the boundary post with the post on his shoulders, asking where he should put it. One night a drunk man answers that he must take the post back to where it came from. The ghost is released and stays away once he has done this.
50044: At night men meet a woman who, when one of them pushes aside her falie (a traditional shawl), turns out to have red-glowing eyes. Two of the men flee in fright. The third later tells, as proof of what happened, that he jumped over a thicket so high that he normally could not have done it.
50045: A farmer who secretly moves the boundary of his field comes back after his death with the post on his shoulder, asking where he should put it. A drunk passer-by calls out to him that he must put the post back where it came from. The ghost is then released, puts the post in its original place and disappears. The drunk man sobers up at once and tells his wife at home what happened, and she passes the story on.
50046: After his death the man who moved a boundary post walks about every night with the post on his shoulder, calling out where the post should stand. The ghost disappears when a drunk man tells him to put the post back in its former place.
50048: A man will not say anything about his encounter with a ghost, but never again dares to pass that place.
50049: After his death, the municipal secretary who had wronged the municipality returns to his house with hauntings. One of the hauntings is a wagon that drives invisibly through the gate and the stable and is suddenly in the attic, driving and rattling.
50051: On the road a man and his horse are bewitched, so that the horse cannot go on, and countless cats sit on the horse's back and collar. After the man has knocked the cats away and prayed, the witches disappear.
50052: At night a carter meets a band of witches in the shape of cats. They disappear when he strikes at them with his whip.
50053: A cat that is struck and disappears, after which a woman further on in a hedge puts on her cap, is the example of how a witch can turn into a cat and back again.
50054: Two places where witches in the shape of cats meet at night.
50055: One night a man sees a line of men in black going to the churchyard, but when he waits for them they do not come. Many people see a funeral procession, but it is thought that only people born with a caul can.
50056: Gnomes leave the area after their chief is shot dead by a hunter.
50057: A man born with a caul sees a funeral procession in the evening. His prediction that his sick wife will die within three days comes true.
50058: Two shots miss a hare, and the hare even runs back into range a few times. With a bullet blessed by the priest, the farmer manages to shoot off its left leg.
50062: A long-held belief that on the Duivelsberg spirits from hell perform devilish tricks. Many see monstrous creatures there that frighten people and put them to flight.
50063: A crowd of cats appears when a man throws his spade at a cat blocking his way. After a prayer is said the cats vanish, but the spade has vanished too and stays gone.
50064: In the evening or at night some people see an animal standing that looks like a horse without a head, and it suddenly disappears when people come closer.
50065: Around midnight passers-by are accompanied for a few minutes by a silent young lady dressed in white.
50066: A headless dog the size of a calf walks along with passers-by for a while in the evening when it is dark, without doing any harm.
50067: Carters nearly always go into a certain woman's pub, otherwise there is a chance she will hold their horses fast.
50068: A landlady tells a man in Germany how his family is doing, and as proof shows a knife from his household. When he gets home, the man finds that the woman told the truth. When the news was being told, she had jumped onto the table in the shape of a cat, thrown the knife on the floor, and vanished, as had the knife.
50069: A Danish woman can tell a man who is far from home news about his family the next morning, and as proof shows a spoon from his household bearing his mark. At night the household sees a cat sneak in, jump on the table, throw a spoon on the floor and run off with the spoon.
50070: A woman in Luxembourg tells a man that his wife has given birth. As proof she shows a piece of the childbed meal. Indeed, the family had seen a cat eat a piece from the pot and disappear again.
50080: A man who has heard voices underground saying they will leave the next night because Kyrië is dead tells others about it. Another man hides to watch, and from midnight until the next morning hundreds of gnomes pass by.
50085: One evening invisible beings lift a man up, and he hears the words over hedge and bush; they take him on a journey through the air, during which he bumps his foot against a tower. After coming back down to earth he walks home, and is delayed on the heath by the fens. The man believes the Bokkenrijders (goat riders) or Kaboutermannen (gnomes) were the cause.
50087: Neighbours of the man who is a werewolf search for the leather belt from which the werewolf draws his power, and throw it into a burning oven. After the belt is burnt, the man stops being a werewolf.
50088: After his belt is burnt, a man is no longer a werewolf.
50089: On the way home the suitor goes into the woods. He tells the girl to walk on slowly, and if a dog comes she must throw a handkerchief in front of it. A dog appears and she throws a handkerchief in front of it. Back home she sees remnants of the handkerchief between the boy's teeth, so he must be a werewolf. The planned marriage is called off when it turns out that the boy has a secret power to bring harm to people and because he is a werewolf.
50090: While her boyfriend has left her alone for a moment on the way home, a girl is attacked by a big dog that tears her apron. When he comes back the boy reassures the frightened girl and nothing more happens. At home, however, the girl sees bits of her apron between his teeth, and she breaks off the courtship.
50092: A boy twice strikes a cat sitting on a bridge railing so that it falls into the water, but both times it jumps back onto the railing. When the cat then tells him to do it again, the boy knows it was a witch in the form of a cat.
50093: One evening a man meets a hare standing on its hind legs, dancing and leaping. The man tries three times to chase the hare away, but the animal comes back three times.
50094: A man who speaks to a cat on a turnstile gets an answer from the cat in the form of a question in return.
50095: The death of newborn calves at a farmer's is blamed on a large cat that the farmer's wife sees sneaking to the stable.
50096: A cat that a boy carries home in the evening jumps away, thanking him for carrying it. The boy understands that it was a witch in the shape of a cat.
50097: Villagers chase a hare; at the spot where they thought they had seen the hare sits a woman who has not seen any hare. The people believe the woman is a witch who has turned herself into a hare.
50098: A hare hit by bullets scratches itself behind the ears and otherwise seems unharmed. People claim the hare is a neighbour woman who is regarded as a witch.
50099: Travelling in the evening, a boy and a girl notice that a dog is following them. As soon as the boy goes at the dog with a stick, they hear the terrible rattling of a chained dog, though nothing can be seen. The boy goes into the field and sees a sheep standing there. Meanwhile the girl has fainted, and the boy takes her to a house. At midnight the boy passes the spot and nothing unusual is going on.
50100: A drunken man challenges a ghost to show itself, whereupon the ghost appears and walks home with him.
50101: On his way in the evening a man hears strange panting and groaning and thinks it must be a fearsome ghost. So the man takes a detour, but ends up right at the ghost he thought he had avoided. The ghost turns out to be a monstrosity as big as a horse, without head or legs.
50102: At night three friends meet a woman who, when the narrator pushes aside her falie (a long hooded cloak), has red-glowing eyes. As they flee, one of them claims to have jumped over a high hedge.
50103: At a haunted spot a man sees a silent woman sitting and spinning. He does not dare say anything and goes home frightened.
50104: A miller plagued by witches in the shape of cats is helped by someone who stays the night in the mill by the fire with an unconsecrated and a consecrated candle and a kettle. The man asks the cat that appears where she comes from and invites her to warm herself. In the end there are 42 cats dancing paw in paw around the fire. The man strikes at the cats with a sabre and cuts off a middle finger with a gold ring. It is the ring of the miller's wife, for her name is on the ring. The next day the miller's wife lies in bed with a finger cut off.
50105: A number of encounters with a phantom dog that accompanies people and makes noise or roars terribly.
50106: A girl's health suffers from her encounters with a spirit. Asked why it appears, the shade answers that he is her father and can only enter heaven once three more Masses have been said. After the girl has done this, her health improves.
50107: A dead father appears as a ghost to his son and charges him to make a pilgrimage and give a loaf of bread to a poor person, because the father did not fulfil an obligation during his life.
50108: On the priest's advice, a silent spirit that appears to a girl is asked what must be done. The spirit turns out to be her mother, who wants a Mass said. The shade disappears after the request is promised and fulfilled. An imprint of the spirit's hand remains on her hand, even though she had wrapped it in a cloth.
50109: A dead parish priest appears to a woman, asks her to do a good work for him so that he will be saved and she will be happy, and disappears again.
50110: On his way home at midnight a man is stopped by a ghost. He does not manage to drive the spirit away with a stick. Just outside the village he hears clear whistling and invisible people. He also sees a ghost floating in front of him.
50111: One evening a person, pale and thin as a ghost, enters a house and demands that the man present let himself be shaved. After being urged several times, the man no longer dares to refuse. The shaving goes in the usual way, but the ghost's hands are ice-cold. Afterwards the shaved man never grows a beard again; he also loses the hair on his head and it never comes back.
50112: Seven boys plan to frighten the girls walking home in the evening by dressing up as ghosts. When they notice that an eighth person has unexpectedly and unnoticed joined them, they run away and decide never to play such pranks again.
50113: The place where a woman sits reeling yarn is avoided. In the evening cats block the road and scratch people who touch or bother them.
50114: Crossroads are places where witches gather in the dark. A man who does not believe this goes and stands at a crossroads on Christmas night and indeed notices nothing, but on the way home he is overtaken by an old woman muttering about how she will manage the cooking for so many guests. After the student has called out something mocking to her, he is attacked by cats.
50115: Witches from the whole area, in the shape of cats, have their meeting place in a linden tree, where they play and dance and confer about secret arts. That their coming and going is not noticed is not strange, for it is believed that a witch can change into a cat and back, and that they are invisible to people.
50116: A parish priest is held fast and can move on once he has read from his breviary. If priests do not read their hours on time, witches have power over them.
50117: A woman known as a witch asks a man on his way home from a fair whether he has come from the fair. The man does not answer, but a little later an extraordinarily large mole runs ahead of him.
50118: After a strange cat that comes into the house is beaten and chased away, the tormenting of a woman by a witch she knows comes to an end.
50121: In a pit lies a tower bell which is said to strike only at midnight on Christmas Eve. The woman who calls on the bell to make a miracle happen immediately gets a stiff neck from which she never recovers.
50122: Stories about sunken bells in various places, and how the bells came to be there.
50128: A young knight is attacked by a band of robbers and taken to the chief's dwelling, where there is also a young girl. The girl, who is given leave to visit the nobleman, turns out to have been abducted from her cradle at her parents' castle. Together they manage to escape, return to their families and marry each other. The band is driven off and the robbers escape; only the woman is tried and burned. The robber chief vows revenge by picking up a bullet stained with blood and saying that whoever refuses will walk about burning and glowing. He manages to get a night's lodging at the nobleman's castle, but a servant foils his plan to kill the nobleman by shooting the robber chief dead. From that time on a glowing human figure appears at night.
50150: One evening a man sees cats dancing paw in paw and singing, and then drinking from a silver goblet. He declines the invitation to drink from the cup too, but does take it home with him. A woman's name turns out to be written in the cup. When he comes to her house to return the cup, she is lying ill in bed, but she recognises his voice.
50265: A hunter does not believe the story about a hare that cannot be hit. He puts it to the test; before midnight he sees two ordinary hares that stay out of range. At midnight a large hare comes straight at him, but is not hit by his shots. The hare mockingly asks whether the two little ones are far ahead yet.
50270: A black tomcat asks a farmer who gives him a mocking answer to repeat it. As soon as the farmer tries to strike the cat, he is attacked by so many cats that he cannot fight them off. He flees home without his horse.
50279: A cat that sits in the same spot every evening answers a question.
50281: In the morning there are dog's paw prints on the hearth of a bewitched house. The next morning the sausages made the evening before are hanging in the tree in front of the house. Every evening a cat sits in that tree and answers back. A man who strikes at the cat is at once surrounded by countless cats that chase him all the way home.
50282: On the third night before someone dies, a funeral procession goes about. Someone who passes a medlar thicket that night gets a hard blow from an invisible hand, from the mispelman (medlar man).
50283: Cats that make a racket at night are witches holding a meeting.
50286: One evening a priest is thrown into the water by someone invisible. When he says that whoever made him wet will also see to it that he gets dry, an invisible witch tells him that the next morning his shirt will be hanging from the church spire, which is indeed the case.
50289: A ghost walks on a meadow that is up for sale. A woman sees that the ghost has human legs. The ghost is probably someone trying to give the land a bad name this way so he can buy it cheaply.
50290: A farmhand has to open the gate across the road for a funeral procession. But at twelve o'clock at night before the funeral, the farmhand already has to open the gate for the same procession.
50291: On the night before the death of guild brothers, the brothers hear loud knocking on the chest where the funeral cloaks are kept.
50292: A man foresees the building of factories, houses, etc.
50294: Will-o'-the-wisps are the souls of unbaptised children. When they float above the water, they want to be baptised.
50337: Two rhymes indicating that no meaning is attached to dreams. Two examples of belief in dreams as omens.
50338: Unexplained noises in the house, such as a thump or a tap on a window or door, are an omen of an imminent death.
50339: If the cart hook falls while a cart is being driven, it is an omen of a death.
50341: Omens of a death are two bells ringing in confusion together, and a clock striking at the moment the host is elevated during Mass.
50343: Giving a knife or scissors as a gift cuts off a friendship. This can be prevented by paying the giver something and asking that it be given to a poor person.
50346: A hearse horse pawing the ground in front of a house of mourning means another death within six weeks.
50347: Where little lights can be seen in the evening, money lies buried.
50349: A painting or mirror falling off the wall means a death or brings bad luck. Breaking a mirror when moving house brings bad luck.
50350: Animals as omens of a visit, a wedding or a death. The striking of a clock is an omen of a death.
50351: An owl sitting and calling near a house in the evening means a death.
50866: There was a farmer who could change into a werewolf; he would then come over the bridge as a black dog to roam as a werewolf.
50868: An old miller is pushed aside by an invisible force while out walking.
50869: Poachers shoot a cat off the roof. The witch, in the form of the cat, died.
50870: Poachers are out hunting. When they come to a pile of wood, one of them says he wishes a hare that can talk would come out of it. When a talking hare really does come out of the pile, the poachers run away in fear.
50874:
If a witch has bewitched a child, one can burn the witch by boiling her in the form of a black hen.
A sign that there is witchcraft in a house is roses in the pillow.
Witches used to be weighed in Oudewater.
50875: Use of little dolls in the shape of the enemy, to transfer pain to the enemy.
50892: In the past there were people who could sense that the eels were coming up out of the mud (and so it was time to fish).
57771: If you walked on the bridle path at midnight, you risked being pushed aside by a funeral procession of blinde belies (blind ghostly figures).
57772: A farmer was on his way with a horse and foal to a market in another town. While he is walking on the dike he is suddenly thrown off it and a little woman comes up to him.
57774: When the wind was right, in Goudriaan you could hear a witch flying over the chimney. A white bird was also seen then.
57776: When a family's daughter falls ill, everyone is convinced she has been bewitched. They try to lure the witch and lock up an old woman whom they accuse. This turns into a riot. In the end the girl turns out to be pregnant.
57777: A girl and a boy are walking along the dike. When the boy goes off for a moment, the girl is attacked by a black dog. When her boyfriend returns she recognises him as the dog, since there are threads of her apron between his teeth.
57789: At midnight you could meet a funeral procession on the dike; if you were in the way, you were pushed aside.
57791: Many cats have gathered by a barn. Sometimes they chase someone, at other times they have vanished.
57792: People thought that some spots on the dike were haunted, because the mats in front of the houses there often suddenly disappeared and were found rolled up in the attic.
57799: Sometimes the churn was bewitched, so that butter could no longer be made.
57820: A large group of polecats sat by a mill, but when people walked over there was nothing to be seen or heard. Sometimes they ran around the mill.
57821: Certain places were haunted. There were black/white shades that could not be caught. They held people fast. If people took a detour, the shades went along with them.
57832: When the narrator was young, his neighbour's place was haunted. Other places were haunted too. His mother knew how to protect oneself against it.
57833: In the past there were mysterious fires; they came from the friction of ghosts.
57834: In the past people thought that cattle disease came from haunting.
57838: In the past several people were accused of witchcraft. They were able to lead others off the road, or make doors open and close by themselves.
57839: There was a woman who often saw a black cat walking about. But she could never catch the cat.
57841: People warned that you had to watch out for the witch. You were not to accept anything from her, nor let her stroke your hair.
57843:
To protect the horses against the nightmare, one had to lay a cross in front of the threshold.
Someone whose hair was in a mess was sometimes compared to a nightmare or a werewolf.
57849: If the churn did not work, people thought it was bewitched.
60744: When the churn would not produce butter, a red-hot poker was thrust into it. The churn worked again, but afterwards the neighbour woman went around with a burnt arm.
60746: The narrator's great-grandfather, while walking through the fields, was set back across the ditch. Others were put in the water. This happened in many places.
60747: People were warned to walk on the horse path, because walking in the wheel track was dangerous. On this path haunted the people who had been born without a caul. They threw walkers off the road.
60750: When a horse stood overkoot (an abnormal position of the hoof), the person blamed for it was called a werewolf.
69279: In the old days an old woman lived in Goudriaan who was thought to be a witch.
69310: When a house was haunted, all the things moved by themselves. There was a woman who could do witchcraft who went haunting with a sheet around her, and this seemed to attract ghosts. Nobody dared to pass her house any more.
69315: Near a haunted house people were led off the road; people were afraid to come near it.
69318: One should not go onto the bridle path.
69361: The wife of S. de J. was named as a witch. People found it frightening to walk past their house.
69363: In Leerbroek there is talk of a haunted castle, devilry and hauntings. A priest exorcised these activities.
69364: In Bergambacht Overlek there used to be unexplained fires in which several farms burned down. It is said that the people were warned beforehand. The culprit was never caught.
69454: At night on the road, a witch's cat asks a man whether the kovelet (hood) fits him. The man does not respond and flees into his house. The next morning a little hood with a little cloak is found hanging on the back door.
69613: Three boys each get an apple from a witch. When they later take the apples out of a basket, they are toads.
69614: A man gets a pear from a witch and puts it in his pocket. When he gets home and wants to give the pear to his children, it has changed into a toad.
69615: A man from Vessem in Brabant outwits the devil. As long as the leaves are on the trees, the devil does what the man wants, but when the leaves fall from the trees the devil may come and take him. The man, however, ties the leaves to the trees with string. When the devil sees through the trick, he goes away.
69616: A farmer from Duizel goes to Riethoven to sell his cow. On the way home he passes a linden tree where he is startled by a black cat. When he tries to hit the cat with a stick, eleven black cats suddenly appear and dance around him. A witch crawls out of the linden tree and then chases him.
69619: A man is offered a glass of sweet wine by a cat. He does not drink it, but recognises the glass and returns it to its owner.
69620: On his way home a man feels a big dog walking between his legs. Neither his friend nor the man himself can see the animal.
69621: On his way home a man meets a dog. The dog follows him all the way to his house and keeps growing larger.
69625: A man is walking home with friends in the evening and feels a dog brushing past his legs that starts to bite him. Neither the man nor his friends can see the dog, but the next day the man is covered in scratches.
69627: A farmhand always disappears during supper. His friends decide to follow him and so find out that he is a werewolf. They call in a priest to free the farmhand from his enchantment. The priest does this by burning the werewolf's skin.
69630: A cruel lord of the castle haunts his castle for centuries after his death. Because of this the castle is abandoned.
69631: The rattling of chains is constantly heard in a house. One of the villagers is not afraid to go and investigate. After an hour in the house a ghost with chains appears and leads the man to a spot where the ghost disappears. The next morning a skeleton with chains is found in the ground at that spot. The bones are buried and the ghost does not return.
69632: A poor beggar woman knocks on a door to spend the night somewhere. She is offered a place in a haunted room. The second night she is woken by the shrieking of a ghost that takes money from the windowsill and sits down to count it. The next morning she tells her host and they find the ghost's money. The host offers the woman half, but she says he should give it to the poor. After that the ghost no longer returns.
69633: During a crossbowmen's procession in Valkenswaard, a hare starts running at the front. Boys chase the hare, which dashes into the woods. When they have almost caught the hare, the animal changes into an old woman.
69635: In Eersel a white horse appeared that accompanied the people who had died of the plague to the churchyard. There was also an invulnerable hare that turned into an old woman after being shot at three times.
69636: A farmer's calves keep dying. One day his wife sees a hare hopping to the stable. The next morning another calf was dead.
69637: A castle near Eersel is haunted. A brave man from the village goes to investigate. While waiting, he bakes pancakes over a fire. Each time a pancake is done, a limb falls out of the chimney, until at midnight they form a skeleton that comes to life. The skeleton points him to the cellar, where there are three chests of gold. When the chests are divided between the man, the church and the poor, the ghost can rest.
69665: On his way home Kobus always came across dancing and singing cats. One evening he crept into the ditch to see them better, and then they sang to him.
69666: While out hunting, a father and son come across a cat. The son shoots at the cat, but the cat jumps into a ditch. When they come home that evening, grandmother is sitting in front of the fire drying herself.
69699: A woman dies in childbed and for several weeks afterwards keeps haunting the bridle path near her old home. Only when the baby dies does the woman go away.
69707: In a house there is banging every time it gets dark. One day Hannes decides to turn the whole house upside down to stop the banging. While doing so he finds a chest of money. The banging does not stop, however. Then he decides to ask for help from an old woman, who sprinkles the rooms with holy water. The banging goes away, and the once poor family now has the money that was left behind.
69708: A miller wanted to grind at night as well, but at night the mill could not process a single grain even though it was turning. To solve this the miller called in the help of his farmhand. One evening the farmhand kept watch and saw seven magpies come flying to the mill. The farmhand shot at the biggest magpie and hit the bird's toe, which had a ring on it. The next morning it turned out that the ring belonged to the miller's wife. So she was a witch.
69710:
A miller is pestered by a woman almost every day. When, on his farmhand's advice, he removes the ladder so the woman cannot climb up, she is still found with the miller the next day. Strange things also happen at night in the miller's room.
The farmhand decides to spend a few nights in that room and, to his horror, sees two big, stinking, green animal claws come under the door at twelve o'clock each time. On the third night he chops off the claws with a machete. The miller and the farmhand burn the severed claws, and the next morning they hear that the woman who pestered the miller has been found dead in bed with her arms chopped off.
69727: A hare could not be hit by bullets. Only after the priest had blessed a bullet was the hare struck in its leg. That same night a woman was walking around with only one arm.
69728: A farmer kept seeing a hare around his farm and decided to kill it. But the hare could not be hit. After three days the farmer decided to crush a dime and use it as a bullet, but on the fourth day the hare did not come back.
69729: A farmer's son kept seeing a hare in the cabbage field and decided to kill the animal. The bullets kept missing the hare, and the farmer's son was advised to put silver on the bullet. He used a dime for this, and when he then shot at the hare he managed to kill it.
69730: There used to be a magic hare in Hoogen. Two hunters tried to shoot it, but every time they tried, their guns would not work. Another hunter from the area also tried to kill the hare, but when he had his gun ready to shoot, there were dozens of hares standing in the field. It was a hare that had been bewitched by the clog maker.
69733: During the Belgian Revolution several posts were stationed along the southern border of Brabant. A captain would make unexpected rounds of the guardhouses at night to check that the soldiers were at their posts. One night the hated captain vanished without a trace, but from then on a large black dog came to inspect the posts. The large dog had a rattling chain and no shot could hit it. When the troops left the border, the dog went away too.
69736: People do not dare to pass a black dog in front of the church door. The priest strikes the dog and declares that it shall vanish in the name of God. The dog, a recently deceased man who wanted to see his wife and children, asks him to pass on his greetings to them.
69737: On his way home a man met a large black dog. But the man was not afraid and said: "If you are the devil, be gone; if you are of God, speak." The dog went away and the man could continue on his way.
69738:
A farmhand from Bladel was walking home with his girl when he felt the urge to play the werewolf. He sent the girl ahead with an excuse and told her that if she met a big dog on the way she should throw her handkerchief to it and keep walking. No sooner said than done, and when they got home she told the story to her family. During supper the girl's family saw fibres of a handkerchief between the farmhand's teeth and concluded that he had been the werewolf.
Because they thought the farmhand a good man, they went to the fathers of Hei-Tongeren for advice. These told them to burn the werewolf's belt, and that the farmhand would then be rid of his werewolf playing for good.
69740: When a plague epidemic broke out in Oirschot, a white horse appeared out of nowhere and carried the victims of the disease. The white horse was always ready to carry the dead and did not need to be fetched. When the last plague victim had been buried, the white horse disappeared too.
69741: In Veldhoven, during a plague epidemic, a white horse roamed about as a herald of death. After people made a pilgrimage to Werbeek, the plague disappeared together with the horse.
69742: Near a little village in Belgium a headless foal haunted the area. The bravest man in the village once came across the creature and was terribly frightened. After that evening the foal was never seen again.
69743:
After a few drinks, a man is challenged by a stranger to a cursing contest. On his way home he meets a foal that stares at him devilishly with flaming eyes, so that he cannot move. Only when the sun rises can he move again.
Out of fear and regret for taking part in the cursing contest, he goes to the priest to confess. But because the cursing was so serious, the priest cannot help him and sends the man to the brown friars and a dean. After the man has been to those friars and the dean, he never cursed again.
69749: A woman ends up in hospital, where strange things happen, and suddenly disappears. A policeman looking for her is harassed by a black cat. At the hut a jet of fire sets bushes alight, which the policeman attacks with buckets of water. At the same time he sees a cat and a woman fighting, and throws a bucket of water over both, after which nothing is left of the cat. The woman says the water has freed her from the devil, because the devil cannot stand it.
70091: The werewolf was in the polder, you would sometimes hear people say. Then they heard a kind of roaring. They also said that the sheep had been torn apart by the werewolf.
70094: The howling of a dog means a death within three days.
70207: A man asks a priest who can drive out the devil for help for his wife, who has not been able to speak for seven years. The priest advises him to go to the fathers of Hei-Tongeren. On the way the man suffers all kinds of trouble; the fathers realise it was the devil and bless him with holy water. He must make his wife eat scalding hot porridge. While eating, his wife struggles for breath, then a bluebottle flies out of her mouth, after which she can speak again.
70208: A possessed man goes on a retreat, where he must first confess before the fathers can help him. The man starts roaring like a wild animal, so he cannot confess. The fathers push him into the confessional, bless him with holy water and walk around the confessional three times with a crucifix. Then a terrible noise breaks out as if two men are fighting, and a cloud of smoke rises, after which the church smells of sulphur. The man is freed from the devil.
70209: Witches' rings, found around beech trees and on bare patches in meadows, are places where witches dance. To be able to fly they rub themselves with an ointment and speak a formula.
70210: Man has seen singing cats dancing paw in paw.
70238: A bare ring in the fields is the place where witches in the shape of cats gather and dance. Whoever dares to enter the circle is held fast.
70239: Cats dance around a ring of mushrooms; at night witches hold witches' meetings; people who go to watch lose their way as punishment; cat pits where cats dance. A man who goes to watch must dance with the cats; they drag him into the cat pit, where he drowns.
70240: A boy is woken by the yowling of cats and sees something float out of the girl. He cannot wake her; later the floating thing returns, whereupon the girl wakes. She dreamed that she went to the churchyard, where she turned into a mottled cat. The next night at midnight the boy goes to the churchyard, sees the mottled cat among black cats, picks it up and throws it away, shouting that the cats must vanish. He is startled when the girl speaks to him, for the spell is broken.
70241: At midnight witches in the shape of black cats dance by a linden tree. A man who refuses to join the dance strikes at the cats, but they cannot be touched.
70287: If you saw a black cat walking along the road in Goudriaan in the evening and struck it, the next day you might meet a woman with her arm in a sling.
70289: The narrator once heard of a bewitched churn that started running by itself.
70390: A farmer who walks past the tree where witches in the shape of cats are holding a cats' dance is forced to drink from a cup. When he speaks the name of God the cats disappear. The name of a woman is discovered on the cup.
70395: A man who on Christmas night throws a stone among cats dancing in the churchyard is attacked by the cats. By making the sign of the cross he makes the cats disappear.
70402: A miller's farmhand who is troubled by cats, especially at night, makes a fire, lights a blessed and an unblessed candle, lets a black cat sit by the fire, and notices the number of cats increasing. During the cats' dance he hacks at the cats with a sword, and they disappear. The finger with a gold ring that the farmhand finds turns out the next day to belong to the miller's wife.
70407: A carter who is surrounded by cats throws a knife at them to chase them away. At the first house he comes to, he asks if he may rest. The woman who opens the door has a cloth around her head with fresh blood on it.
70438: The werewolf was talked about in the old days too. Then they would shout: "Woman, bring your cat inside, it's starting to weerwolven (werewolf about)!"
70443: There was clairvoyance in the old days too, at the fair in Gorrekom. They had to see your fingers, and then she told you all the joys and sorrows awaiting you.
70489: When will-o'-the-wisps/stalkaarsen could be seen, it was something mysterious. In Gorkum there is still a piece of land named after them. That land is called 'De stalkaars'.
70490: In the old days, when old people got together, you heard stories about how they had suddenly been shoved to the side of the road, and more things like that.
70491: The werewolf is something in a horse's tail. A smith in Gelderland did something about it, stroking or something like that. Then the horse was better again.
70492: At the time of the cattle plague, some people saw omens in the sky. In Noordeloos there was a farmstead with two separate stables. In one all the cattle were gone, and in the other the cows had nothing wrong with them.
70494: In the old days, if the butter would not come in the churn, it was bewitched. Then you had to put a handful of salt in it. And when the cows had to go into the cowshed, salt was strewn under the turfs, so that they would not lose their calves.
70496: If there are many magpies near the farmstead, you will get a lot of visitors.
70497: If a dog whines plaintively, there will be a death in the neighbourhood.
70570: In the old days curtains hung on wooden rods. If a curtain fell from the window, it was said, there would be a death within a week.
70571: The screeching of a magpie or an owl at night means impending disaster.
70580: The wheelwright's wife was a witch. There was also a witch at the Sluis. The little house by the Sluis was a haunted house. If you went there in the evening, you could not get past it properly.
70584: I once heard my grandmother talk about the bewitched churn; then boiling water had to be added.
70587: If the cat washes her ears, you will get visitors.
70588: If you spill sugar, you will also get visitors: if it is fine sugar, gentlemen will call; if it is coarse sugar, ladies will call.
70674: It was said of witches that the broomstick stuck out of the chimney.
70727: A house in Deil was haunted. A sort of skeleton was apparently seen there.
70729: A young man was coming back from his girlfriend's and saw a ghost. Someone else also saw a white figure when coming back from his girlfriend's. It turned out to be a white shirt hanging over a wire.
70732: They had seen signs in the sky of the cattle plague.
70735: If the butter would not come in the churn, you had to hold a red-hot poker in it.
70737: A horse can have a wolf in its tail. Then the root of the tail is very limp.
72499: Centuries ago a monk is said to have been murdered on the Kapittelstoep. He apparently still haunts it.
72502: Girls fled from a boy in a white boiler suit because they thought he was a ghost. A traffic policeman was mistaken for a ghost by a man.
72511: According to the saying, it will thaw when an old woman wearing a bonnet goes onto the ice. That is why old women in bonnets on the ice are jeered at by the young people.
72513: A barn owl making a racket at night foretells great disaster.
72515: If a corpse lay above ground on a Sunday, another person would die within a week.
72717: Father went along the church path, it was all like silver. Most went back, because there were so many leaves. A ghost. They called the tree the climbing tree.
72719: At twelve o'clock at night a ghost walked across the road near Capelle. It was a fellow wearing an animal skin who frightened people. But another man went up to him and hit him, and that was the end of the ghost.
72720: At a farmer's place a cow often broke loose at night. His son kept watch at twelve o'clock and then a cat came along, and it was a man!
72723: In the old days there were people who could do magic. They were called toverkatten (witch cats), because they could change into a cat. They could not be shot, but if silver was put on the shot they were crippled.
72725: A cat came up to him and he kicked at it, and then more and more came.
72726: While he was hunting, more and more animals came the more he shot. And he could not hit a single one. But when he put a dime in his gun, he shot one in the backside.
72727: In the past people often told about Mien Spook. When a man came home, they told him that there was haunting going on at the cemetery. So the man went there and grabbed Mien Spook by the arm. After that it was over.
72728: A farmer came to an inn and drank some beer. When he left, the innkeeper's wife said he had to bring something back, or else she would make him drive into the water with his horse. And that is what happened.
72730: People often read a book about witches and witchcraft in the evening, and while they read it all came out. Then they threw the books away, but the witches stayed all the same.
72731: In the old days there were those magic cats everywhere. They were strange creatures, and you couldn't hit them either.
72732: If you follow that will-o'-the-wisp, you end up on the dwaalpad (path of straying). In the old days they called them stalkaarsen.
72735: The farmhand had to ferry people across the Drongelse vaart at night. When he sailed back he saw a rowing boat going faster, but with nobody in it.
72737: In Hoge Vaart they also had a witch. When a horse refused to be harnessed, a witch came, and then the horse was suddenly willing.
72739: In Drongelen there was a woman who was said to be able to do magic. But if you keep that in mind, she cannot bewitch you. So when she came by, I said she could do nothing, because I was thinking of it.
72740: A boy had to go to the doctor and met a woman who could do magic. She asked why he was running so fast, and when he told her he had to go to the doctor, she said he had better hurry. And then he started running faster and faster.
72743: In the evening you saw will-o'-the-wisps moving over the ground. The Roman Catholics said that if you had not baptised your children and they had died, they became will-o'-the-wisps, because they did not go to heaven.
72747: There was a hunter shooting at a hare. But that hare was a witch who had turned herself into a hare. Every shot missed, until he put a dime on the barrel of his gun; then he shot her in the backside. So the woman said she had fallen down the stairs and that was why she was limping.
72752: When I was going to Zevenbergen, I suddenly saw a black animal running across the field and suddenly heard a splash in the ditch. I thought I had seen a wonder.
72754: When the farmer went along the road with his horse and cart, the horse always stopped in the Kakhoek. Every single time, because a woman suspected of witchcraft lived there.
72755: People from Capelle had warned my father not to accept anything from a woman who could do magic. But he had sold his cow and she wanted to give him an apple and a cup of coffee. He also had a little boy with him, but the woman said she would not harm the child.
72756: A woman who was born with a caul said that she always gets upset before something happens.
72762: A man from Capelle went with other farmers to the polder near Werkendam. One of those farmers could do witchcraft, and he was in the Oude Straat at night with horse and cart when suddenly two cats jumped out in front.
72763: There was a witch who went haunting in the churchyard wearing a white shirt.
72768: At the market in Zeeuws Vlaanderen a little man sat in the grass mending his trousers. He could not get the patch onto the hole, and the farmhand made a remark about it. But then he was sitting soaking wet on his cart. That must have been a water devil.
72769: My father sometimes saw a dead son of the farmer sitting on the gate, and he also sometimes went into the barn. The parish priest said they should follow him.

127613: When the magpies called, it meant news.
127614: If an owl called near the house in the evening, there would be a death in the family.
127622: Two people were working together. One lay down to sleep. He was dead, he lay cold. But the horses next to him snorted. That was a kind of nightmare, a kind of devil. If you put a handkerchief over the man's mouth, he could not come back to life. Then his spirit could no longer return to his body.
127627: There used to be little streets there where werewolves roamed. A kind of black dog with very big eyes, fiery eyes. There were people who could change into something like that.
127631: You were warned not to walk in the cart track or on the bridle path at night. Because there you could meet evil spirits.
127632: If the magpies fight, something is going to happen.
127635: A boy sees a cat sitting on a gatepost and pins the cat to the post with his knife. In the morning a woman lies dead in bed, pierced by a knife.
127659: There were people who never went to church. On Sundays a group of four played cards, cursing and raging. Until one time a horse's hoof appeared on the wall and knocked a hole in it. They could not close the hole, because it remained invisible. After that they could no longer go there to play cards.
127662: There was a dealer to whom the farmers went in the evening to say they had cows for sale. When they came to that man, he would say: "Sit down." Then the chairs came dancing towards him.
127673: At a baker's, the whole family was bewitched. The children crawled over a narrow plank. Priests advised him to lay birch wood crosswise on the fire. Then someone would come in. Whoever came in would be the witch. The witch came in and grew very restless. At last she cried out in despair: "Jan, where must I get out?" Jan said: "Go out where you came in." Because Jan spoke, she was free. Otherwise she would have jumped onto the fire and burned.
127682: In Hulst there was such a ghost, called Ossaart. People imagined it as a very large head, a kind of ball with arms and legs. The creature lived in the reeds of the outer moat of the ramparts of Hulst. People who walked along that rampart were seized by Ossaart. He came rolling up the rampart, grabbed people and threw them into the outer moat.
127683: The Bonte Hond (Spotted Dog) was a large spotted dog with fiery eyes. It walked silently beside certain people, neither malicious nor friendly. It kept walking beside them for a while. These people died within a few days.
127685: Someone was walking past the churchyard late in the evening when he saw a white rabbit running over the graves. He caught the rabbit, put it in his apron and tied it shut. He went home and opened it, and inside were human bones.
127692: There was a knacker who bought shrubs and bushes from us. Van W. says: "Van den Berg, that fellow will never get away on that motorbike." And the knacker wants to ride off, but the motorbike won't work. Then Van W. grabbed the motorbike and rode off on it, and he stayed away with it for two days too.
127699: In the evenings a white lady holding a candle always floated in an alley. Several people saw her. When they saw it, they turned back.
127708: At full moon all the cats came together from twelve to one for a drink for the cats' dance. Someone did not believe it at first, but went to look. With a piece of wood he then chased away the red tomcat that was leading the dance.
127714: If the farmers did not give an old woman any grain, she got it anyway the next day when a wagon of grain overturned close by her.
127715: It was said of a man in the village that he could make people stand stiff.
127716: The werewolf was a kind of bogeyman; you had to watch out for it.
127720: If a hunter could not hit a hare, he had to put silver dimes in the cartridge.
127722: In the old days people sometimes saw a wagon with two horses driving through the air. This was also said during thunderstorms.
127734: Saartje van Rijswijk is suspected of being able to work magic.
127746: The top of the load of a cart of peat falls off. A woman suspected of witchcraft fills her apron with peat.
127758: Although there is no wind, the baker's boy's hat blows off and the rusks and rolls fall from his cart off the dike, where a witch grabs them up.
127759: A woman could make horses and carts drive off the dike.
127778: If you were given a sweet in the shop of the woman who could work magic, you were not allowed to eat it.
127779: She could also make the cart drive into the ditch. If she did not go inside, the hay wagon went into the ditch.
127782: If you walked along a dark road in the evening and saw a cat, you had to remember never to kick a cat. Otherwise you would have an accident.
127795: You had to watch out for people who could make others stand stiff. The person had to touch you, otherwise nothing happened. If he touched you, he made you stand stiff until he gave the command that you could go on again.
127796: People have seen the iron foal.
127797: A poor woman visits a rich farmer but is refused help. She bewitches the farm and the farmer's horses. The priest does not believe the stingy farmer.
127798: If you heard an owl call in the evening, an accident would soon happen.
127802: There used to be a man with a magic wand. If he touched you with it, you stood stiff. You had to be careful with that. He could make it so that you couldn't open your hand again, or your eyes stayed open, and if your mouth was open it stayed that way too.
127803: People went out to have a pee and then they came back in and had seen a whole procession of fiery horses go over the dike. That always happened from December to mid-January.
127806: If an owl came and sat on the house three times, that was dangerous. It meant there would soon be a death in the house.
127807: Witches can bewitch people, so you had to avoid them.
127811: They came up in an old ditch. In the distance you saw them burning. That was a faded devil.
127813: The werewolf was an old man; in the evening and at night he went out, as if he had a white sheet around him. With those fiery eyes. Everywhere at the neighbours' he threw open the door latches and made a racket. The girls hardly dared go outside anymore.
127814: The iron foal lived in the water. It was a kind of dragon in the shape of a horse.
127815: In Poederoijen lived an old woman who was considered a witch. Once a man drove his carriage off the top of the dike, by the wiel (a pool left by a dike breach). That was the witch's doing. But nothing was wrong with him. The man simply drove on along the bottom until he reached the steps.
127817: Werewolves wore a shaggy hide. At midnight they put on a hide and then walked on four legs. They did people no harm; they just trudged along with them.
127819: Here in Brakel, when the wind was from the north, the bell could drone, such a heavy sound. Then people said: Before it is Sunday, there will be a death.
127820: You could see a white lady floating near the Kleine Weeltje.
127822: A woman could turn a farmer into a dog with a human head.
127830: A stork on the roof: good luck.
127831: An owl screeching at night: a death in the neighbourhood.
127905: If the night owl screeched right above someone's house, someone in that house would die very soon.
127913: That was in Rhenoy; the man was so convinced of it that he was being followed. That was the werewolf.
127920: One of those old women had to bless someone. The pillow was cut open. You were not allowed to accept anything from that old woman.
128004: A woman with special powers made sure, when she quarrelled with the neighbours, that the threshing machine would no longer run. You must never accept anything she gave away, or you could fall ill. But if you put a little cross under the doormat, nothing could happen to you, as the evil influence was held back.
128005: There was a woman they had quarrelled with, and she came into the house in the shape of a toad. The toad was thrown into the stove, and then the woman's evil influence was gone.
128006: In the evenings a lady walked up and down to draw people's attention to the fact that a farmer had moved a fence post. That way the farmer had gained a piece of land that was not his.
128008: They were children who had died without being baptised. They came back in the form of little lights. The people who saw them were upset by it.
128039: If you walked through the barn in the dark and the cats climbed up into the beams, then there was an evil spirit in the barn, you could count on that. Then they always went to check on the cows and the horses one extra time.
128046: If the rooster crowed while a dead person was laid out, there would be another death within three days.
128047: If the magpies screech in the tree: another death within three days.
128050: A maid in a café in Macharen was a witch. The priest, however, said that witches do not exist.
128051: If you drove past a little café without going in, you got into trouble.
128075: In the old days there were people of whom it was said that they could turn into werewolves, change into a black dog.
128077: In the old days there were old women who believed they could work magic. If someone was bewitched, little roses grew in his pillow.
128080: Well, in Lithooien there is the Spookwieleken (ghost wheel). When people went over the dike, that happened there.
128081: Here you must never walk along the cart track or the bridle path at night between twelve and one. If you did, you were attacked by a black dog.
128086: The legend of Doctor Faust and his pact with the devil is told.
128088: There was someone here whom they called the werewolf.
128105: If something went wrong with the churn: "That's not right, that's witchcraft!"
128107: Haunting cats, that was always the case; it came through that witch, who worked with a cat.
128117: When the wagon got stuck on the sandy track, the Black Cat was fetched. She then made a little cross and the wagon could move on.
128118: In Chaam the witches could dance hand in hand around the church. There were too many of them to all fit around the tower.
128119: In Chaam the witches could dance hand in hand around the church. There were too many of them to all fit around the tower.
128342: The farmer's daughter milks the cows in the meadow. She sees a white figure. The next evening the farmhand goes with her. Again the figure appears. On the third day the mother goes with her. On the priest's advice, the daughter asks on the fourth day what the spirit wants: "I cannot obtain eternal life because I did not keep my promise to go to Kevelaer." Mother and daughter go on pilgrimage. They and the priest see the figure, the others do not. In Kevelaer the bells began to ring by themselves. A mass was said and the spirit disappeared.
128347: In 1672 a French army crosses the southern borders. Two French soldiers desert the army and settle in Knegsel, where they live by robbery and theft. A weaver from Steensel is attacked and murdered on Christmas Eve by one of the French soldiers. The murderer is hanged, but as a gloeiige (glowing ghost) he returns every evening to the scene of the murder to wander about.
128730: A baker in Kessel was working through the night in his bakery. A black cat came by and the baker invited her in. The baker did not notice that six other black cats then came in one by one. When he did see it, he threw a bucket of boiling hot water over the cats. In the morning the baker found his wife in bed with burns. Apparently she had organised a witches' gathering in the bakery that night.
128733: Every time a suitor went to visit his girl in the evening, a werewolf jumped on his back.
128736: Doeressen Driekske, the narrator's former neighbour, slept in his youth with his brother Pierke in a box bed. In their fear of the dark night they pulled the doors of the box bed shut behind them. Sometimes they could not fall asleep, and it was as if a dark threat hung over them. They both felt as if a heavy creature jumped onto their bodies, pressing on their chest and throat so hard that they could hardly breathe. When their parents came to comfort them, the pressure eased again.
128743: There was once a soldier who was very frivolous and could never make ends meet on his pay. Once he had so much debt that one dark night he sold his soul to the devil, and from then on he never lacked money. When one of his comrades asked where he got so much money, the frivolous soldier replied that the comrade himself would soon be able to get that much money too. One night, when the frivolous soldier and the comrade were on guard, hundreds of coins suddenly rolled across the ground. The comrade bent down to pick up the money; there was a thunderclap and tremendous screaming, and then both the coins and the frivolous soldier had vanished. The pact with the devil had ended.
128744: There was a farmer in Acht who was building a mill. He ran short of money, however, and so could not finish the mill. At his wits' end, he called on the devil for help. The devil declared himself willing to finish the whole mill in one night, before the first cockcrow, on condition that he would get the farmer's soul. The farmer agreed. The devil built all night long. He was missing only one millstone. He went to fetch it on a hill. When the devil bent down to pick up the stone, a cock suddenly crowed. The devil had lost his game. In fury he hurled the millstone off the hill. The farmer laughed, and from that day on, in honour of the devil, he called his property the 'Duivelsmolen' (Devil's Mill).
128745: A strange and generous guest once came into an inn in Mol, a small town in the Belgian Kempen. He paid for everything in hard cash. The stranger stayed at the inn for three days. Then he told the innkeeper to wake him early the next morning and have a horse and cart ready for him, because he had to leave for an urgent reason. The innkeeper, who did not want to lose his strange guest with his well-filled purse, deliberately did not do so. That afternoon a strange rider dressed in a grass-green uniform rode in through the door of the inn on a large dog. When the clock struck three, the rider laid his hand on the strange guest's shoulder and said he had to come with him at once. Trembling with fear, the guest stood up, mounted the hairy dog and sat behind the green-clad rider. The dog flew through the air with both men on its back and then disappeared into a crack in the earth in a large meadow. The guests at the inn crossed themselves in fright, for now they knew that the rider in green was the devil. He had of course come to fetch the stranger because the man had sold his soul to him and his time on earth was up at exactly three o'clock.
128747:
In Best there once lived a witch who kept a little café. Farmers and tradesmen passing by had to stop, because on reaching the café it was impossible to get the horses to move on. Only after having a drink, and paying for it of course, could they calmly continue on their way.

In Oerle too, on the Halve Miel, lived a witch who kept a little café. She ran it with her daughter, who was also a witch. If passing farmers and carters did not buy a drink, they got lost and had to go back to the café. If they then bought a drink after all, they did not get lost a second time. Mother and daughter saw to that.

In Hoogeloon you could only pass with horse and wagon if five cents were paid.

In Veldhoven many peat cutters with their loads of peat passed the cottage of a witch. Their horse always stood stock-still until the witch had taken a few peats off the wagon. That way the witch had free fuel all winter.
128754: In the old days you should never be so careless as to follow a hengstenspoor (stallion track), because then you might suddenly be flung aside by a white horse. A member of the guild of St. Jan in Oerle once rode through such a hengstenspoor on his way home. Something invisible thumped against his body.
128756:
To be able to fly, a bokkenrijder (goat rider) had to sit on a goat and say:

'Over house, over dune, over stake,
and then to Cologne into the wine cellar'

Once a year the bokkenrijders (goat riders; most came from Limburg) gathered on the Mookerhei in Limburg, and the chief of the bokkenrijders (the devil) was there in person. At these gatherings you could become a bokkenrijder by renouncing God and his saints.

In Erp there is said to have been a farmer who was carried high through the air by the bokkenrijders as far as Boxtel, and on the way he is said to have stubbed his big toe on a church tower. In Halsteren exactly the same is said to have happened to a farmer.

And in the Biezenkuilen in Zeelst there is said to have lived a farmer who was once suddenly picked up by a bokkenrijder, carried through the air, and only came down hours and hours later on the Oirschotse Heide.
128762: Four farmers from Oerle wanted to sell their souls to the devil. They went to a so-called witches' circle between Oerle and Zandoerle. When the clock struck twelve at night, three of them stood in the witches' circle and called up the devil. The devil came, but was so terrifying that the three farmers changed their minds and wanted to flee. However, they could not leave the witches' circle. The fourth farmer fetched a priest. The priest got the devil to agree to the following condition: the devil would be satisfied with the last man left standing in the witches' circle. Now one of the farmers had secretly dropped a steel crucifix, which he always carried with him, onto the ground in the middle of the circle. The priest now called the farmers out of the circle one by one. When the third farmer jumped out, the devil leapt at him, for that third farmer was of course his. But then he suddenly saw that the last one in the circle was not the third man but the crucifix. Howling, the devil left the witches' circle, and it is easy to understand that the men were cured of their greed for good.
128764: One evening in Exel a farmer sat drinking with his farmhand. Made reckless by the alcohol, they decided to go after midnight to the small castle opposite the inn, which everyone said was haunted. The farmer and his farmhand wanted to experience it for themselves. At twelve o'clock the men got up and set off for the castle. Hardly had they approached it when both let out a shrill cry, and at the same moment the echo of the cry came back from the ruin; at once all the windows were lit up and a merry company could be heard inside with games, music and dancing. A distinguished gentleman invited the farmer and his farmhand to come and drink a glass of wine. They accepted, and in his drunken recklessness the farmer even said: 'We won't pass up a good glass of wine, not even at the witching hour among twenty-five ghosts.' The friendly gentleman then gave them two magnificent golden goblets filled with exquisite wine. Then the church clock in the village struck six: morning had come. The farmer and his farmhand felt a heavy pressure in the air from a sudden strong wind that blew out all the lights of the castle and plunged the ruin and its surroundings into darkness. When they raised the golden goblets to their mouths, they were horrified to find each holding a skull instead of a goblet. Completely sobered by this adventure, the farmer and his farmhand threw the skulls away in disgust and ran back to the village as fast as they could.
128765: Two farmers once lived next to each other in Baarle-Neeth. One of them asked his neighbour to help him bring his hay to the hay barn. But the neighbour would have none of it. So the farmer had to do it himself, but fortunately his son helped him. Late in the afternoon, when the hay had been gathered, the weather turned bad. A strong wind rose and much of the hay flew through the air. The angry farmer took his scythe and threw it after the wind, shouting: 'If the devil wants that hay, he can take the scythe as well!', and the scythe too flew through the air. A few days later the neighbour fell ill. When the feud had lasted a year and the neighbour was still not better, the farmer began to feel sorry for him and went to visit him. 'Is there no doctor who can help you?' the farmer asked. 'No,' replied the sick neighbour. 'There is no doctor who can help me. But you can help me.' 'Me?' asked the farmer. 'How? Because I would gladly help you.' This show of goodwill was already enough, for at the very moment the question was asked, the scythe flew in through the window. At the same moment the neighbour got out of bed and from then on was completely cured.
129735: A woman dies abandoned. She keeps wandering her house as a ghost until the time her death would have come had she been properly cared for.
129736: People chatter during Christmas Mass. The devil writes the names of the chatterers on a cowhide, but through the prayer of a pious man he falls down and breaks his bones. Since then it has always been quiet in church during the service.
129742: Two men were walking together. One is attacked by a dog. He fled. The other did not see it.
129745: Between twelve and one at night someone saw a funeral that took place five days later.
129749: A clergyman saw his own funeral. Four men with a bier kept walking behind him all night. He later died on that same road.
129750: A woman foresaw the death of a child.
129751: When a man sat down on a doorstep, someone there died. He had been born with a caul, but someone else had stolen it. And so that man became a danger.
129752: Two people are sitting with a man on a cart, which suddenly stops for a funeral procession they do not see. Two days later a funeral procession passed that spot.
129753: Someone born with a caul: has second sight; is not wounded as a soldier; does not drown as a sailor; draws a lot exempting him from conscription; is good at learning. If the caul fell into someone else's hands, the person born with it had to clear away obstacles for the funeral processions he saw. This happened at night.
129754: A child was pulled aside because a funeral procession was going to pass. In another case, another child had to take off his cap.
129755: A woman troubled by the nightmare was advised by the parish priest to lay a cross and a dagger on her chest at night. The second night it moved to her belly and the third night to her feet. In the end it was gone.
129756: Two farmhands slept in one room. One of them was skin and bone, because every night a mare came to the window. He had to ride it all night. One night the fat one rode her and had her shod by the blacksmith. The farmer's wife had horseshoes on her hands and feet and was found to be a witch.
129792: There used to be a little bridge over the Gender where, especially on spring nights, the white women came to sing. They sang a funeral song at the graves of two lovers, a noble maiden and a knight, who were not allowed to love each other because of a feud between their fathers. The maiden's father locked her up in a convent. When the knight came to rescue her, the maiden's father murdered both lovers. They were buried on either side of the convent wall, but on the knight's grave a large weeping willow grew that reached over the wall to the maiden's grave. The knight's father soon took revenge and destroyed the castle and the convent of his enemy, the maiden's father. Only the graves of the two lovers were spared. Besides the white women, the former nuns, the maiden's father also regularly returned to the scene of the crime as a wandering knight.
129793:
Fleeing from farmers, a robber knight and his squire end up in the Dolle Moer and suffocate. The wandering ghost of the knight lures people into the Dolle Moer.
As foretold, the knight's corpse is found, in the form of, among other things, a gilded silver helmet.
129794: A farmhand discovers that the farmer's wife he works for is a witch. She often leaves the farm at night on a broomstick. One night the farmhand also takes a broom, speaks the right spell and follows the farmer's wife to a gathering where men and women eat, drink and dance. When the gathering is over and all the witches have left, the farmhand wants to fly back to the farm, but he does not know the spell for the return journey. He has to walk the long way back. He had put some food in his pockets, but it turns out to have changed into toads.
129796: A miller quarrels with his wife so often that one day he calls on the devil's help to get rid of her. In return for his help, the devil wants to be able to grind in the miller's mill every night. The miller agrees, but soon regrets it. The devil makes so much noise every night that the miller cannot sleep a wink. He discovers that the devil and his one-eyed accomplice grind sacks full of skulls in the mill every night. The devil also wants to grind the miller's skull. Together with his neighbour, the miller manages to drive off the devil and his accomplice. Whether the wife ever came back, nobody knows.
129811:
This story tells the history of the holy linden tree in Eersel. The tree grew from a branch stuck into the ground by the Frankish maiden Odora when, after years of living in solitude in the wilderness, she returned to her parents' home on the back of a white horse.
The linden tree was felled in 1903 after a swarm of bees had settled in it. When people tried to drive out the bees with fire, the inside of the tree also caught fire. A new, young linden tree was planted on the same spot.
At a certain point the linden tree got a bad name because it was said to be haunted. People saw witte wieven (white women) and witches there, among other things. A certain Jan Prinsen witnessed a cats' dance there.
129815:
Steensel is said to have once had two church bells. According to some, one of the bells was stolen by the French; according to others, it hangs in the basilica of Sint Jan in 's-Hertogenbosch. Still others say that the devil stole the (unbaptised) bell. But the devil had to drop the bell between Veldhoven and Zittard because it was too heavy, and so the Klokkuil or Duivelskolk was formed. On Christmas night at twelve o'clock the bell still rings there and the devil's mother makes a fire.
The bells of Steensel and Knegsel talk to each other.
129865: A student teacher on his way to the Rijksnormaalschool (state teacher-training college) in Eindhoven meets a fellow traveller, a farmer. On the way the fellow traveller insists on stopping at an inn they pass for a drink. When they travel on, the little farmer tells him that he once passed the inn without stopping. He had just passed the inn when a big dog came after him and stopped him. Then he heard a woman's voice call out a spell, he was lifted by an invisible hand and flew wildly through the air. According to the farmer, the woman who owned the inn was a witch.
129866: An old man with a divining rod says he knows where a treasure can be found. The narrator's father goes with the old man to the ruins of a castle to look for the treasure. The divining rod does indeed move, but while digging the two men are chased off by soldiers. The father later returns to search further. He digs down to the castle's foundations but finds not a penny.
129867: During a walk a man meets an old woman who turns out to be a witch. She says not a word and suddenly disappears. The next day the man finds his trousers covered in burnt-in little crosses. He goes back to the place of the meeting with his neighbour and they see a pair of priest's shoes under a hedge. The witch most likely put them there.
129869: A bewitched child does strange things, such as walking up the wall and along the ceiling. At first the priest does not want to come, because he does not believe in witchcraft and such things, but when he finally goes to have a look, the child does turn out to be bewitched. He blesses the child, and it becomes normal again and stays so for the rest of its life.
129871: On Christmas night a fiddler knocks at a farmhouse to ask for shelter. It turns out no one is home. When he sits down on a loom to tune his fiddle, the seat floats away. The fiddler thus ends up on the Heksenberg, where the witches force him to play for them. Finally he plays a Christmas carol, at which the witches flee.
129872: A man has heard that a skull turns into a lump of gold if you hold it in a tub of water on Christmas night. When he puts a skull he stole from the churchyard into the water, he is attacked by a great swarm of skulls. The man runs back to the churchyard to bury the skull again. As soon as he has done so, the skulls stop their pursuit. The next morning, however, his frozen body is found in the churchyard.
129875: A sexton discovers that his divining rod has been stolen by the witch Maaike Taaike. When he goes to her house and threatens to break her legs if he does not get his property back, Maaike Taaike predicts that his cornfield will not look fine much longer. The next night the sexton sees Maaike Taaike standing in his cornfield. The witch vanishes, but the sexton still manages to throw a stone at a black cat. Not long after there is a heavy hailstorm. The next morning the sexton's cornfield has been destroyed by the hail, and Maaike Taaike walks around with a bandage on her arm, at the spot where she was hit by the stone as a cat.
129879: A miller cannot keep a farmhand because they are chased away by enormous cats that come haunting at night. One day a man comes who says he is not afraid of the cats. At night he boils milk, and when the cats try to pounce on him, he throws it in their faces. The cats flee, screeching. The next morning the man sees three old women with bandages around their faces.
129949: A soldier called Jan spends the night in a haunted castle in Dalem at Hapert, near Eersel. In the castle he decides to bake pancakes. But with every pancake he bakes, a bone falls into his pan. He throws all the pancakes into a corner. From that corner a skeleton rises, which shows him three treasure chests in the cellar. He may keep the first chest himself, the second chest is for the poor, and the third chest is for the Church.
129952: Two witches, a mother and a daughter called Hanne and Mie, had a café by the road. People who came along that road had to drink a glass of gin there. If they did not, the witches made them lose their way.
129955: The carelessness of walking on a hengstenspoor (stallion track) is punished by a kick from a black horse or the blow of an invisible hand.
131915: Grandfather used to see will-o'-the-wisps and Witte Wieven (white women) in the evenings and at night.
132042: Ghosts come at night and are white.
132043: A man goes into a haunted ruin. He hears the rattling of chains.
132044: A ghost is trapped in an old house where a murder was committed. Someone goes inside and rescues the ghost.
132045: In the haunted house stones flew through the house and through the roof. Yet no hole could be seen.
132047: An old woman is known as Heksenmijntje (Witch Mientje). People think she is possessed by the devil.
132048: The butter will not churn because it is bewitched. By throwing a guilder into it, it does churn.
132049: A witch comes flying at night on a sieve and makes a horse ill.
132051: A farmer's dung cart creaks. Inspecting the wheels, the farmer finds a thirteenth spoke in the wheel.
132052: The lord of the borg (castle) Stenhoesheerd murders a priest because he refuses to say mass. Immediately after the murder the castle sinks into the depths.
132053: The (robber) knight of Hoensbroek is given a monkey as a present, which was part of the loot from one of his men's raids. This monkey turns out to be the devil.
