165839: A witch went with a neighbour to fetch fodder for her animals. When the neighbour reached the field, the witch already had a whole sack of fodder. When it rained heavily, that witch could make the ground under her feet bone dry.
165842: A sorceress could fly much faster than an aeroplane. A boy who was seeing a sorceress pretended to have fallen asleep in his girlfriend's house. Meanwhile, however, the boy saw the girl take a little pot of holy water from behind a painting and rub herself with it. Then she said: "I fly over hedge and heath, over the field and the hedgerows." When the girl had flown away, the boy copied what she had done and also flew to Rome. But the boy had made a mistake in saying the magic formula, so he flew not over the hedgerows but through them.
165852: In an inn on the Zieleberg in Lovenjoel there was often card playing, drinking and cursing. One evening a gentleman came in who wanted to join the card game. When one of the players bent down to pick up a dropped card, he saw that the gentleman had horse's legs. The people were afraid and went to fetch the priest, who had the greatest difficulty driving out the devil.
165900: A witch came to visit a farm, stroked one of the animals along its back and said: "What a fine beast!" The next day the cow lay dead in the stable.
165915: In a pigsty in a wood in Zemst-Laar, the pans were taken away every night, though there was nothing to be seen.
165925: If you could strike a werewolf in a certain spot, he changed into a human and you could unmask him.
165950: In a house where the light was always put out, the priest was sent for to put an end to the witchcraft. The clergyman claimed that witchcraft did not exist, but began to pray anyway. Three days later the light in the house was no longer put out.
165991: The father of F.C. from Moorsel had died. A long time later the maid saw the ghost of the dead man appear in a red waistcoat. The maid fell ill from fright.
166017: Near the Schoolbergen lived a widow with her daughter and three sons. One day, when the daughter was home alone, she heard a knocking at the door at three in the afternoon. "Who is it?" the daughter asked, and the voice of her dead father answered: "It's me, your father." Although the knocking grew louder and louder, the girl did not have the courage to open the door. Finally there was a loud blow, after which everything went quiet. The ghost's hand was burnt into the door. The girl's three brothers, who were at work at that moment, claimed they had felt a blow in their backs at three o'clock.
166018: In Kaggevinne lived a woman who was suspected of being a witch. Because that woman's husband was somewhat infirm and always wore leather boots, people said of the so-called witch: "Look, she did that to her husband too."
166079: A boy apprenticed to a tailor in Aarschot left very early in the morning and only came home late in the evening. Along the road the boy had to walk lived a woman who was said to be a witch. Because the boy was terrified of that witch, he sometimes had his brother, three years younger, fetch him in Aarschot. When the two boys were walking home one evening, the elder suddenly cried: "Look there, a ghost! If you are of the devil, go away. If you are of God, speak!" Because the apparition stayed where it was, the boy threw his iron at the ghost. The iron fell right through the ghost. The boys arrived home out of breath. The next day the boys found the iron again. The 'ghost' had been nothing more than mist in the moonlight. When people could not be cured by a doctor, they consulted a herb woman, who had a book full of recipes. In people's imagination, however, a recipe book soon became a book of magic and a healing hand a black hand. Women who lived alone and had a black cat were often suspected of witchcraft.
166082: In a house in Roodebeek there was much misfortune caused by the evil hand. The farmer's wife went to the priest, who said: "If you see an animal come in, pour boiling water over it. I will pray that it succeeds." One evening the woman saw a toad come in through the water drain. The woman poured boiling water over it. A few days later she met her own daughter, who had a burnt face. The woman was frightened to death when she realised that she had been bewitched by her own daughter.
166109: A man who went off the road with two carts believed he had been bewitched.
166112: A man once saw a black toad that he could not kill. That toad was a witch.
166117: In Kumtich lived a man known as a werewolf. One day the man threw a handful of earth into the air. When the earth fell back to the ground, it had turned into mice. The priest had the man come to the church and baptised him again. After that the man could no longer make mice. A word had been forgotten at his baptism.
166118: A man and a woman who had been married for a year moved house because the woman was expecting a child. When the midwife was washing the newborn child, there was a knock from a neighbour who had come to bring gingerbread for the young mother. Because the mother was afraid of being bewitched, she had the gingerbread thrown into the fire. The next day the father and mother heard that the neighbour had been telling everyone that they had such an ugly child. After that incident the neighbour was no longer let in. This made the neighbour very angry and in the end she stopped coming by. But the child did not grow any fatter and died at the age of seven months. The father and mother were convinced that the neighbour had bewitched their first child.
166132: A man walking home alone stopped to urinate against a tree stump on a church path. Suddenly the man heard a cat meow. A moment later the cat had vanished. That cat was probably a witch.
166160: A woman who was cutting clover saw two frogs sitting there. A moment later an old woman stood behind her and said: "You must not harm those frogs, for they are such sweet little creatures." The woman's child began to cry. The next moment all the frogs had vanished.
166162: If thirteen people sat at table together, it was believed that someone from that company would die within the year.
166168: A man who had drunk too much, and as a result began to sweat and had trouble getting to work, often said he had been bewitched by a woman from the village. Most of that witch's children had died. When her son had come to live with her with his wife, the daughter-in-law died young. The son then remarried and had three children from that second marriage. Those children, however, also all died young.
166178: A man who was a soldier in the British army had gone mad because of the evil hand. The man had been told that a woman would come by in the morning and would say something. That woman would be the witch. The next morning the man was spoken to at the well by a woman from the neighbourhood.
166199: A boy went to the field with his father. When the boy picked up a clod of earth there and threw it into the air, mice ran everywhere. The father had his son prayed over by the priest, after which the boy could no longer make mice.
166216: A sorcerer could fly on a wheelbarrow wheel or on a horse's jawbone after saying: "Over hedge and over hedgerow, from here to Kuringen into the priest's wine cellar." In that wine cellar the sorcerer helped himself to the wine. A man who had spied on the sorcerer and also wanted to fly to the wine cellar for once said: "Through hedge and through hedgerow to Kuringen into the priest's wine cellar." That man arrived at his destination badly injured. Moreover, the man had given himself away through his injuries.
166241: A man was in the habit of going hunting in the Hellegat with two friends on Sundays. Suddenly the men saw a hare that seemed to clap its hands and cried: "Mass missed, Mass missed, Mass missed!" For the hunters had not been to church.
166243: A witch lived in Tienen. At night there were always black cats in a brewer's workshop, and they let all the barrels run empty. One evening the brewer kept watch with a bowl of hot porridge. He threw a spoonful of hot porridge at the backside of every cat. The next day there was a woman from the neighbourhood who could no longer sit because her backside hurt so much.
166280: A man from Meerbeek had a sick cow. Because the man knew who had caused this misfortune, he went one evening to someone who could overlezen (read prayers over) the animal. On the way the man was approached by the witch, who stood in front of him with a revolver and said: "If you dare tell, I'll shoot you."
166322: When a child stopped growing, people believed the child had been bewitched by a woman from the neighbourhood who dealt with evil.
166354: A spiritist claimed that after his death he would come back in the shape of a blue cow. When the man had died, however, he was never seen again.
166374: On a farm in the Koninklijke Kasteeldreef all the cows died through the evil hand. A black cat was always seen walking near the farm. One day the black cat was shot dead. The next day a woman from the neighbourhood lay dead in her bed.
166383: Vuurmaden (fire maggots) were little worms. Some people claimed that seeing vuurmaden brought bad luck. According to others, the little lights brought good luck instead.
166465: A pigeon fancier would go back home if he had met a witch. He knew then that he would not win a prize with his pigeons anyway.
166475:
In Tielt there used to live so many witches that they could form a circle around the church hand in hand. They were children who had not been baptised properly.
A girl could make mice come out of the parish priest's pocket, and she could also flatten a field of grain by magic. One day the girl had to bring coffee to her father, who was mowing the field. When she arrived, the girl said: "Isn't the work done yet? Come, I'll finish it." Although half a zil (1) still had to be mown, the girl did the job in a few seconds. After the girl was baptised again by the priest, she lost her magic power.
166483: A mother with a two-week-old daughter was visited by someone from Galmaarden who wanted to buy the child. Before the mother had seen the woman come in, the woman was already standing with the child in her arms. The mother explained that the child was not for sale and sent the woman away. After that the child was bewitched. It lay completely stiff in its cradle. After a friar had overlezen (read prayers over) the child, it was cured. The mother also had to do a novena.
166497: A woman had as many as a hundred and fifty needles in her heart. Her husband sought advice from an old man, who said: "At midnight you must take your gun." That night at twelve o'clock there was a knock at the door. The man opened it and saw a neighbour woman standing there, who said: "How is your wife?" The man fired a shot. At that the woman turned into a hare, which then ran away.
166508: A mother had a baby that always started crying at midnight. The baby died. Some time later the woman gave birth to a second child. In the first weeks the baby behaved normally, but at a certain point it also began crying at midnight. Her neighbours advised the mother to take a piece of the child's clothing to a nurse on the Kapelleveld. The nurse prayed over the child's little shirt and had the mother return two days later. The next two nights the child cried much less. The nurse said to the mother: "The day before yesterday around midnight I passed your house. On the doorstep sat a woman sticking pins into the mat. With every pinprick your baby feels pain. I grabbed the woman and asked what she was doing, but she said nothing and ran off. But it is already too late for your baby." Shortly afterwards the second child did indeed die too. The nurse gave the mother a prayer with a picture of the Blessed Sacrament, which she had to put under her threshold. After that the woman had five more perfectly healthy children.
166512: In Roosbeek lived a rich man who was bewitched. Sometimes it happened that the man suddenly could not go any further.
166513: In Jette lived a sorceress who could turn herself into a hare. This sorceress was always out at night. A man who saw a hare sitting on the road looked the animal straight in the eyes and shot at it. The animal was hit, but was not dead. The next day the sorceress lay in her bed. She said she was ill.
166517: A child went to the fair with his father. At a wheat field the child said: "Father, shall I make some white mice?" and suited the action to the word. The father had the priest read prayers over the child. After that the child could no longer make mice. Perhaps that child had not been baptised properly.
166520: In a house a pot of porridge had been put on the floor to cool. At a certain moment a cat came in through the water drain. The people struck the cat with the ladle, whereupon the animal ran off yowling. The next day a woman walked around the village with half her face burnt.
166537: In Orsmaal-Gussenhoven lived a little boy who could make mice by throwing little balls of earth on the ground. After the boy had been baptised again, he could no longer work magic.
166540: When the children came back from catechism class, they had to pass the house of a witch who wore a red headscarf. The witch was always ready with apples, but the children were not allowed to accept the fruit. Otherwise they would have been bewitched, because apples were one of the means used by maren (witches).
166567: A gentleman with a top hat and fine clothes came into the home of people in Tienen who were struggling to pay their debts. The gentleman had eyes like a Chinese man, big hands and exceptionally long fingers. He offered the people money. When the man was about to accept the money, he had to sign a contract in his blood. At that moment the wife looked into the gentleman's eyes and became very frightened. After the wife made the sign of the cross, the gentleman flew out of the house with all his money. That had undoubtedly been the devil.
166573: Anyone who had pointed at a stallicht (will-o'-the-wisp) had to make sure he got indoors quickly, before the light came and struck the door three times. It was said that stallichten were the evil spirits of the dead. The lights mostly settled on the heads and harnesses of horses.
166594: In an orchard in Melkwezer, during a thunderstorm, one could see a circle in which the witches danced. The farmhands would then get up to watch the witches. Drumming could also be heard.
166599: In Meerbeek a woman had put the evil hand on the animals. Every time that woman had been at the farm, something went wrong.
166602: A café owner who did good business was visited by a gentleman who said: "Landlord, have you got anything for my dog? He has a stomach ache." The café owner gave the man something, after which the animal was cured. A little later, however, the gentleman came back to the café to say that he now had a stomach ache himself. The café owner said: "I can take away your stomach ache, but then I'll have to give the pain back to the dog." After the gentleman had sat in the café a while longer, he said: "I'm going home", to which the café owner added: "God willing." The gentleman replied: "God willing or not, I'm going home." In the morning the gentleman's children came to the café to see where their father was. The café owner said: "He was here yesterday and then left for home. He's probably still on his way. I'll send him home. He'll arrive there at six o'clock." The man had to jump over ditches and crawl under wires. At exactly six o'clock he arrived home.
166611: A family in Houwaart had a little child that cried every night from two o'clock until half past six in the morning. The child was probably bewitched.
166616: If you could make a werewolf bleed, you could unmask him.
166628: Three brothers lived in Opwijk. One of the brothers was ridden by the mare every night. The mare was a woman who crawled on top of the man, so that he could no longer move. The man no longer dared to sleep in his bed.
166637: Two girls had gone to buy a torch. In the shop the torch worked. On their way home the girls met a witch, who said: "Take my milk jug along for me!" The girls were too shy to refuse and took the milk jug. A little further on the girls found that their torch no longer worked.
166662: A farmer who had an exceptionally good harvest made a pact with the devil, who would build him a new barn. The devil had to finish the barn before the first cockcrow the next morning. In exchange for the barn the farmer had to give up his faith. Because the rooster crowed half an hour too early the next morning, the devils had not finished the barn. That barn could never be completed. Because the farmer sweated heavily every night, he sought advice from various people, who advised him to go on a pilgrimage. After the farmer had returned to his faith, he had no more problems.
166677: Some people claim that the mare that came to ride people was nothing more than poor circulation or digestive problems.
166705: People who were ridden by the mare lay moaning in their beds at night, stiff as a board.
166721: Every week a woman came to buy six eggs from a man who sold eggs. The woman always paid too much, for example twenty or fifty francs, while the eggs cost only three francs. The man always had to give change. Strangely, the money he had received from the woman disappeared from his pocket. In the end the man refused to sell that woman anything more. Money that a witch had held in her hands went everywhere with her.
166724: At midnight a man from Oppem saw the cradle in which his child lay dancing. It was his mother-in-law who caused this evil.
166755: In Humbeek lived a woman whom all the children feared. One day the woman was visiting a farm while carrots were being cooked there. The woman said: "Oh, I would love a little carrot like that." So the farmer's wife let the woman eat a carrot. After that the farm had much misfortune. Now a cow died, then a calf. The farmer and his wife finally went to the friars of Dendermonde.
166777: After the fair a boy had taken his girlfriend home. When the boy then had to go home himself, it was raining hard. The girl said to him: "That doesn't matter. There's a horse in the stable here. Take it and you'll be home at once. If the horse doesn't go fast enough, you must say: 'Through hedge, through bush.'" The boy did as he was told and was indeed home in no time. The girl had turned herself into a horse.
166780: A girl went to the fair with her boyfriend. While the girl was sitting in the inn, the boy said: "I'm going for a pee. If you meet anything, throw my handkerchief at the apparition." When the girl saw her boyfriend again in the inn a little later, she noticed that he had the fibres of the handkerchief between his teeth.
166796: At a blacksmith's in Wilderen the food always spoiled unusually fast, so people believed it was bewitched. After the witch died, the blacksmith had no more problems.
166797: When people had misfortune, they often believed they were bewitched.
166805: A witch from Beigem could make people have accidents. That witch's grandmother could also do strange things. Sometimes at night she stood by someone's bed without the people having seen her come in.
166825: A woman from Ruisbroek had a little son who was ill and would not get better. A neighbour came to drink coffee with this woman every week. Someone who believed the child had been struck by the evil hand told the mother: "When that woman comes again, put a wedding ring under her chair. If she can't get up any more, you can be sure it is she who bewitched your child." When the mother followed the advice, the visitor indeed could not get up. A short time later the child died.
166847: An old witch often visited people who had a farm with two horses, three cows and some pigs. Every time the witch had been there, one of the animals fell ill and died. The farmer's wife went to the parish priest, who came to overlezen (read prayers over) and bless the whole house. Then the clergyman said: "You must keep that old woman out of here, because she is the one causing the misfortune. She is a sorceress."
166853: A man went to his field to mow the grain. He mowed a stretch and then said: "I mine and you yours!" The next moment the whole field was mown.
166855: When people saw a black cat, they threw stones at the animal. After all, they believed black cats brought bad luck.
166868: A woman who had vowed to go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel died before she had fulfilled her promise. Every night the widower J. had a vision in which his wife appeared wailing and lamenting. The neighbours advised the man to make the pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel his wife had promised himself. When he left, the man had to put a broom by the gate. When he came back, the broom was gone. Since then the man never had the vision again.
166870: Sometimes a horse began to sweat at night through the evil hand.
166876: A farmer's wife had been given a packet of mints by a woman from the neighbourhood. On her way home the woman vomited the whole time. When she got home she had the parish priest overlezen (read prayers over) her, and he sweated heavily while doing so. The woman was bewitched.
166877: On his way home a man saw a packet of tobacco lying there. When the man tried to pick up the tobacco, a strange force threw him into the woods. A witch had done this.
166878: While people on a farm were working in the rapeseed field, one of the farmer's sons was given candy sugar sweets by a sorceress. Afterwards the boy fell ill and had to go home. On the way he fainted. The doctor visited the boy twenty-seven times, but he did not recover. Someone took the boy in a carriage to the monastery of Hekelgem. On the way there the boy sweated terribly and on the way back he was cold. The friar had said: "The mother must sprinkle hayseed in a tub of water and put the child in it. The next day she must put the child in bed with a damp bandage wrapped around his body." The mother did not do that, but she did keep a nine-day penance, because the friars had advised her to do so as well. Nine days later the child was cured.
166895: A man from Peizegem had shot at a hare at night. Although he had hit the hare, he found the animal had vanished when he went to pick it up. A little later the man hit the hare again. This time too he could not find the dead animal. A little later the man saw an old woman walking with a bundle of wood on her back. The man was terrified and hurried home. For that old woman was a witch.
166913: On the Oemsberg stood a castle where the ghosts of the dead returned.
166918: In front of a woman's house a girl found a little bag with two sweets. The girl put the sweets in her mouth. After that the girl had to dance for a long time.
166941: In Laar lived a woman whom people feared. That is why that woman was never allowed into the stables of a farm. One day there was a party at a farm, so people had forgotten that the woman would come to fetch her milk. Quite unexpectedly the woman stood in the room, and the people jumped up in fright. The woman said: "Ha, there's a party here. Never mind. Stay seated, I'll fetch my milk myself. I know where it is." When the woman then also said "enjoy your meal", the twenty-five forks of the people fell to the floor.
166957: A man who wanted to sell his soul to the devil had been advised to lie stretched out on the ground at midnight by a small chapel at a crossroads. When the man lay there and heard the church bells strike twelve, he changed his mind and stood up. The man felt something jump on his back and was beaten by a figure with a horse's foot.
166967: People who had a lot of bad luck said that a black cat came into their house. That was a woman who had put the evil hand on them.
166969: A man went to fetch fifty kilos of lime from a woman who had had nine children but had already let eight of them die. The woman pointed at a cat and said: "Look, that cat there, that is our misfortune." The man advised the woman to burn the cat, but she did not dare. Whenever someone kicked at the cat, it always went to the fire or to the children's room.
166972: A woman from Kessel was ridden by the mare at night. In the morning the woman was dead tired. In the moonlight the woman could see the mare come in. It was a neighbour who appeared in her nightgown.
166978:
A farmer from Bierbeek did not have enough room to store his harvest. He met a man, who said: "If you sell your soul, you will have a barn tomorrow before the first cockcrow." The farmer agreed and had to stay indoors that evening from ten o'clock. When the farmer and his wife were in bed, a hellish noise could be heard. The farmer told his wife what he had agreed to. Towards morning the farmer's wife went to the stable, where she clapped her hands and imitated the crowing of a rooster. At that the rooster woke up and began to crow too. Only when the farmer's wife had made the rooster crow three times, and only a hole in the barn still had to be closed, did the devils run away.
The ridge of the barn was completely bent. A priest tried to lay roof tiles over the hole in the roof, but the tiles always flew off. Only by laying a cross of red tiles could the hole be closed.
166979: A farmer who had seen a toad sitting there had bad luck with his harvest. One day the farmer threw a stone at the toad. When he did so, he heard a scream, for he had hit the witch.
166991: At the fair in Galmaarden, Fiel P. had said that after his death he would come back in the shape of a horsefly. During the next fair, Fiel's widow saw a horsefly flying in her house. Convinced that the horsefly was her late husband, the woman said: "Oh Fiel, there you are. How is it over there?"
167002: In Bos lived a woman who could make mice by throwing earth. A farmer who was harvesting had chased the woman away or scolded her. The woman then said: "You won't get off the field with your wagon." When the farmer was almost off the field, his wagon tipped over.
167006: One evening a vet was called by a woman whose cow was about to calve. The vet told his wife that he had to go to the Langdonken and left. The vet stayed away a very long time, so that his wife and children grew worried. After the calf was born, the vet was in a wood where he had lost his way. The whole night the man walked around in the wood, looking for a way out. When at six in the morning the vet heard the bells of the church of Wolfsdonk ring, he found his bearings again and found the way home.
167016: A sexton suspected a certain woman of being a witch and decided to put it to the test. After Mass the sexton left the missal open at the Gospel of Saint John. The woman stayed seated in the church and at a certain point began to cry and shout: "Let me out, let me out, let me out!" When the sexton closed the missal, the woman could leave.
167018: A boy was coming back through the woods from the fair in Averbode with his girlfriend. When the boy said on the way that he had to relieve himself, the girl said: "I'm too scared to stay behind here alone." The boy then said: "Here is a red handkerchief. If you meet a dog or something like that, throw the handkerchief at the beast." A little later, to her great fright, the girl saw a black dog coming with its jaws open. The girl threw the handkerchief at the animal's jaws. When her boyfriend appeared a little later, she saw that he had the fibres of the red handkerchief between his teeth.
167020: A woman came to a farm to ask for butter while the girls were still churning. The woman had probably touched the churn, because for the next two months no butter could be made on that farm. The farmer had a Passionist friar come, who overlas (read prayers over) everything and gave a medal to put under the churn. When the visitor came by again and the farmer's wife invited her in, she answered: "No, I have no time" and left. After that the farm always had good butter. The farmer warned everyone about the maar (witch) who had bewitched him.
167021: A man with special powers could turn himself into a dog in the evening and at night. In the evening that man often went to the café. When that happened, flames could be seen at the house opposite the café. The next day there was no trace of the fire.
167023: Two men were tormented at night by two cats that kept walking between them. The men prayed a lot and did not dare kick the animal.
167026:
A farm that a sorceress always visited began to have problems. When the animals were in the meadow, they suddenly fell to the ground. The vet was called, but he did not know what to do. Someone had seen a woman always walking among the animals in the stable, making signs of the cross the whole time.
Because the animals in the meadow could not get up any more, they had to be dragged home. People went to a friar of Dendermonde, who said: "You must take me there and bring me back before sunset, or else I will die." The friar came and went into the stables to overlezen (read prayers over) the animals until drops of sweat rolled down his face. When it was done, the friar said: "Drive me back as fast as you can, or else it will be over for me." The friar reached the monastery in time. He also advised the people to be careful from then on about whom they let into the animals' stables.
167029: In Dormaal stood a bewitched house. The farmer's wife fell ill and the livestock died. The son went to the brown friars of Sint-Truiden, who advised him to put a pot of consecrated oil by the door. Then no one could come in any more. The people were often visited by an old woman who came asking for alms or a slice of bread. When that woman came again, the farmer's son invited her in to eat with them. The woman answered that she had no time. But the man kept insisting and meanwhile removed the pot of oil. Then the woman did come in. When the son asked: "Are you to blame for all our misery?", the woman denied all guilt. But the son persisted and said: "If you don't confess everything, you'll burn!" Then the witch said: "Go to my house, take fifteen pins from the cushion under my bed and burn them." The man fetched the whole cushion and burned it in the oven. After that the witch was powerless. The farmer's wife soon recovered. That witch was never allowed near a baby's cradle.
167059: In the old days people told of those who had been ridden by the mare.
167063: People who were ridden by the mare dreamed and made noise in their sleep.
167073: In the old days, when people heard a strange noise, they believed a dead person had returned.
167091: People who were ridden by the mare had a bad dream that left them lying stiff as a board in their beds, unable to do anything.
167115: A woman was always visited by a neighbour who came to ask for water to bake bread. After the woman once gave the neighbour water to drink, she found that her bread always went bad.
167127:
A man was ridden by the mare every night. Once, when the man was wide awake, he saw the mare appear at the window. The man took his knife and said: "Filthy bitch, this time you won't get me!" The mare took the man by the arm and sat on his chest.
The man often went to sleep with his knife on his chest. In the end he was freed from the mare by a Crosier friar from Diest. The man went to confession and told the priest about his problem. The priest answered: "You shouldn't put any faith in that." The Crosier friar read prayers over the man and also gave him a scapular, which he had to wear at all times. After that the man was never ridden by the mare again.
167183: Toads were sometimes associated with wizards in the past.
167212: In the past people were very afraid of a rag woman from Tienen, because that woman could give people the black hand.
167224: A stalkaars (will-o'-the-wisp) was the soul of an unbaptised child.
167228: In Wemmel people were very afraid of the white madam. The children in particular were afraid of that apparition.
167239: A girl had got convulsions because of a witch.
167264: Near the church of Vorst will-o'-the-wisps flew back and forth. Such lights were mostly seen near churchyards. Will-o'-the-wisps were dead people who had to come back because they had promised to go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel but had not kept that promise.
167285: In Tremelo lived a witch who always tried to bewitch the children by giving them something. Sometimes she offered them a piece of wheat bread with a coin on it. Many schoolchildren who accepted such a thing were bewitched.
167291: A butcher who met a cat by the Steenweg to Ninove said to the animal: "Well, Blonde Minne, where are you off to now?" The cat answered: "Well, Jan the butcher, how do you know me?"
167321: On the road to Tienen lived a woman who wore a bonnet. One day the woman had taken the tram to Leuven. When she returned it was raining. The woman came into a house and asked the people whether she could leave her bonnet there so it would not get wet. The woman put the bonnet on the kitchen cupboard and went home. That night, as the people lay in bed, they heard the lid of the Leuven stove rattling. Because they were afraid, the next day they had an uncle come to spend the night in the house. When the lid began to rattle again, they put some paper in the stove. At some point the people realised that the woman who had left the bonnet with them was probably a witch. When the lid rattled for the third time, they put the bonnet in the fire. After that the lid did not rattle any more. The witch never came back to ask for her bonnet.
167338: A man walking home through the woods saw a black dog lying on the road and said twice: "Get out of the way." But the animal stayed where it was, so the man said: "Because you don't do what I say, you'll have to lie there a long time." The man fixed the dog in place by magic. When he got home he told his girlfriend what had happened. The girl had to beg him to let the dog go again.
167344: When a man had to bury a coffin, he was startled by a creaking sound that seemed to come from the coffin. The man sent for the parish priest, who said: "Don't worry, he's well and truly dead!"
167352: A woman who saw a toad sitting in the hallway said to the animal: "Filthy beast, how did you get in here?" and she gave the animal a kick. Shortly afterwards the woman heard that a little woman from the village was injured.
167425: A farmer's wife who found that the milk always went sour drove a cork into a bottle and said: "Now she'll come, the witch!" In the evening a woman came running up in tears, asking whether she could come in and whether they would release her. The cork had to be pulled from the bottle to release the witch.
167427: Some children who lay talking in their beds in the attic one evening heard the roof tiles rattling. That was the mare crawling in through the tiles. If you stayed lying on your back, the mare would seize you by the throat for five minutes.
167442: In the past some people believed that black cats were witches.
167458: A boy from Rummen had a relationship with a girl from the village. One day when the boy was taking his girlfriend home, he said on the way: "Go on ahead. I still have to tell a friend something. If you see a dog here, throw this handkerchief at its jaws, then it can't harm you." The girl stayed behind alone and a little later saw a big dog come running. The girl threw the handkerchief at the animal, as she had been advised. Some time later she saw her boyfriend again. He had the fibres of the handkerchief between his teeth.
167470: When people had misfortune in their house or in their stable, they believed they were bewitched.
167487: One morning a farm was struck by witchcraft. The children became so fat they could no longer get through the doorway. The animals crawled around on their knees and ate dung from the dung heap. The friars of Winge and the friars of Leuven could not help. A healer from Charleroi freed those people from the witchcraft.
167488: A vet who travelled on horseback could fix people to the ground by magic, so that they could not move a foot.
167503: People who were ill sometimes believed they had been ridden by the mare. Such people would then go on a pilgrimage or have the priest read prayers over them.
167534: A man out walking saw a woman standing outside who was suspected of being a sorceress. The man said to the woman: "I've already fallen twice on the way." The woman replied: "You'll fall plenty!" A little further on the man fell again. The husband of the woman standing there said: "He shouldn't have drunk so much!" But the man had not touched a drop.
167561: People who were ridden by the mare had fallen victim to others who wanted to torment them.
167571: One day a farm began to have problems with the calves. The animals ran up the walls in fear. When many calves and chickens had already died, the farmer went to look in the stable one night. There he saw two pheasants sitting, and he did not know where they had come from. A friar from Gent came to look and said: "Are there strangers in the house? That must not be. You must stand by the gate and watch who walks past. The guilty one will pass by." The friar sprinkled everything with holy water until he sweated terribly. The farmer had seen a woman walk past who always came to fetch butter and milk from him.
167581: On a Saturday, a farmhand from Booienhoven went to take his laundry home and fetch clean clothes. At a turnstile the man saw a big dog lying. Because the dog would not move, the man had to take another way. When the man went home, he took a dung hook with him. The dog was still lying in the same place. The man stabbed the animal in the snout, so that blood flowed. The next moment the dog had vanished and a man stood there, who said: "If you dare betray me, you're dead." The man promised not to betray the werewolf. Two Sundays later, however, he told the people in church: "Whoever says that X is a werewolf is lying, but watch out for that man!"
167605: A Flemish girl worked in Holland as a nanny. One evening the children's mother and father went out, so the girl had to stay home alone. The girl put an armchair against the door and had a little sleep there. Suddenly the girl felt a tap on her shoulders. When she looked, she saw a black apparition, which disappeared a moment later. The girl thought she was dreaming and went back to sleep. A little later, however, the same thing happened again. She heard the children crying. When she went to look, she saw that the medicine cabinet had fallen over and everything lay on the floor. A window was open in the children's room. The girl was very frightened. She sat in the children's room until the mother and father came home.
167606:
In Blauwput lived a farmer who was looking for bricklayers to build him a new barn. The farmer met a gentleman who claimed he could build the barn before the rooster crowed for the first time the next morning. In exchange for the job, however, the farmer had to give up his soul. The farmer agreed. When he lay restless in his bed that night, he told his wife what he had done. The farmer's wife got up immediately and began to clap her hands by the henhouse, so that the rooster crowed early. At that moment the barn was not yet finished.
Whenever the barn was torn down, it was standing again the next morning.
167642: A man in the woods shot at two hares that were playing. The man missed, whereupon the hares clapped their paws and said: "You surely want them all, but you can't hit us!"
167681: In Elingen lived an unkempt woman who was suspected of being a sorceress. Sometimes the woman walked around in her shift. When a cow there had calved, the calf was laid under the table in the house.
167696: A man went poaching in a wood in the moonlight. When the church clock of Boskant (Merchtem-Peizegem) struck midnight, however, he had not yet seen a single hare. A little later a gigantic hare came running, and the man quickly raised his gun and fired. The man, though a good hunter, had missed. A little later a second hare came running, and the man fired again. This time too he missed. When the church clock struck for the last time, a third hare came along, limping. The hare came up to the hunter and asked: "Did the others pass by long ago?" Terrified, the man went home.
167717: The Blauwe Schuur (Blue Barn) was built in a single night, but in the morning there was still a hole in the building that could never be closed afterwards. Every time the hole was bricked up, the brickwork fell out again the next day.
167718: Toads were witches, so people said.
167728: Some people who were about to move had gone to clean everything. They stayed there to sleep at night. In the middle of the night they heard the pump start pumping by itself. In the stable there was a noise as if plates were falling out of a cupboard. The people went to look, but there was nothing to be seen. The cows started lowing at night for no explicable reason. The dog must have seen something too, for the animal went wild.
167741: People who had been ridden by the mare were in reality suffering from a standstill of the blood. This could be caused, for example, by eating badly baked or burnt rye bread, or other food that was hard to digest.
167761: Some young people coming back together from the fair in Kauberg saw a priest approaching along a lane in the woods. The priest was reading in a book the whole time. When the young people said "Good day", the priest answered: "Let rest what is at rest. The night is for us, the day is for you." Terrified, the young people ran away. The priest had once been murdered for two and a half cents.
167781: In Baardegem lived a man from Denderbelle whose half-sister was ill. The man blamed the illness on witchcraft and went to stand by the sorceress's house with a dung fork. He lashed out with his dung fork but could not hit the sorceress.
167794: Near the churchyard people often saw will-o'-the-wisps. Although the lights were really little worms, people believed they were the souls of the dead.
167817:
In the past there were women who were said to be able to work magic. Then it happened that the cows on a farm always jumped into the manger at a certain time. When butter could not be made on a farm in Pepingen, the friars of Halle were called. After the friar had overlezen (read prayers over) the farm, he said: "The guilty one will come to borrow something from you, but you must not give anything." A while later a woman came to the farm to ask for a pen and ink. That was something she certainly did not need.
To break the power of a sorceress, one always had to strike higher.
167824: Rie V. was a poacher who was seldom at home. Two weeks after his youngest child had died, his wife came to see him. "Our child is dead," said Rie, to which the woman replied in disbelief: "No, that's not true at all!" "Yes it is," said the man, "last week the child came to haunt me. It was wearing a little shirt that was much too short."
167857: A woman who lived alone in a little house heard knocking on her door every evening, as if a dog were hitting it with its tail. There was also knocking behind the cupboard. The woman always asked: "Are you there again?"
167871: People lying in bed could sometimes be ridden by the mare. They then felt as if a millstone were lying on them and sweated terribly.
167877:
In Asse lived a woman everyone feared. One night that woman had been seen at midnight standing on her dung heap with her arms spread. It looked as if a herd of animals came running up and passed right through the woman. That was evil. When a hundred-kilo pig had been slaughtered, the meat was rotten after only eight days. A family who had a bakery and a shop was constantly struck by misfortune. They said many prayers, but it did not help. The cows and pigs died. In the end the wife went to the parish priest. That clergyman, however, did not believe in witchcraft. The wife went to the witheren (Norbertine canons), to whom she said: "I have always held to the good, but if this misfortune does not stop, I will have to seek counsel from evil." One evening, while the husband was kneading bread dough, there was a knock at the door. After long hesitation, they let the visitor in. The visitor asked for a glass of beer but did not drink it. Then he said: "Is this where so many misfortunes happen? I am here to help. All that is awake must stay awake. All that rests must stay at rest." The man took something from his wallet and went around the house with it, talking. The man's face twitched convulsively. Then the man went to sleep in the stable. No one was allowed to wake him before twelve noon. The next afternoon the man said: "You will lose one more of your children. The person doing this to you is standing at your door. If you want, I will make her come in." The husband wanted that, but the wife did not. Then the healer said: "I am powerless, for man and wife are one." Some time later a little daughter of those people died. The woman responsible for the evil never came into those people's shop again.
Because the people in the neighbourhood also had much misfortune, they came to that family to get the healer's address. He was a witheer (Norbertine canon) from Aalst, but he was never found again.
167881: In Kraainem lived a witch. Whenever that witch had visited a woman, that woman always had misfortune afterwards.
167891: When people had misfortune, they believed they had been ridden by the mare or touched by the evil hand.
167901: One evening a cattle dealer was coming back from the market with his friend. On a little road the two saw a big cat walking. When the cattle dealer wanted to stroke the cat, the animal grew larger and larger. The two men walked home as fast as they could. Whatever you meet at night, you must leave alone.
167903: A man coming back from Ternat was always followed by a white cat. When the man got home, he saw that the cat had disappeared.
167909: People who had fallen victim to a witch had the parish priest read prayers over them.
167938: People coming home from work in the evening saw a calf lying in the middle of the street near a castle in Booienhoven. When the people had passed, the calf had suddenly vanished. It was said to be a werewolf. Some time later the people came there again, and the calf was lying there once more. Werewolves were pranksters who disguised themselves to frighten passers-by. If you could make a werewolf bleed, you could unmask him.
167939: If thirteen people sat at table together, misfortune would follow, or so people believed.
167946: In Herfelingen lived a woman who was said to be a witch. That woman always went to visit a child who had convulsions. In the end the child died.
167956: At a factory in Zoutleeuw a good five hundred grey cats sat in the wood. A man coming back from the cinema one night saw a good twenty cats sitting there. The man threw a stone at the cats, after which the animals ran away. When the man came into his house and opened the window, a whole pack of cats was sitting there again.
167966: In a house in Keerbergen a ghost always appeared.
167973: A seamstress was visited by an old woman who came to ask whether the seamstress would sew buttons onto a garment. The seamstress did what she was asked. When she lay in bed that evening, she was shaken violently. Every evening at eight o'clock there was a knock at the seamstress's house. When the door was opened, no one was to be seen. Shortly afterwards one of the seamstress's cows died. The animals were always being untied and butter could no longer be made. In the end the people went to the friars of Dendermonde, who advised them to put an Easter nail under the door and to pray the Gospel of Saint John every evening. The bewitchment lasted for weeks, but thanks to the friars' intervention they were finally freed of it.
167991: A man always came home around midnight together with an accordion player. On the cobbled road from Ninove to Leerbeek the two men were flung from one side to the other by the witches.
168028: A small, feisty little man worked on a farm in the village and lived there in the bakehouse. At a certain hour of the night this man had to roam about as a werewolf. At that moment the animals in the stables were set loose. The animals sweated terribly and everything went up in flames. Towards morning everything was back to normal. Only after the man's death was his skin found above the bakehouse.
168053: On the Alverberg a white ghost was always seen appearing. When Pier V.H. went to chop down some stumps on the hill, he found a chest with eight hundred silver coins and also some leather money. The man went to the priest of Bekkevoort and asked: "Shouldn't we have a Mass said now?", to which the priest replied: "No, that is not necessary, for the soul has now found rest." Since then the ghost has no longer been seen on the hill.
168058: An unmarried girl who lived in de Rode went to the fair in Testelt with a boy. At the fair the girl saw her former boyfriend, who kept watching her and her companion the whole time. Later that evening the girl walked home with her former boyfriend. On the way the boy said: "Here is my handkerchief. If you meet a dog, throw the handkerchief into its jaws, because I have to relieve myself." Further on the girl saw a big dog with glassy eyes standing there, staring at her with open jaws. The girl threw the handkerchief, and the dog left her alone. When her boyfriend came back a little later, the girl noticed that he had the fibres of the handkerchief between his teeth. When she got home the girl crawled into her bed. She never got out of it alive again.
168061: In a house in Sint-Joris-Winge someone had caught pneumonia. People believed that person was bewitched.
168073: A man always dragged chains around in the attic so that people would think the house was haunted.
168082: A butcher kept seeing a white cat running in front of his feet. Finally the butcher struck at the animal with his axe. The next day the man saw a woman sitting in the inn who had a large wound on her head.
168104: A man who owned a mule and sold mint drops at the fair was married to a woman suspected of witchcraft. For one day the man had given someone a packet of sweets, saying: "Here, this is for you, but make sure she doesn't see it, because she is a witch."
168105: In Vlezenbeek lived a farmer whose barn was too small to store his harvest. One day the farmer met the devil, who told him: "If you give me your most precious possession, you will have a barn in a single night." The farmer agreed and sold his soul. The barn had to be finished before the rooster crowed for the first time the next morning. In the night, however, the farmer grew worried and told his wife what he had done. The wife got up, went to the henhouse and began to clap her hands, so that the rooster began to crow before three o'clock. Because the barn was not yet finished at that moment, the farmer could keep his soul. That barn was called 'the Duivelsschuur' (Devil's Barn).
168123: In Kerkom lived a witch who could bring people much misfortune. If that witch had been in a house with children, the children fell ill. After the people had fetched a relic from the friars and put it under the threshold, the witch could no longer get in. In the end the witch then made her own children and her husband ill. She had to do evil until the devil came to fetch her.
168142: People who lost many animals believed they had fallen victim to the kwade hand (the evil hand, bewitchment). They would then go to a friar, who gave them small loaves. The friars sometimes also came to read prayers over the animals. The people then had to make a novena.
168144: Some boys who slept in the attic always put a blessed palm sprig on their chests because they were afraid of a woman who always came to them at night to bewitch them.
168174: The wife of Sus V.R. had recently died. One evening, when Sus wanted to go to the toilet, he saw his dead wife sitting on the toilet and said: "Trees, is that you?" At first the ghost was white, but as soon as the man had spoken, the ghost turned black. When Sus spoke again, the ghost turned white again. In this way the apparition changed colour as many as six times.
168185: A woman had blackened her hands completely and said: "Now I fly over hedge and over hedgerows and over the 'towers' (?) of pavilions!" Then the woman was gone. A man who had seen all this and wanted to follow the woman made a mistake in saying the magic formula and said: "And now I fly through hedge and through bush!" The man arrived at his destination badly injured.
168194: On a farm on the Heikant, horse bones were seen rattling by themselves.
168213: If a piece of a blessed candle had been put under the threshold, no witches could come in. If one picked up a pin that a witch had dropped on purpose, one could be struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, bewitchment). For witches often deliberately dropped things in people's houses.
168218: In the past it was often said of old women that they were witches. Children were not allowed to accept anything from those women, for otherwise, it was believed, they would be bewitched. Such things were told, for example, about a good woman who liked to help her neighbours a lot.
168222: A woman who was running an errand in Wemmel saw a nice little stick lying in the Reekstraat. The woman wanted to pick up the stick, but found that it stuck to her hands. When the woman began to pray the Gospel of Saint John, the stick fell to the ground again.
168230: A man went to the friars of Edingen because his child had worms. People believed the child had been bewitched. After the friars had removed the evil, they said to the man: "If you see anything unusual on your way home, you must not do anything." In the field along the Waddenstruik (1) the father saw a toad. He put the animal in his pocket and, when he got home, threw it into the stove. The next day the man's neighbour was burnt all over.
168248: In Opheule there was a circle of maren (nightmare witches). A woman who had been there wanted to leave the society. When she announced this, the maren said to her: "You have seen your first child make his solemn communion, but with your second child you will never see it." The woman's second child died of meningitis. That was the revenge of the maar (nightmare witch).
168254: If you met a witch, you could protect yourself by giving her something. A farmer who went to his field early in the morning had to pass a little house where a witch lived. The farmer greeted the woman, who then asked: "Are you going to manure your field so early?", to which the farmer replied: "Yes, the sooner it's done, the better." The witch went on: "You won't go." The man went on, but he could not get onto his field. It was as if there were a wall holding him back. The next morning the man decided to try a second time. This time, however, he brought something along to give to the witch. After that he was able to get onto his field.
168255: Two tailors from Avendoren went to play music at the fairs. One evening, when the two men were on their way again and had to pass under the Boog (1), a witch said to them: "You may pass under the Boog now, but don't think you'll manage it on the way back!" When the men went home that night, they indeed could not get under the Boog, because the road was full of black cats. The men had to make a detour behind the Mijnke.
168256: A witch from Landen often went around peddling all sorts of things. That witch suffered a great deal before she could die. She could do people harm. For example, she made sure someone could no longer move forward or got the 'spot' on his eye.
168273: A witch who was sleeping in church suddenly knocked her clogs together. The next moment the church was full of mice.
168274: The castle of Sint-Pieters-Rode was haunted. At night the gate there was always flung open and shut, without anyone to be seen.
168296: On her way back from Tienen, a woman was taken by the hand by a rag-picker who was said to be a witch. When the woman came home, she said to her mother: "Isn't my hand swelling? That witch touched my hand." Of course the hand did not swell at all.
168303: At a certain spot in Keerbergen a stallicht (will-o'-the-wisp) always appeared. People believed that this apparition was the soul of a dead woman who had hidden a pot of money somewhere and came to point it out. On seeing that light, you had to say: "If you are sent by God, speak. If you are sent by the devil, be gone".
168340: A woman who always brought something with her often came to visit a family. When the son and daughter of that family died shortly after one another at the age of eighteen or nineteen, the people believed the children had been bewitched by the visitor.
168349: In Mijlbeek lived a witch. When a man from the village died after tumbling into the brook with his horse and cart, the witch was the first at the scene of the accident. It was claimed that she had caused the accident.
168356: A woman was often ridden by the mare. There was not much one could do about it, but one could go to the friars, though even that did not always help.
168361:
A farmer who had a boar was often visited by people who wanted the boar to cover their sow. One day the boar had broken loose. A woman from the neighbourhood, who was suspected of being a witch, drove the boar back to its sty with a stick, shouting: "You shouldn't keep that one any longer, not a single piglet will come of it!" The farmer did indeed have to sell his boar.
Everyone was afraid of that witch and people always tried to keep her away from the children of the neighbourhood.
168380: After Mass a certain woman stayed seated in the church. Suddenly the sexton saw that the missal was still open. After the priest had closed the book, the woman left the church.
168398: Some people went to the house of a witch who was said to have bewitched someone. When they entered the house, the witch's children said: "Mother is in the coffee pot." They looked in the coffee pot and saw that there was a toad inside.
168421: A man had gone to work at the house of a woman in Meldert. People had warned the man that the woman was a witch. On his way home the man had to cross a brook. Suddenly there was so much water in the brook that the man could not get across. The witch had done that.
168425: A man whose daughter had a fever of forty degrees walked the Lieve-Vrouwweg (Our Lady's Way) around the church every evening for nine days. People who saw that man there in the dark believed they had seen a ghost.
168448: On a farm twenty-eight animals died within one year. When a cow was taken to the bull, a woman stood watching along the way and said: "It won't work!" Two days later the cow was dead. The people fetched a relic to put under their threshold. The parish priest of Scheplaken came to read prayers over the farm. Moreover, the people had to enter and leave the stable backwards. After that things improved.
168466: The northern lights were a star with a long tail. When people had seen that star, they knew misfortune was coming.
168499:
In the old days people often said: "The more left, the better; the more right, the worse." If your right hand itched, you would soon have to spend money. If your left hand itched, you would receive something.
If you met a black cat, a nun or a priest, misfortune would follow.
168514: A woman visiting her father suddenly noticed that the old man began to speak strangely, so that he became almost unintelligible. The man claimed he had been bewitched by a woman from the neighbourhood. His speech impediment was said to have begun after he had seen the woman appear the night before.
168523: In Bever lived a woman whom everyone feared because they believed she had special powers. A baby of that woman's daughter-in-law died. Because the woman had stood by the cradle, she was accused of having bewitched the baby.
168535: On the Kattendijk in Haacht a man is once said to have seen witch cats dancing around him.
168556: A woman from Willebringen worked as a maid on a farm in Kumtich. Strange things often happened on that farm. The cow was untied and the maid often saw something at the window at night. Another night the maid saw in front of her a hand that was on fire.
168560: In Kumtich lived a boy who could make white mice. After the priest had read prayers over the boy, he could no longer make mice.
168561:
In de Borcht (a hamlet of Grimbergen) a baby died through the doing of an old woman who was said to be able to bewitch. Such witches could free people from illnesses, but then they fell ill themselves.
A sick woman called in a witch from Mechelen. After the witch left, the woman was cured, but her grandchild got diarrhoea. The child died.
168573: A man was home alone one Sunday afternoon. He decided to bake cakes for when his wife came home. Because his wife kept the money, he went to a shopkeeper to fetch some flour on credit. That shopkeeper, however, was a sorceress. While the man was baking, he saw a toad come in through the water drain. Twice the toad said: "Hand over hand, paw over paw, Jan isn't dead yet and he's already baking cakes and his flour isn't paid for yet." The man then hit the toad with his pan, whereupon the animal jumped away. In the evening he told his wife everything. When she went to pay for the flour the next day, she saw that the shopkeeper was burnt all over.
168590:
A man from Meerbeek moved to Herfelingen. Because his child was ill, the man went to the witheren (Norbertine canons) of Affligem with a photo of the sick child. The priest walked around the table until drops of sweat rolled down his face, as if he had to push a cart with a load of a thousand kilos. The priest gave the man a prayer card to put under the child's pillow. But the child could no longer be saved.
That man lost two of his children to witchcraft. In the attic of the house the most beautiful music could often be heard, but when someone went to look, there was nothing to be seen or heard. People were also struck by an invisible force.
168596: In a café a man struck at a rat that was running about. A while later the man saw that a woman from the neighbourhood, who was suspected of being a sorceress, had a scratch on her face.
168623: Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of people who had been killed in the fields. Several rapes and robbery-murders had once taken place on the Meigemheide. People avoided that place like the plague because many will-o'-the-wisps floated about there. The souls came back to torment their murderers.
168628: On a farm good butter could no longer be made. There were always red and blue maggots in the butter. The people went to the friars, who told them: "The woman who comes to wash her cap at your pump every day is the guilty one. Beware of her." The people chased that woman away and had no more misfortune.
168639: In Opvelp a witch often came to visit her mother. Wherever the witch went, people heard noise and music in the attic, though nothing was to be seen. The witch claimed she was accompanied everywhere by a black man, even into the wine cellar in Cologne. When the witch was in Opvelp again and said she had come to visit her sick mother, the people said: "You shouldn't be here, your mother isn't ill." To which the witch replied: "But she will be." The poor woman did indeed fall ill, and her daughter stayed with her until she died. The witch had caused her own mother's death. After the woman's death, the witch no longer wanted to see her mother.
168653: In Oudenaken an old woman came peddling oranges. Because their mother was ill, the children did not want to let the woman in. The peddler could not get the door open. The sick woman crawled over the scaffolding that had been put up to paint the ceiling and was given an orange by the peddler, who said: "Here, eat this." But the woman immediately threw the orange into the stove.
168668: A man often visited his girlfriend in Noduwez. When the man returned to Bost, he had to go through the fields. In Goetsenhoven a big black dog was often waiting for him, and it accompanied him to the end of the street. One day the man took a heavy stick with him and said to the animal: "If you touch me, we'll measure ourselves against each other with the stick." But the dog did him no harm. The man was accompanied by the dog for months, until one day he no longer saw it.
168679: Along the Kleine Gete people often saw will-o'-the-wisps, to their great fright. Those were the little souls of children who had died unbaptised.
168681: If people believed the animals in the stable were bewitched, they put something under the threshold. At a farmer's in Halle a cow had died shortly after the farmer's son had gone swimming with the school in Halle. The farmer then believed his cow had been struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, bewitchment).
168692: Two men walking past the Kattebeek saw a dance tent there. They went into the tent and were given silver cups of beer. When one of the men said: "God, where have we ended up now!", the whole scene vanished. The men only had their cups still in their hands.
168727: A woman walking past the churchyard one evening saw a little light appear above a grave in unconsecrated ground. Someone told her that such lights were the souls of people who had died unbaptised. If such lights were baptised, the souls went to heaven. Later that day the woman went back to the churchyard with her husband. The man took some holy water in his hands and said: "I baptise that grave above which a little light hovers in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen." The next moment the little flame was gone.
168747:
People who were ridden by the 'maal' (mare) were in reality suffering from a standstill of the blood.
A woman who had a five-month-old baby always saw a head wearing a bowler hat appear above her bed. In the end it got so bad that the woman no longer dared go to sleep. She was allowed to sleep at the neighbours', where she did not see the apparitions. When the woman had regained some strength, she went back to sleeping at home. She no longer saw the apparitions. That woman had been ridden by the maal.
168766: A drunkard lay ill in bed for a long time and finally died. The man claimed his own mother had bewitched him.
168772: In the past, little lights were seen in the Delle every night at the same place and the same time. They were the souls of children who had been murdered right after birth without receiving baptism. When Octavie and Sidonie were coming back from Aarschot one day, they saw a will-o'-the-wisp come flying towards them at full speed, although there was no wind.
168787: A man from Jette saw a stallicht (will-o'-the-wisp) flickering under the trees. Liza V. went to baptise the light.
168791: A woman went to cut grass with a scythe for her animals. Every time the woman put the jute sack of grass on her shoulder, the sack tore. A witch caused that.
168797: Sometimes an unrecognisable figure resembling a goat could be seen floating through the air.
168802: In a family where a child had died, it was found that the child's body was full of pins.
168814: On a farm in Grimbergen nobody was allowed in the stable after eight in the evening, because then the ghosts walked on the beams. That farmer owned the two finest stallions in all of Brabant. Within two days both stallions were dead.
168841: One evening a woman went with her seven-year-old son to fetch milk at a farm. When the woman reached a crossroads around eleven o'clock, she suddenly saw the devil standing there. The woman stood rooted to the spot, but the devil did her no harm and disappeared a little later. That crossroads was notorious at the time. Anyone who wanted to make a pact with the devil had to go there at midnight with a black hen under his arm. After that incident the woman had two fathers from the Keizersberg in Leuven come to her house. The fathers examined the whole house and found that the place was still under the influence of the evil hand. The fathers said prayers and hung crosses above the doors. The mother begged the fathers to tell her which witch was responsible for that evil. The fathers answered: "We may not say who it was, but we will show you that person. Next Friday between three and four o'clock you will see the witch." That Friday, shortly after three o'clock, a car stopped by the house. The man inside held his hands over his eyes, stayed there like that for ten or fifteen minutes and then drove on. Years later that man died after a terrible death struggle. The priests had to pray for a long time to let that man die.
168847: On the Plein there was a farm where a coach with black horses drove around every night. Two gentlemen sat in the coach. At that moment the child's cradle began to rock back and forth and the mill to turn. The animals in the stable were drenched in sweat.
168866: A boy who worked on a farm in the Kerkstraat always met a piglet on the way. One day the boy kicked at the piglet. The next moment, however, the boy saw little piglets everywhere.
168870: In a house where the children had been struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, bewitchment), the father went outside to tie thorns around two lime trees. The man's mother came by and said: "Are you going to tie them to it, son?", to which the man answered yes. Before it was dark, a child died in that house.
168877: A shopkeeper gave a girl a bag of sweets. The girl ate some of the sweets and also gave a few to her friends and her dog. Her mother would not accept a sweet. When the girl married a short time later, she had much misfortune. The girl had a child, after which her breast swelled terribly. The doctor found that there was not milk but blood in the breast. A spiritist from Charleroi was sent for, who spoke with the parish priest about the girl's health. The spiritist sent the priest away and predicted that a woman would come by and knock on the door. Some time later the shopkeeper came knocking at the girl's door. The spiritist read prayers over the girl's breast, but the next day three doctors came to amputate the breast.
168890: In Attenhoven lived a woman who could give children lice by touching them.
168897: Whenever the people of Beert came back from the fair, they always saw a big black cat standing in front of their feet. Because the cat kept growing bigger and bigger, the people walked back home.
168908: A man who went to Leuven to sell butter let three or four women ride along on his cart. On his way home the man stopped at the church to drink a glass of beer. When the man then wanted to leave again, he could not; the horses stood stock-still. Finally the man shouted to the women riding with him: "If my horses don't move within a minute, I'll beat to death everything sitting on my cart." The next moment the cart started moving.
168917: A man who was often ridden by the mare tied a knife around his chest with the blade pointing upward before going to bed. That left the mare powerless.
168941: A woman could not churn butter because a witch had put the kwade hand (the evil hand, bewitchment) on her cow. From the moment the witch died, the woman could churn butter again.
168957: In Bunsbeek lived a woman who was suspected of being a witch. A man bringing in his harvest in the field suddenly could not go on when he saw that woman standing there. The horses would not take another step. The man then said to the woman: "If you don't make my horses pull, I'll burn you right here," to which the woman said: "Your horses will pull." Then the cart started moving.
168958: If one carried a little cross, witches had to turn around when they came near. A man working in his asparagus field saw a farmer coming with his wife. The man quickly turned around. After that the woman did not go to the strawberry field for three days. The man also fell out with that woman afterwards.
168961: In an inn where money always disappeared from the drawer, a man decided to keep watch one night. At a certain moment the man heard a creaking, though nothing was to be seen. Terrified, the man went to the bedroom. When the two got up the next day, they found that the whole drawer had disappeared. The people were convinced that a witch had been in their house.
168965: Black cats were witches in animal shape.
168970: Toads and black cats were witches in animal shape.
168985: On the Neerveld lived a woman who liked to torment people. If one agreed with that woman, a piece of the ceiling fell, a chair toppled over, or a child fell ill when one came in. Usually those illnesses were not serious. If the illness could not be cured with anise, one had to have prayers read over one by the friars of the Vosseplein.
168987: Two men coming back from the fair saw an old woman standing by the street. That woman was suspected of being a witch. A little later one of the men found that his wallet had disappeared. When the two men parted and each went his own way, they lost their way.
168988: A girl who was standing outside with some friends one afternoon saw a farmhand from a big farm ride past. That farmhand was suspected of being a sorcerer. Because he was eating an apple on the cart, the girl asked: "Do you have one for me too?" "Yes, hold your apron open," the sorcerer replied, and threw an apple to the girl. When the girl went to take the apple out of her apron, she saw only two or three mice sitting in it.
168991: On a farm where butter was being churned, a woman who was said to be a witch came to visit. That day the people did not succeed in making butter. Whoever had to contend with such witchcraft went on pilgrimage to the abbey of Affligem.
168999: A farmhand from Meldert returning from a visit to his girlfriend in Domijt had to carry a horse on his back along the way. The boy fell ill. When he lay on his deathbed, a clergyman read a blessing over him. The parents were advised to hang a bottle on a cord in the well and let the boy drink from that bottle every day. The boy was cured. Afterwards he had to go with a gun to the place where the horse had leapt on him and say: "You are the oldest witch of Meldert." Then his own girlfriend appeared there.
169015: A neighbour woman always came to a farm to fetch milk. On Fridays that woman always went briefly into the cowshed before going into the farmhouse. If the farmer's wife made butter on that day, it failed. When the farmer's wife went to the friars of Ghent, she was told: "It must be that witch of Mijlbeek again!" The friars came to read prayers over the farm and advised the farmer's wife to make butter only once a week, namely on Friday. The farmer's wife followed the advice and could make butter every Friday. The witch had a hard death struggle. After her death her daughter took over her witching power.
169023: Black cats were witches. People who met a black cat in the evening were bewitched. Such animals had to be caught or beaten to death.
169025: A light was always seen in the churchyard of Wemmel. People believed it was the ghost of the old mayor floating there.
169026: A woman suddenly got a headache and swelled up completely, so that even three beds were not enough for her to lie on. The woman woke her husband so he could go and get a pill. The man tried to get up but went completely stiff and fell. A little later the woman's brother got the same symptoms. All this lasted two hours. After that the sick began to crawl.
169053: People believed that stallichten (will-o'-the-wisps) were the souls of unbaptised children. In fact, stallichten were sulphur that formed where horses lay buried.
169055: In Perk, yllichten (will-o'-the-wisps) were often seen. They were the souls of unbaptised children.
169060: A boy went for a walk in the woods with a friend. At a certain moment the boy said to his friend: "Go on ahead, I have to do a big job. If you see anything, throw my handkerchief at the apparition." When the boy came back a little later, his friend saw that he had the fibres of the handkerchief between his teeth.
169073: People who had bad luck were said to have been ridden by the mare.
169075: Because P.'s house was haunted, nobody dared to live there. Someone was said to have once been buried in the ground on which the house was built. Widower B. from Oplinter woke up at night because a strange cat was in his room. Frightened, the man threw the cat out of the window. The next day the man found that the neighbours' dog had been strangled.
169088: A man who had to go and ring the church bells saw a white ghost in the church tower. It was the spirit of the late sexton, who had once promised to make a pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel and could find no rest until that pilgrimage had been made.
169120: At a watermill lived people who had much misfortune. Their three horses stood there for three days with their heads against the wall, and the vet was at a loss. The son of those people died. In the end the friars were called in, which put an end to the evil. A woman who lived in the neighbourhood moved to Edingen.
169150: When one went somewhere to buy or sell something, one knew one would have bad luck if the first person one met on the way was a woman. A boy going to draw lots for the army met a witch first and was drawn for service.
169165: On a bewitched farm many cows and pigs died. When the curate came by and asked whether the people had let a stranger in, they remembered that an old woman had visited. They had not known that the woman was a witch. After the priest had read prayers over the place until he was drenched in sweat, he advised the people never to let anyone into their stable again.
169180: At the Schaliënhof the cows were untied every night. Nor could anyone manage to get a calf or a piglet onto the cart. The people sought advice from friars in East or West Flanders, who put an end to the harassment.
169195: A man who had vowed to go on pilgrimage died before he had kept his promise. After his death the man had to come back to haunt. When his relatives went on pilgrimage for the dead man, they put a stick by the door and said: "You go ahead, we'll follow!" Otherwise they would have had to carry the ghost the whole way.
169198: In a house in Zichem something always came and lifted the cellar door, although nothing could be seen. When the people told the priest what was happening to them, the clergyman said: "I will come by tomorrow and pray a little. You will catch a rat." The people did indeed catch a large black rat in their cellar. The priest had changed the tormenting spirit into a rat, for an ordinary rat would never have been able to lift that door. The rat had to be burned, and after that the haunting stopped.
169217: When someone had died, people often believed that the dead person came back. They then went to the friars to find out what vows the dead person had made during his life.
169228: A boy was taking his girlfriend home over the Schoolbergen. On the way the boy said: "Go on ahead, I have to relieve myself. If you meet anything on the way, you must wave your apron." Further on the girl saw a big black dog come out of the woods. She remembered her boyfriend's advice and waved her apron. When she got home she noticed that her boyfriend had the threads of the apron between his teeth.
169246: A man with a bad leg sold sweets at the market. One day the man had given a sweet to a woman who had special powers. From that day on, the man's house was plagued by ants. The people went to the priest and told him they had perhaps been struck by the evil hand. The clergyman replied: "You mustn't believe that".
