172537: An old woman who could hardly walk once lived in Waasmont. When the children came back from school, she often asked them to run an errand for her. One day a girl was given money by the woman to go and buy a loaf of bread. The girl said the money itched terribly in her hands. She believed she was bewitched.
172549: On a farm where people were sitting at their evening meal, they suddenly noticed a man with horse's legs sitting at the table. The place was haunted.
172567: Will-o'-the-wisps that flew through the woods were souls who had to do penance.
172570: A woman who was ridden by the mare suddenly received a blow to her face while lying in bed. She could see nothing and went completely stiff. To protect yourself against the mare, you had to place your shoes with the heels under the bed.
172571: When a farmer's cows were sick, the farmer was advised to lift up the cows' trough, because a witch in the shape of a snake might be underneath it.
172577: One evening a woman was visited by a neighbour who had never been to her house before. Afterwards the woman's grandchild fell ill. The woman took the child to the priest, and it recovered.
172581: A fifteen-year-old girl had been bewitched by a woman from the village. After the girl's mother made the sign of the cross, the spell was broken.
172602: In Meise a little child was given a lump of sugar by a woman every day. One day the child fell ill. The friars advised the child's mother to bury the lump of sugar the next day and to look at it again a few days later. When the mother did so, she found that the sugar had turned into slime infected with tuberculosis. The friar had said that the mother should take her child to the doctor. He also gave her a medal so that the woman who had caused the harm could no longer come in.
172618: A sexton who had gained much knowledge from books had a reputation for having special powers. But the man did no one any harm. When some horses from Vollezele were on their way to the competitions at the half-century jubilee palaces, the innkeeper said to the sexton: "Look, sexton, what fine horses are coming." The sexton replied: "Fine horses? Those aren't fine horses. They're lame for good." The horses could hardly get past that spot. Then the sexton let the animals go on.
172620: One always had to make sure not to be tapped on the shoulder by a sorceress, because that was dangerous.
172632: A man going to Lot to fetch soft white cheese saw a cat as he drove up a hill. At that moment the horse began to rear. The man said: "You sorceress, there you are again!"
172647: In Merchtem lived a sorceress who had learned her magic from her mother. On a cold day a man had to take chaff to the sorceress with the dog cart. He had brought his little son along. The sorceress gave the man and his son a cup of coffee and stroked the son's head. A few days later the child was so ill that the doctor had to be called. The child grew visibly thinner and the doctor did not know what was wrong. One day a spider was seen crawling out of the child's bed. The doctor sent the people to the friars of Dendermonde. The clergymen said to the parents: "We can do something, but then you must do something too. Go to that sorceress and tell her she must take the spell off your child." After the child's father had been to the sorceress, the child recovered.
172664: A man who had pulled up a boundary post during his life walked about the churchyard with the post every night after his death, asking: "Where shall I put it? Where shall I put it?" One day a drunkard came by and answered: "Damn it, put it where you found it!" The ghost went and put the post back and was released.
172711: A man had promised a friend: "If you die first, I will have a mass said for you." But when the friend had been dead for two years, the man still had not had a mass said. After a while the man heard knocking on the door every day. Since he did not know what the sound meant, he went to the parish priest, who asked him: "Did you not promise something?" After the man had the promised mass said, he no longer heard the knocking.
172722: In Overhespen there once lived a woman whom people thought was a witch. In those days all the children had lice. Many people believed that the witch had given their children lice.
172767: An old farmer who had died had to come back and haunt after his death.
172771: In Bierbeek stood a barn that had been built in a single night. In the barn was a hole that could never be closed. There was also a tree standing in the barn that was not allowed to be cut down. If someone did so anyway, the tree was just as big again the next day.
172780: In the past people did not like to see owls or crows coming, because they believed those birds were omens of death.
172782: People who practised sorcery could send rats or mice to a particular place.
172796: A woman who went to the inn one evening saw an unknown gentleman sitting at a small table there. Suddenly the woman saw that the gentleman had goat's legs. The woman quickly made the sign of the cross and left.
172802: A sick man from Kampenhout was visited by a friend. At that moment a woman from Antwerp came in. When the man died a few days later, the woman went around proclaiming that he had been bewitched by the friend who had visited him. So the friend got a bad name. In reality the man had died of appendicitis.
172806: In Hakendover lived a girl whose father had died young. At the age of twelve the girl had to go to work on a farm. After Sunday mass the girl was allowed to visit her mother. She had to be back before dark. Since the farmer's son had returned from the seminary, strange things had been happening on the farm. Between midnight and one o'clock people saw a werewolf roaming the Tommenveld. When the girl turned sixteen, she was allowed to go home from Saturday. She always took the shortest way, which ran past the Drie Tommen. One winter's day the girl heard a growl at the last burial mound. Frightened, she ran to the house of the broom-maker. The woman who lived there walked part of the way with her. After that the girl was advised to make a detour by the Piepelboom because it was safer there. A farmhand who worked on the farm had also advised her always to carry something red. The girl always took a red shawl with her. One day at the Piepelboom the girl was leapt upon by a big black beast. The girl struck three times with her red shawl and fled. After that incident the girl's mother sent her daughter to the factory in Tienen. When the girl came to fetch her things from the farm, the farmer's son was standing at the gate. He had always had an eye on her. The boy smiled at her, and at that moment she saw that he had the red threads of her shawl between his teeth.
172810: The devil is often depicted as a goat with rattling chains. On winter nights you could hear the devil walking and leaping in remote streets. A man who dared to go and look one night saw a large white goat dragging a chain behind it. The next day the goat's footprints were found on the ground.
172811: The priest was the only one who could recognise the witches in the church. If he left his missal open, the witches could not leave the church and had a beehive on their heads.
172817: People who had a lot of misfortune in their stable believed they had been bewitched by someone and had the friars of Affligem read prayers over them.
172822: Two friends going to the fair of Walfergem saw a cat sitting in the middle of the street on the way. One of the men wanted to give the cat a kick, but the other advised him against it. When the men were a bit further on in the fields, they were chased there by a good hundred cats. The cats kept asking: "Uncle, may I come along?" At a certain moment the cats had disappeared.
172852: In the Oude Kattenstraat there was a werewolf that sometimes made passers-by carry him.
172871: In Oppem-Brussegem stood a barn that had been built by the Freemasons. The barn was used to store the tithes that the white canons of Grimbergen demanded from the people. One day, however, the barn became too small, so the farmer sold his soul to the devil in exchange for a barn that had to be finished before the first cockcrow. Because the farmer regretted his deed in the night, he got up and woke the chickens, so that the rooster began to crow early. The devils flew away, but there was still a large hole in the barn.
172872: On the ramparts near the Ijzerenmolen, three white ghostly figures always appeared at night.
172879: Houses where many children died of illness had been ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit), people believed. Sorceresses had caused that misfortune. A family that had just been freed from witchcraft was in trouble again when someone picked up a beautiful white handkerchief from the street. A sorceress had put that handkerchief there.
172900: A girl coming back from Oudegem met an old woman, who gave her a pat on the shoulder. Afterwards the girl fell ill. She was never healthy again.
172913:
If one met a cat at a crossroads at midnight, it was best to turn back.
Witches passed their magic power on to their eldest daughter.
172941: In Booienhoven lived a sick man. He always heard something in his bed, but nobody dared to look. The friars read prayers over the man's house and cut open the mattress. There was a rosary inside. After the rosary was destroyed, the man recovered.
172948: Witches could take the shape of a toad. That is why people were afraid of toads. If one saw a cat in the evening, one was not allowed to touch the animal, certainly not if it was a black cat.
172958: A man who went for a walk in the evening heard a rustling in the ditch. The man struck with his stick at the spot the rustling came from. As a result, however, the man lost his stick. The next day a woman brought the man's stick back with the words: "If I hadn't been there, you would have been dead!"
172977: Some men were playing cards in an inn. At a certain moment a stranger came in and asked if he could join in. The men agreed. The stranger, however, always won and in that way swindled the other players out of all their money. When one of the players bent down to pick up a dropped card, he found that the stranger had cow's legs. The stranger then said: "That's not all. You can't give me a single task that I can't carry out". The men challenged the stranger to stick his nose through an anchor hole (1) in a wooden beam. The stranger climbed onto a table and did what had been asked. Meanwhile, though, one of the card players had gone outside and climbed up a ladder. When the stranger stuck his nose in the hole, the card player drove a nail into it. At that the devil cried: "That's cross-work!" and he disappeared.
172988: A man who had taken away a boundary post had to haunt the Bist after his death with a boundary post in his hands. The ghost kept calling: "Where shall I put it? Where shall I put it?" One day a drunkard answered: "Put it back where you got it!" Since then the ghost has not been seen again.
173005: In Tielt someone lay dying. A witch came to visit the sick person to heal him, but she did not succeed. At the end of her visit the witch could no longer leave by the front door. She had to go out by the back door.
173020: Some pigeon fanciers took their birds to a man who lived by the station in Opwijk, since the pigeons were to fly to Noyon (France). When the men went home, they got lost, although they knew the area very well. When the tower clock of the Boskant (Merchtem-Peizegem) struck three, the men were standing in the Ravenstraat. The men walked through the fields and were home in no time. They believed they had been ridden by the mare.
173026: A man was always attacked by the werewolf when he came home late. The man resolved to give the werewolf a thrashing one day, although his wife had advised him against it. So a long fight broke out between the man and the werewolf. The man managed to strike the werewolf on the forehead until it bled. Because of this the werewolf took on his human form. It turned out to be one of the man's neighbours.
173049: In Ezemaal a child had got lice after a witch had taken off its little cap.
173053: In the past people often said that black cats were witches.
173080: A man had to go and fetch the midwife for his wife at night. Although there was no wind, the man saw the trees in the pine wood swaying back and forth.
173090: A woman from Grimbergen was visited by a pedlar selling socks. When the woman explained she needed nothing, the pedlar took her hand and then touched the wall. After that incident the woman never again found suitable socks for her child or her husband; the socks were always too big or too small.
173110: In Lubbeek lived a witch who had sold an animal to her neighbour. The neighbour had been warned beforehand by other people. The animal was always sick and the man had nothing but misfortune with it.
173133: In a house the butter churn started working by itself while nobody was in the house.
173137: People who had problems with the animals in their stable believed they had become victims of the kwade hand (the evil hand, a curse). In reality they were simply people who had a lot of bad luck.
173148: A man from Sint-Pieters-Leeuw could no longer make butter. When the farmer's wife had milked the cows and carried the milk inside, she found that it had gone mouldy. Because the farmer and his wife believed they had been struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, a curse), they had the friars come to read prayers over the stable. After that, the farmer and his wife had no more problems.
173154:
A girl from Drieslinter got up in the morning to light the stove. To her great astonishment she saw that three legs had been knocked out from under the stove. Yet the people had heard nothing during the night. The girl's mother was so afraid that she no longer dared to use the stove and sold it to a rag-and-bone man. Three weeks later the father died in that house, leaving the mother alone with eight children.
Strange things had happened in that house before. One evening the girl was milking the cow while her parents were at the Kaarskensprocessie (candle procession). When her little brother went inside to fetch a glass so that he could drink some fresh milk, he saw an old little woman sitting behind the door. The little woman was no taller than half a metre and pulled an ugly face. Terrified, the boy ran back outside to tell his sister what he had seen. After that the girl did not dare to go inside either, so the two waited outside until their parents came home. When they went inside, there was nothing to be seen any more.
173155: A woman whose daughter had been ill for a long time and who had misfortune in the stable blamed her mother-in-law, whom she suspected of being a witch.
173156: If the church bells of Sint-Martens-Lennik and Sint-Kwintens-Lennik rang at the same time, someone would soon die.
173161:
In 1600 a plague epidemic raged in Scherpenheuvel. The people then prayed to Our Lady that the disease would be wiped out. Because Our Lady answered the people's prayers, the tradition arose of holding a candle procession on the first Sunday after All Saints' Day.
One year it rained cats and dogs on that day, so it was decided not to hold the procession. The next morning the statue of Our Lady was found completely smeared with mud. Our Lady had walked the procession alone. After that incident it was decided always to hold the procession, whatever the weather.
173203: On a farm there was always misfortune whenever the farmer's son had been to visit his girlfriend. When the boy stopped seeing the girl for a while, the misfortune ended. Some time later the boy secretly visited his girlfriend again without his parents knowing. Shortly afterwards the horse on the farm fell ill. In the end the animal even died. Another boy who had a relationship with the same girl fell ill and went to the friars, who told him he had only three months to live. The boy did indeed die soon.
173227: Anyone going from Rummen to Geetbets saw thousands of will-o'-the-wisps. People believed those lights were the souls of unbaptised children. In reality they were grubs.
173234: A twelve-year-old girl was ill and had to stay in bed. She was bedridden for twenty-four years. After her mother died in 1903, the girl gradually recovered. On her deathbed her mother had predicted: "When I die, you will be cured." The girl then had to learn to walk again and sought advice from the friars of Edingen. She lived with her father until he died around 1910. So as not to be alone, she then worked as a maid in two different places. She died at the age of 58 or 60. She had been bewitched by her mother.
173249: An altar boy had a swelling on his head. People believed the boy had been struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, a curse). When the friars of Sint-Truiden were in the village for the mission, they asked the boy what was wrong. They took him to the sacristy, read prayers over him and gave him some holy water with which he had to wash thoroughly two or three times. Five or six days later the boy was rid of his swelling.
173253: In Leuven lived a woman who stayed up late every evening. One night someone saw the woman take a little black man out of a cupboard. The woman must have found out she was being spied on, for in the following days nothing more was seen in her house. But one night a terrible noise was heard in the woman's house. The neighbours went in and saw that the hatch leading to the attic was completely overgrown with grey hair. The house was burned down. The woman was never seen again.
173314: A man with special powers could make a carter's horses stand still. Thus a farmhand returning from Diest with shop goods had to wait until four o'clock before his horses would move on. The man who did this owned evil books.
173315: Being ridden by the 'moel' (mare) had something to do with witchcraft and evil.
173348: A farmer's wife who had many horses was visited one day by a woman who stroked the animals. The next day the horses lay dead and the butter on the farm had gone sour. The friars came to pray at the farm and said: "You will meet the sorceress in the lane, but you must not speak to her." The friars also put an Easter nail under the door. The sorceress did not visit again, but the farmer's wife was ruined.
173350:
A friar who had read prayers over a bewitched house said: "Now the witches can no longer get in here, but you must also avoid the witches."
Three girls went to the fair in Meerbeke together with three boys. On the way they went into the house of a witch. When the girls came out, they were covered in lice.
173416: A woman working at P.'s saw a will-o'-the-wisp settle beside the water barrel because it wanted to be baptised. Will-o'-the-wisps were unbaptised children who had ended up neither in heaven nor in hell.
173418: A drunkard walking home in the evening kicked a skull, which said: "Leave alone what leaves you alone." Because the drunkard had been badly frightened, he immediately ran to the presbytery. The priest said to the man: "Come to mass early tomorrow morning with a small child and then go to confession. Otherwise your neck will be broken." The drunkard did what the priest had advised. When the man went out sober two days later, he came across the skull again and heard: "Lucky for you that you went to confession, otherwise I would have broken your neck and your legs."
173419: A witch is said to have lived in Kester long ago. People believed she went about bewitching the farmers' stables. On a farm she visited regularly, the farmer had much misfortune. His cow miscarried, a heifer would not get in calf, and so on. On another farm she often visited, an Easter nail was put under the threshold of the door, so the woman could no longer come in.
173437: In one house a child had been struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, a curse) after a sorceress had visited.
173443: The wife's family always came to borrow bread at a certain house. When they had baked themselves, they brought back a few loaves. But the people had to stop, because they got misfortune in their house and stable. When they no longer lent bread, they had no more misfortune.
173467: People troubled by witchcraft had a priest come. The clergyman asked them: "Do you think it is a woman from the neighbourhood?" But the people were reluctant and did not dare simply to make an accusation.
173473: People who were ridden by the mare had to place their clogs upside down.
173497: A witch from Sint-Martens-Lennik always came asking people for bread. But the people were not allowed to give her the bread themselves; the witch had to take it.
173498: The brother of a woman suspected of being a witch was always ill. The doctors could not help the boy. The child ate normally but stayed just as thin. Moreover, the child still lay in the cradle when other children his age could already walk. After the child had prayers read over him, he recovered.
173503: During the First World War a woman went to the shop, where many people were queuing. Among the crowd was a witch who kept trying to touch the woman's shoulder.
173532: When someone in Beert wanted to pick up a cat, the animal broke in two. It was probably a witch.
173557: A boy who met a supposed witch said: "You won't get me, old mother!" The witch replied: "Just wait!" The boy had to be taken home in a cart, and some time later he died. That witch caused all her children to die.
173560: Witches could turn themselves into animals and roamed about at night in that shape.
173574: Two men had agreed: "If one of us dies, the other must have a mass said for the deceased." But when one of the men had died, the other did not keep his promise. After his friend's death the man grew thinner and thinner. Moreover, at midnight he always saw a light appear. His wife did not see the light. During the mission the man told a friar what his problem was. The cleric said: "Did you ever promise anything to someone who has since died?" At that moment the man remembered his promise and decided to have the mass said as soon as possible. The friar had also said: "If the strange apparitions do not stop after you have kept your promise, hold a cloth at night. A glowing hand will be burned into the cloth." And so it happened.
173579: A miner had always said that after his death he would come back in the shape of a horsefly. When the man was dead, his wife saw a horsefly fly into her house during the Whitsun fair. The woman asked: "Ha, boy, is that you? How is it over there?" Of course the horsefly did not answer, but the woman was convinced that it was her husband's spirit.
173586: Near the Gaspeldoorn farm on the road to Vlezenbeek there was a spring in which a bell is said to have sunk once. It was called the Holy Spring because clear water always flowed from it.
173594: A man going from the town hall of Molenbeek to Brussels got lost. The man had been ridden by the mare. That had something to do with hypnosis.
173612: A man who lived alone was about to fry some meat when he saw five cats come in through the water drain. When the man had briefly gone outside to fetch water, he saw that the animals each had a piece of meat in their mouths. Furious, the man poured hot fat over the cats, burning three of them. The next day the man saw three women in church wearing bandages around their faces.
173619: A black cat roaming about in Kester was suspected of being a witch.
173674: The Wilderhof used to be haunted. Every morning the animals lay strangled in the stable there. The people kept watch in the stable, but the slightest moment of inattention was always fatal to the animals. Then the people had seven strong friars armed with clubs keep watch in the stable. The horses had the greatest difficulty reaching the farm. For two nights they had to fight against evil. Then they went home. On the way they still had to use their clubs to keep evil away. The horses had foam on their lips.
173676: A girl had fallen into the power of a sorceress after accepting strawberries from her.
173703: If you saw a crow fly past, you could expect misfortune.
173711: During a party in Lebbeke, a woman was sent to the shop to buy jenever. On the way the woman met someone with a sheet over his head. Convinced that it was some joker, the woman pulled the sheet away. Because the woman was holding a skull in her hands, she ran in fright to the priest. The clergyman advised her to bring the sheet back and to take a young child with her. When the woman went to return the sheet, the ghost said: "If you didn't have that child, I would break your neck!"
173737: In Rillaar lived a woman who could throw eggs from the attic into her apron, which she had hung ready downstairs, without breaking a single egg.
173770: People who were ridden by the mare had a kind of illness. Those people had prayers read over them.
173807: A man walking home suddenly noticed, at the little white chapel of 't Bolhuis, that he was in a beautiful avenue. The man walked and walked until morning came. When the man said: "God, where on earth would I be now", he found himself at the edge of the wood. The man knocked somewhere and asked the way to Okselaar. When the man came to Engsbergen, he found his bearings again. There a little woman opened her door and called: "Where have you been so early?" When the man made to attack the woman with his hook, the woman jumped inside and shut the door. It was that woman who had made the man lose his way.
173812: The Winning van Pachtes used to be a monastery farm. Every night a dead priest came to haunt that farm. His gravestone had been broken when the church was rebuilt. The farmhands always threw nutshells at the haunting priest.
173818: A man in Denderbelle had a meadow in which he had put calves. A sorceress had stolen one of the calves to put it in her own meadow. After a while the sorceress had to come and bring the calf back. "She won't get past the cellar hole," a friar had predicted. At the cellar hole the sorceress did indeed stand turning nervously round and round.
173820: People struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, a curse) had much misfortune. At the Stayenmolen in Sint-Truiden all the animals died through the kwade hand. One day an animal disappeared. It was never found again. A witch had bewitched the animals in that stable.
173835: In the house opposite the Heimolen lived a miller who had special powers. When the miller sat in an inn with his friends, he always made bets that won him many glasses of beer. From the balcony of the mill, the man could open the bolted door of the café, thirty or forty metres away, by throwing his cap against it.
173839: A man with an injured leg was home alone with his grandmother, who lay ill in bed. At a certain moment an old woman came to visit and wanted to see the cow in the stable. When the woman asked when the cow would calve, the man answered: "That will surely be another two weeks." The woman said: "That won't be true," and left. A little later the man heard a cry in the stable. Behind the cow lay a calf in the straw. The animal died at once.
173845: A carter was on the road with a wagon and two horses. When the carter had to pass the house of a sorceress and saw the sorceress standing outside, his horses suddenly could not go on. The carter took off his coat and made the sign of the cross with it on the cobbled road. Then the horses stepped over that spot and went on.
173851: A woman with a child in the cradle was visited by someone who came to ask for beans. The woman went to another room to fetch the beans. Eight days later the woman's child was dead. Perhaps the visitor had stroked it.
173855: A woman sitting outside her house said to the children coming home from school: "Would you thread my needle for me?" Then the woman threw the children into the water and bewitched them so they were covered in mice.
173865: A toad was a witch, so people claimed.
173870: In an inn in the village there was haunting on the upper floor. One evening, when people were talking about the haunting again, they decided to go upstairs and take a look. The people searched everywhere but found no ghost. Then they went back downstairs. Then one of the men said: "Come on, come down now." The next moment a donkey came down the stairs. Yet nothing at all had been found upstairs. Perhaps that donkey was a wizard who could turn himself into an animal.
173877: A woman could make mice because the priest had forgotten something at her baptism.
173897: A farmer from Wever had moved the boundary post of his land to enlarge his field. After his death the farmer haunted at night with the words: "Where shall I put it?" One night a drunkard answered: "Put it back where you got it!" Since then nobody has seen the haunting farmer again.
173899: A farmer from Bierbeek who had no barn to store his harvest was visited one evening by a man, who said: "If you sell me your soul, a barn will be standing for you before the first cockcrow tomorrow morning." The farmer agreed. After the man had left, however, the farmer grew worried and told his wife what he had done. When the farmer's wife saw that night that the roof of the barn was almost finished, she ran to the henhouse and imitated a rooster's crowing. At that the rooster woke up and began to crow itself. The devils fled and the farmer could keep his soul.
173919: A wizard could make someone have a fever for six weeks or make a woman in childbed suffer great pain. If people paid the wizard, he came with his magic books and took the evil away again. The wizard sat in the café from morning till evening, drinking all the time. He always had enough money to pay the bill. He would take a piece of copper from his pocket and pay. Strangely enough, the coins in his pocket could never be heard jingling. He probably got his money from the devil.
173939: A woman had lost her way in broad daylight because of a sorceress. That sorceress had come to milk the cows for her because she herself was a little ill.
173942: Near Tienen lived a farmer who had no barn to store his harvest. Suddenly the farmer saw a black gentleman standing there, who said: "If you give me your most precious possession, you will have a fine barn before the first cockcrow." The farmer signed the contract and went home, not knowing that by his 'most precious possession' his soul was meant. When the farmer lay restless in his bed, he told his wife everything. The farmer's wife got up and clapped her hands, so that the rooster began to crow early. Then a tremendous bang was heard. Outside stood a large barn with a small hole in the wall. To build the barn, the devil had pulled up trees everywhere. People tried several times to close the hole in the wall, but in the morning it was always open again. Only when a crosswork of beams had been placed in the hole did it stay closed. The devil's barn still stands near Tienen.
173949: A woman had visited a sorceress, where she drank a dram and ate a biscuit. When the woman lay sweating in bed that evening, the sorceress said to her: "Now I've got you too, eh!" That same night the woman had to call the doctor.
173951: On a farm where an old woman came to visit every afternoon, there was much misfortune in the stable. Pigs and cows often died, so the people had to buy other animals. Someone had said: "As long as the farmer doesn't throw that old woman out, he will keep having misfortune." The woman found out and never came to the farm again afterwards. There were no more problems there either.
173969: If one had been touched by a witch, one always had to strike her higher up. One day in church a woman met a friend she had not seen for a long time. The friend grabbed the woman by the arm. When the woman got home, she was deathly ill. She had forgotten to strike the witch higher up.
173995: A man fell victim to a wizard who made him lose his way, so that he did not get home until five o'clock in the morning.
174000: A healthy man had fallen ill after a woman gave him a glass of beer. Shortly afterwards the man died.
174002: A man transporting chickens in a dog cart began to curse because the cart kept tipping over. When the man held the cart firmly, he heard a tomcat meowing behind him.
174021: Stallichten (will-o'-the-wisps) were children who had been buried unbaptised and could not get to heaven. If someone had gone on pilgrimage to the rock of Okkerzeel for those children, the lights were no longer seen, because the children were in heaven.
174040: A black cat was an animal sent by a witch.
174080: A young mother worked on a farm, where she had to help milk the cows. A woman came to visit that farm every day. One day that woman had been with the mother's little daughter. The child was two and a half years old at the time. One night the girl began to cry at twelve o'clock, calling out that she saw all sorts of things. Her parents, however, saw nothing strange. Because the crying went on for several nights, one evening the mother put a knife under her pillow. She said to her husband: "Tonight we will stay awake and lay our daughter between us." When the child began to cry, the mother struck out with the knife at an apparition that looked like a wolf. By the time she called her husband, the apparition could no longer be seen. Afterwards the mother had her daughter overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell). A few days later the strange woman came to the farm again. She tried to get near the child and shouted: "Filthy brat, dirty brat!" After that the woman could no longer harm the child. When the mother told her mistress what had happened, the farmer's wife replied: "You mustn't believe in such things. That woman has been visiting here for years and we have never had any trouble with her."
174089: A woman who had to take the tram to Brussels could make the tram stand still until she was on it.
174100: If you slept in the moonlight, you could be ridden by the maar (nightmare). The priest said one must not say such things; according to him, being ridden by the maar was a stagnation of the blood.
174154: When a witch was sitting in church, the altar boys stuck a piece of the Easter candle under the threshold. The witch began to curse because she could not get out.
174166: In Kapellen lived a witch. When the Germans tried to move that witch's wagon during the war, they could not manage it in any way. The same witch also made animals die.
174188: A man coming back from the Eppegem fair saw a black cat in front of him in the field and kicked at it. A little further on the man saw the cat standing there again. This time the animal said to him: "Go back and set upright what you kicked over." After that the man was instantly sober.
174190: A man who kept pigeons became the victim of witchcraft. A neighbour woman had laid her hand on the pigeon loft. Because of this the man did not win a single prize with his pigeons that year, which was very unusual. To protect his pigeons, the man always scattered salt near the loft. A medium had also taught him to draw a pentacle with its point upwards in chalk on the loft to protect the birds.
174209:
A man who had to bring in the harvest got the work of three people done. That man was involved with the devil. After people had taken him to Edingen, he lost his magic power.
That man's wife walked on crutches. A neighbour who had been in the army had seen the woman flying on a broomstick there and said to her: "God, here you go about on crutches and over there you could run so fast!"
174211: A man who went to cut heather saw the wife of a sorcerer dancing in the field with heather on her head. When the witch saw she was being watched, she vanished. The trees could no longer be seen either!
174219: A girl from the Sollenbeemd in Halle was ridden by the mare. The girl lay stiff as a board in her bed when she saw the mare coming, and she could not go to work in the mornings. After the girl had the friars read prayers over her, she was freed from the mare.
174222: A farm in Neerlanden was haunted. The table and chairs moved there and at night noise was heard. When the farmer got up to look, the sounds could no longer be heard. The next night the sounds were heard again. The people were afraid and had a friar come to exorcise the house. After that no more ghostly sounds were heard on that farm.
174238: Many witches used to live in Linden. A farmer's wife turned herself into a crow every night and flew along with the Tillekesjacht (a wild hunt). One night a farmer had shot at the Tillekesjacht and hit the witch from Linden. After that all of that farmer's children died.
174256: If you walked under a ladder, misfortune would follow.
174257:
A woman always saw a comet at the stroke of twelve when she was working in the field. Letters could also be seen on the cabbage leaves then.
Because of this apparition, people believed the world would come to an end.
174279: A woman had had eight children, who had all died. When the woman was again lying in childbed, her husband saw a toad crawl out of the water drain outside the house. The man took a shovel and struck at the animal. The next day the witch had a broken leg or arm. She had always appeared in the form of a toad to bewitch that woman and make her children die.
174292: A man who worked at a brick kiln always had to be at work early. One morning the man arrived earlier than needed, so he lay down to sleep for a while. The man saw two women coming towards him, who said: "Wait a moment, because he is not sound asleep yet". Then one of the women leapt on the man. The woman squeezed the man's throat shut, so that he could no longer breathe. Only when the other workmen arrived was the man freed from the woman.
174295: Two sisters whose father had just died were so sad that they still set a third plate on the table every day. After a while the girls actually saw their father sitting at the table, but he did not touch the plate. When the girls told the priest what they had seen, he did not believe them. The girls nevertheless managed to persuade the priest to come with them. During the meal the girls saw their father again, but the priest saw nothing. After the priest had read in his breviary for a moment, the girls suddenly cried: "Father, our father is gone!", to which the priest replied: "You will not be troubled by it any more." Afterwards that priest had much misfortune and died very poor.
174304: A woman who was bewitched and suffered epileptic fits went to the parish priest of Bierbeek. Twelve people had to sit at the communion rail. The woman's husband had secretly come along and was also sitting at the rail. Although the priest had not turned around, he said: "There is a person sitting there who has to leave." After the woman had been overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell), the priest said: "You will have it one more time and then never again. The person who did this to you will come to your house the next day, but you must not let her in." After the procession on 15 August the woman had another fit. The next day a woman came by carrying a basket filled with pins. The sick woman opened the door and said: "You may not come in here unless you undo the harm you have done." After that the sick woman was cured.
174318: A man in Zellik was walking past the Bohemians. One of the Bohemians called to him: "Stop!", but the man walked on. The Bohemian went to a bag, took out a coin and gave it to the man, saying: "Make sure you don't lose it." The man walked on, and a little further along he saw that the coin was no longer in his hand.
174339: One had to watch out for some people because they had been ridden by the mare.
174341: A woman did not dare to buy her parents' house, although as the youngest daughter she was entitled to it. There had been much misfortune in that house. The friars came to look at the house. However, one room had to be left free so that the witches could hold their sabbath there. That place was the barn. The man who bought the house was told by a dowser with a pendulum that he would never have luck in that house.
174344: In the past people often saw stalkaarsen (will-o'-the-wisps) by a hedge in Sint-Katherina-Lombeek. They believed these were the souls of unbaptised children who came to dance. You were not allowed to point at stalkaarsen, or they would come and sit on your finger. In reality stalkaarsen were glow-worms.
174370: A miller's hand who had been out on Sunday turned up late for work on Monday morning, which made the miller very angry. The hand had got lost and ended up in Bever. The young man had been ridden by the mare.
174373: In a street in Hakendover where the town hall was later built, a hare used to come and sit at midnight that no one could catch or shoot.
174377: In Meise stood a barn that had been built by the devil. A farmer had sold his soul to the devil in exchange for a new barn, which had to be finished by the first cockcrow in the morning. The farmer's wife had got up at three or four o'clock in the morning and knocked her clogs together, so that the rooster began to crow early and the devils had to flee. There was still a hole in the barn.
174394: Some people who had seen a black cat believed the animal was the devil.
174396: A sexton who got into bed at midnight heard a knocking on the wall. Convinced that it was his brother, who slept in an adjoining room, the man paid no attention to the knocking. Because the man heard the knocking every evening, he moved his bed. After that the knocking was heard on a different wall. One day the sexton told the priest what was happening at his home. The priest did not take him seriously, so the man threatened to leave the house. The following Sunday the priest had a father from Edingen come to the house. The father sprinkled all the rooms of the house with holy water and said to the sexton: "If you still hear knocking, ask whether it might be the ghost of your dead aunt. She might be returning, for example, to point out money." After the father's intervention, however, the strange knocking came to an end.
174397: In Kampenhout there lived women with a bad reputation. A woman driving to the mill met a witch, who asked: "Are you driving to the mill?" The woman lied and said: "No." When the woman came back later that day, the witch was standing there again and said: "I know very well that you did drive to the mill."
174457: Black cats brought bad luck, so people believed. People who saw a black cat in the dark in the evening were convinced that the cat was a witch.
174466: A divorced card reader who was often drunk and who wrote with a lead fork (?) came to visit a house where a sick child lay in the cradle. The mother sent the card reader away, at which she reacted angrily: "I wish your child would get convulsions tonight!" That evening the child did indeed get convulsions. Only after three days did the child get better, after it had been overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell) by a friar. While this was happening, the sorceress sat facing the wall.
174467: In the village lived a witch who was always out and about at night. Wherever people went, every night they ran into that woman.
174479: A boy was followed on the road by a spotted cat and asked: "Spotted little cat, where are you going?" Then the cat said: "Jan asked me, pretty spotted cat, where are you going?" The man ran home terrified.
174497: A boy could make mice by pushing against a molehill. When the children told the priest during catechism what the boy could do, the clergyman took the boy into the sacristy. Afterwards the priest said: "Now go and make mice again!", but the boy could no longer do it.
174502:
A man and his wife had joined the freemasons. They had both had to sign with blood. When that man died, he was not allowed to be taken to church. When the man was dead, he was buried with a torch.
The wife of another freemason who had died wanted her husband to be buried in church. So cobblestones were put in the coffin, so that people would think the man had been given a church funeral.
174519: A man making a pilgrimage on foot to Diegem went to the Hof van Bollebeek to ask whether he could spend the night there. The people explained that the man could certainly sleep there, but that every night around half past eleven a ghost appeared that rattled chains and bells. The man was not afraid, however, and decided to sleep in the hayloft. When the ghost climbed the stairs to the hayloft at night with a great deal of noise, the man was terrified after all. In the morning he told the farmer of his experience and then continued his journey. In Diegem the man went into a little café where people were playing cards. When the man came in, the card players all stormed outside. The hole this made could still be seen years later.
174523: In Landen lived a woman who could make mice.
174524: If you had been in an inn whose landlady was a witch, you were covered in vermin. A girl who had to take lunch to her father, who worked in the factory, went into the inn to fetch a bottle of beer. The landlady said to the girl: "Well, are you taking your father his food again?" and grabbed hold of her. Then the girl began to scream and fell to the ground. The parish priest had to be fetched and the friars overlazen (prayed over to lift a spell) the girl. But the girl was never quite herself again. The girl's father then went to the witch and said: "You must undo the harm you have done to my daughter at once, or I will beat you to death here." The girl was never cured and died very young.
174536: A curate could fix horses to the ground by magic.
174552: Black cats that roamed about in the evening were witches, so people believed.
174559: A boy had been to Zelk with his father. On a telephone pole under the bridge as many as a thousand cats began to screech. The boy had briefly got off the cart to relieve himself, but he quickly left again because he heard loud screeching. That was the Tillekesjacht (a spectral hunt).
174582: In Schaffen a little boy worked who could conjure mice in the church. After the priest had freed the boy from his magic power, he could no longer make mice.
174584: A man from Bassily whose aunt had died went to fetch furniture from the woman's house. The man threw a statue of Christ into a meadow because he did not want it. When the man got to his cart, he was run over and killed by a car.
174594: Everyone was afraid on the Pelsberg. A merchant from Zoutleeuw asked a man from the neighbourhood whether he would go with him, because he was afraid to cross the Pelsberg alone.
174614: One evening a man was walking from the wood to the church of Butsel. When the man was halfway, a groaning apparition jumped onto his shoulders. It was the werewolf. The man said: "Is that you? You're damn lucky I don't have my knife with me, or I'd teach you a lesson!" At that the werewolf cried: "You mustn't do that. If you make me bleed, I have to start my term all over again."
174618: One morning when she woke up, a woman found that her head was full of fat black lice. The woman combed all the lice out of her hair. There were at least two hundred. A witch had given that woman lice.
174620: In Boekhout people were driving a cart with two horses. Suddenly they could not go any further with the cart because of witchcraft. Only the next day did they get the cart moving again.
174629: Witches could put the evil hand on someone. When that happened, people put a piece of a blessed candle under their threshold, so that the witch could no longer come in. When people could not make butter, they went to the monastery to be overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell).
174645: Every night a foal came to the chapel of Zeven Weeën in Sint-Pieters-Kapelle. Four fearless boys went to have a look. But when the foal followed them, the boys jumped into a stable out of fear. The foal jumped against the stable door with its forelegs. It looked as if the foal had two torches in its eyes.
174652: Three poachers had heard that a dog often appeared in Zoutleeuw. The men sat with their guns at the ready behind a dunghill on the Ossenweg. When the dog passed by, not one of the three men was able to shoot at the animal.
174655: When people had a sick animal, they had the parish priest come to overlezen (pray over to lift a spell) it. They believed the animal had been struck by the evil hand.
174668: A sorceress walked past a house that was being demolished. A beam was to be pulled out of it. Although thirty men had been summoned for the job, the beam would not come loose.
174671: Some men were resting in the field after their meal. When a carter came by with a cart full of grain, one of the workmen said: "The cart will tip over." On the hill the cart did indeed overturn. Another time the workman predicted that the cart would get stuck halfway up the hill. That happened too. The wizard advised the carter to unhitch the horses because they had not been fed. With one finger the wizard pulled the cart along.
174692: A woman coming back from an inn met Kledde (a shape-shifting spectre) on the way and threw her apron, saying: "Unweave it first." Kledde had to unravel the cloth before he could leap on the woman. This gave the woman the chance to run away. Just after she got home she heard three loud knocks on the door.
174702: A mother who had already lost several children believed that her children had been bewitched by someone. The mother went to be overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell) by a friar, who gave her relics.
174712: In Sint-Joris-Winge a little boy of seven or eight and a young woman died of a throat ailment. A midwife used to visit those people at night. She was said to have made them ill.
174734: In the past people believed that stallichten (will-o'-the-wisps) were the souls of unbaptised children.
174744:
A man whose child was sick said to a woman: "If you don't cure that child soon, I'll throw you in the fire!"
Then the woman took a cushion with pins, pulled the pins out and left.
174745: A woman had been bewitched by a witch from Meldert.
174751: In Oppem (Brussegem) a farmer had sold his soul to the devil in exchange for a new barn, which had to be finished by the first cockcrow.
174752: A woman who was often ridden by the mare (here called the moon) felt as if something fell on her body and strangled her. The woman always heard it come up the stairs to her, but she could never see anything.
174761: If two dead people were laid out in a village at the same time, a third death would soon follow.
174783: A farmer walked worriedly through his field because he would not be able to store his harvest in his small barn. In the field the farmer met a gentleman, who promised to build a new barn in a single night on condition that the farmer would sell his most precious possession. The farmer agreed. In the evening he told his wife what he had done. At that the farmer's wife cried out: "But you have sold your soul!" Before the rooster had crowed for the first time in the morning, the farmer's wife knocked her clogs together, so that the rooster began to crow early. Because the barn was not yet finished at that moment, the farmer could keep his soul. There was still a hole in the barn that could never be closed.
174787: If you met a werewolf, you had to throw a handkerchief at the beast. The werewolf then had to unravel the handkerchief completely, so that it could not harm its victim. If you could wound a werewolf on the forehead, it took on its human form and you could recognise it. An old man who had unmasked a werewolf in this way never dared to say who the werewolf was.
174810: A rag-picker who was suspected of being a witch always came to Hoegaarden. People all hung a ring on their bell so that the witch could not come in. When one day a woman had also hung a ring on her bell, the witch patted her on the shoulder and said: "Ah, you've hung a ring too. You are bewitched." The next day the woman had a stiff shoulder, so that she could hardly move.
174846: A farmer and his wife needed a new barn, but they had no money to build it. One day the farmer said: "I would gladly sell my soul to the devil if he would build me a barn." The farmer's words had barely been spoken when the devil appeared in a stinking cloud. The devil sold his soul to the devil, on condition that the new barn would be finished the next morning before the first cockcrow. If the devil succeeded, the farmer would have to go with him to hell within seven years. The farmer's wife got up in the night, took off her clogs and knocked them together, so that the rooster woke up and began to crow. But the barn was not yet finished, for there was still a large hole of two by one metres. The devils screamed loudly and then went home.
174848: People who were bewitched sometimes said they had been ridden by the mare. A woman who could no longer walk because of witchcraft went for advice to the priest of Elingen, who helped her. The priest had told the woman: "On the ninth day the guilty one will pass by, but you must not answer him". The priest's prediction came true.
174863: A woman who went outside with her child always met her neighbour, who said: "You do have a good child!" When the woman later moved house, the child became gravely ill. The little one was always coughing and vomiting. Every night the doctors feared for the child's life. After a while the child's father decided to drive to Tongerlo. When the mother thought her husband must be about there, she saw the child was dying. She had to pick the child up and shake it. When the man came back, the child was cured for good.
174881: Anyone bewitched by a witch sometimes had a stiff arm.
174886: Stallichten (will-o'-the-wisps) were glimmers of light seen above marshes. They were luminous vapours produced by rotting. People believed such lights were the souls of children who could not get to heaven and therefore had to wander.
174935: A sorceress who had made a pact with the devil laid a piece of chocolate near a farm. Because of this the animals grew fat, for they were bewitched. The people then went to the friars and the curate. The clergymen advised them not to pick up the beets lying in the road any more.
174943: At a farm where many animals had died, a parish priest was sent for, who said: "Put some wood in the oven." Then a woman came by to ask for fire. The woman sat by the fire and kept shifting towards the flames. In the end she was forced to pull all the pins out of the animals, which put an end to the witchcraft.
174957: A witch used to live in an inn in Langdorp. When a carter drove his horse past the inn over the cobbled road, the horse suddenly could not go on. Because the horse could not be made to move in any way, the carter went to drink a glass of beer in the inn. When he came back, the horse was willing to go on again.
174960: A woman was very sad when her little nephew had died. At night the woman dreamed that the little boy was with her. The woman said: "Well, what have you come for?", to which the boy replied: "Don't you know your catechism? Then you would know where I come from!" When the woman told the priest the next day what she had experienced, he said: "The dead person you dream about is asking you to pray for him. Once you have done that, he will not appear any more." What the priest said was true.
174982: In Beert lived a man who owned evil books with which he could send a plague of rats to a house. With his books he could also summon priests or make people coming from the station lose their way. Only once those people had asked the sorcerer the way could they find their bearings again.
174985: A mother had a baby that would not drink. Because the baby was becoming completely emaciated, they went to the brown friars of Sint-Truiden, who overlazen (prayed over to lift a spell) the child. The friars also gave the people relics to put under the threshold. They were not to let a certain woman in any more. When the witch came by, she could not come in because the mother had not said: "Come on in." The witch grew angry, pulled her own hair and left again. The friars had also advised the people to cut open the child's pillow. Inside the pillow they found lots of roses. The witch had just been working on the last rose. Because that rose was not yet finished, the child did not die.
174989: Women who had given birth were not allowed to accept anything from anyone before they had been churched. A mother who had not yet been churched gave a woman in her café a glass of beer. However, she did not accept the woman's money.
175003: In Neerhespen lived a woman who liked to be near small children. The child would then cry or fall ill. In the end people became very afraid of that woman.
175004: If you put a nail from the Easter candle under the steps, no witches could come in.
175023: Some people had to come back after their death because they had failed to keep a promise. When someone else had fulfilled that promise, the ghost no longer appeared.
175040: Some people were coming back from Linkhout along the Esselse Straatje. There they were followed by two mewing cats. When one of the men walked towards the cat, the animal backed away. When the man came to a crossroads where there was a little chapel, the cat disappeared.
175041: When animals had been touched by a sorceress, they sometimes gave no milk. People to whom this happened had the friars of the Paterskerk near Halsput come, but they could not help. Then they had the friars of Affligem come. If the sorceresses knew that friars were coming, the clergymen had no power over them.
175044: A mother was visited by a neighbour woman who rubbed her little son's head and said: "What a lovely child!" After that the child would not grow any more. The mother had the friars come, who put blessed palm under the door and advised the woman not to say "Come on in" to anyone. After that the boy gradually recovered.
175050: If you heard magpies chattering around you, misfortune would follow.
175071: Between Oud-Heverlee and the Zoet Water stood a small chapel with 'twin trees' (?) dedicated to Saint Anne. A man walking past one evening saw a large black man coming towards him, with hands like claws and eyes like balls of fire. The black figure walked past the frightened man without harming him.
175082: In the baron's castle in Meldert a returned dead person always appeared at night in the form of a black lady. Music could then always be heard in the castle. A witheer (a Norbertine canon, believed able to drive out spirits) who had been called to the castle could not keep the ghost away. One evening the baron and baroness were followed all the way into their bedroom by a tall lady dressed in black. Since then there has been no more haunting in the castle. A murder had probably taken place in that castle.
175088: One winter night a man was woken by loud knocking. When the man was again woken by the knocking the next day, he decided to go to the priest. The priest advised the man not to believe in such things. Some time before, the man had inherited money and had promised to give part of it to the church. However, the man had not done so. On the priest's advice the man decided to have a mass said. During the night after the man had requested the mass, he heard the knocking again, together with the ringing of the bell used during mass. Since then the man has heard nothing strange.
175107: In the old days people said that a little white rabbit could be seen in Zoutleeuw every evening. A boy who had to go to Zoutleeuw one evening hoped to finally see the rabbit, but he did not see it.
175111: If people saw a stallicht (a mysterious light in the stable), they believed disaster was coming.
175115:
A man who saw a cat sitting there on his way home in the evening often believed that it was a witch sitting there.
One could only become a witch after reaching a certain age.
A woman had hens that were bewitched. The animals always ran off and laid their eggs along the edge of the woods.
175122: People who were often visited by a witch put a piece of a blessed candle under their door, so that the witch could no longer come in.
175126: A woman whose seven children always fell ill after her mother had visited went with the children to the friars of Affligem. When the friars asked whether she suspected anyone, she answered: "Yes, my own mother." The mother bewitched the children by means of a doll into which she stuck pins.
175136: On a farm the hens stopped laying eggs after a strange woman had come to feed them.
175144: Opposite the church of Eliksem stood a clay house with a little shrine to Our Lady on its front. One day the husband of the woman who lived there was seriously ill. The woman promised to go on pilgrimage to the Black Our Lady of Halle. After the woman had made that promise, her husband's health gradually improved. Once her husband had recovered, however, the woman no longer thought of the promised pilgrimage. One evening the woman came back from the shop and saw a large black dog lying next to the door of her house. The woman did not dare to pass the dog and could not chase the animal away. The woman asked her neighbour for advice, who told her to throw a slice of bread to the dog so that the animal would run off. The dog, however, lay there unperturbed, so the woman called to her husband: "Open the window at the back of the house, so I can crawl in that way. If I come through the door, the dog might slip inside." The next morning the dog had vanished, but every evening it was lying there again. One day the woman remembered the promise she had made. After she had gone on pilgrimage to Halle, she no longer saw the dog.
175159:
There used to be barracks at a spot in Aarschot. Some people claimed that witches lived there.
In 2003 there were still people in Aarschot who did not dare go outside for the rest of the day if they had seen a black cat.
175184: Some people whose child was bewitched went to the heksenmannetje (witch doctor) of Meldert. The heksenmannetje said to the parents: "Go home. Your child will be dead. Then you must cut open the child's pillow." In the pillow the parents found lots of witch's pins. The heksenmannetje had also foretold that the witch would come by. The people had to put a bundle of brushwood on the fire and threaten to burn the witch. Then she would ask forgiveness. And so it happened.
175209: A man carrying a sack of bran got lost in the fog. In the past, people who got lost often believed they had been ridden by the mare.
175211: A girl who had sore eyes and always cried at night had been bewitched by a sorceress. At night the child saw a horse's head approaching, which poked its ears into her eyes. The child's parents went to a fortune-teller, who said: "At a certain time the woman who bewitched your child will come by to ask for something." The woman did indeed come at the predicted time. The child's mother had boiling water ready to pour over the sorceress, but when the woman stood in front of her, she did not dare.
175228: The P. family's house was haunted. The plates and cups could always be heard rattling in the cupboard. The woman who used to live in the house had promised to go on pilgrimage if her husband came back unharmed from the First World War.
175231: A man who was out in the evening was suspected of being a pleudde (a shape-shifting sorcerer). When that man passed a hedge, a cat jumped out and he kicked at the animal. The animal leapt in front of the man's feet until he was home. The man kicked at the animal and was not afraid.
175233: A man taking plants to the market in Vilvoorde was afraid of a cat that kept walking around his legs the whole time. The man's hair turned grey from fear.
175238: On a farm where many horses died, the misfortune was blamed on a witch who lived nearby. The farm was overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell) by a friar. The clergyman told the people to break up the floors of the stables. There they found poisonous toads that were killing the horses. Even so, that woman was still suspected of being a witch.
175268: Two drunkards coming back from Leuven late in the evening saw a parish priest in Linden. The clergyman claimed he was doing his night round, and the drunkards said: "You don't need to go back. Come and sleep at our place." When the drunkards lit the light in their house, they saw that the priest had horse's legs with horseshoes. It was the devil!
175280: A barber who lived by the station in Ketsingen went to work in Plutsingen (a hamlet of Heikruis) every Sunday. When he came home one evening, three little white rabbits jumped out in front of him. The man kicked at one of them, but the animal would not be chased off. In the end the man was surrounded by countless little rabbits, so that he began to believe evil had something to do with it. When he got home he was drenched in sweat. The next morning his hair had turned completely white. Six months later the man died from the effects of the fright he had suffered.
175291: A woman had decided to give a piece of land to her godson on condition that he would have a mass said when she died. When the woman died, however, no mass was said. At night the man always woke up because there was knocking against his bed. After the man had a mass said, the knocking stopped.
175301: A widow from Meldert came to a farm in Sluizen to fetch butter and milk. The farmer who lived there felt someone shaking his bed at night and heard chains rattling. He also heard noise in his stables and found that all his animals had been untied. A friar advised the farmer always to make the widow pay for what she took, even if it was only a centime. When the farmer did this, he had no more trouble.
175336: A woman was always visited by the ghost of her mother, who had died of grief because her sister wanted nothing more to do with her. The dead woman asked for a prayer or a mass to be said for her. After the woman said to the ghost of her dead mother one night: "I am happy", the ghost appeared no more.
175339: A woman was ridden by the mare every night at twelve o'clock. Victims of the mare tried to call out, but could not make a sound.
175357: If the church bells of Sint-Martens-Lennik and Sint-Kwintens-Lennik rang at the same time, there would soon be a death in one of the two parishes.
175365: A farmer did not have enough room in his barn to store the produce of his rich harvest. In the field the farmer met a gentleman, who said to him: "If you sell me your most precious possession, I will help you." That gentleman was the devil, who wanted to get hold of the man's soul. The farmer agreed to the proposal on condition that the barn would be finished before the first cockcrow the next morning. When he got home, the farmer told his wife what he had done. Before daybreak the farmer's wife got up, walked to the henhouse and began knocking her clogs together there. This made the rooster crow early. Because the barn was not yet finished at that moment, the devil lost his right to the man's soul. In the roof of the devil's barn there was still a hole that could never be closed.
175383: A woman whose ten-month-old child was ill went to several doctors, who all found that the child had pneumonia. But a relative of the woman said: "Come with me to Charleroi. Your child doesn't have pneumonia." The night before the woman was to go to Charleroi, she heard knocking and ringing in her house. The next day both women went to a fortune teller who lived in Charleroi. Under the fortune teller's table lay a large black dog. When the fortune teller predicted that the child would live only three more days, the mother had a priest read prayers over her little son. The clergyman took mother and child to the chapel, where he hung a chasuble over the child and prayed until the sweat rolled down his face. "The child will not die," said the priest, and he also promised to say a Mass, for which the mother paid three francs. One day the mother saw a toad in the house. The woman struck off the animal's legs. The next night the woman experienced strange things. The toad had vanished. In the lamp in the house three flames sometimes appeared, and the child was very restless, as if it saw something strange. The woman laid the bread knife beside her and called out: "If there's something there, show yourself, you rascal!" In the stable someone threw a ball about. The child was flung from its mother's hands and thrown against the wall. This game went on for no less than ten months. On top of that the people's house burned down, so they had to move in with someone else. At midnight the child always began to cry and a toad could be heard screaming. The man and woman went to the brown friars of Hasselt, who asked: "Who do you think it is?", to which the father answered: "My mother." "She will do you no more harm," said the friar. On their way home the man and woman heard rumbling the whole time. They were followed by the witch, but did not see her. After that the witch still sometimes walked past the child saying: "God, what a lovely curly head!", but the mother then pretended not to hear. When the witch lay on her deathbed, she had all her relatives come to her, except her son and her daughter-in-law. She had never been able to bear that her son had married that woman.
175428: Two friends had planned to go to the chapel of Bijstand in Zétrud. One of the girls died before she had been to the chapel. From then on the friend heard "Oo, oo, oo" called at her window every night. The friend immediately went to the chapel of Bijstand, where she lit a candle for the dead girl. After that she no longer heard strange noises at night.
175434: A man from Humbeek went on pilgrimages to Oppem on behalf of people for payment. When the man came back slightly drunk one night, he saw a brooding hen with chicks sitting on the road. Since the man owned only a goat, he decided to take the hen with him. At home he shut the hen and chicks in the stable and went to sleep. At midnight, however, the man heard a loud growling. He looked through the window and saw a devil with twelve little devils sitting in the stable. The next morning the man went to tell the priest what had happened to him. The priest said to him: "Yes, that is your punishment for stealing. If you wait until next night, you will see that the devil turns back into a hen with chicks. You must then take that hen back to the place where you got them." The man was also given the priest's stole to protect himself on his way. The next night the man took the hen and chicks back. He had barely set the animals down when they turned into devils again. The man held the stole in front of him for protection and walked home backwards.
175437: By the Galgerstraatje in Hekelgem there used to be a castle. Criminals were hanged on the gallows by the lord of the castle. The corpses of the dead were thrown into the devil's pits. At night the ghosts of the dead could be heard making noise; they had been turned into devils as punishment for their crimes.
175442: A woman who had bought a large piece of ham was visited by a sorceress. Afterwards the ham was rotten. The woman went to the friars of Affligem. After that no more food went bad in her house.
175474: A zwarte madam (black lady) was a sorceress. A zwarte madam could put the evil hand on someone. Such people then fell ill. If a sorceress had been in the stables and a cow fell ill afterwards, people went on pilgrimage to Diegem, Leest or Londerzeel.
175481: In Hoegaarden lived a woman said to be a witch. Her hair always hung in her face. After this witch had bewitched a little dog, the animal walked on three legs instead of four. The witch had picked up the little dog three times and slammed it on the ground.
175487: A witch could only be shot down with a gun on which a blessed palm sprig had been placed.
175496: A sixty-five-year-old man had died after an illness of three weeks. As was the custom, the man's coffin was kept at home for a few days. On the third day a knocking was heard. When the coffin was opened, it turned out that the man had come back to life. The man lived for another eight years after that.
175498: Some people believed that black cats were witches.
175531: A man coming back from Kattenbroek through the snow at nightfall in winter got lost and wandered about until midnight. Then the man saw that he was standing by the mill and had only five minutes left to walk to his house. The man had been ridden by the mare.
175540: A boy who had been to the fair in Neerwinden with his girlfriend passed the little chapel of the Heilig Kruiske with her at midnight. There the boy said: "I have to relieve myself. You stay here for a moment. Should a dog or a werewolf come at you, throw this handkerchief at its jaws and you will be unharmed." The girl was afraid, but when a werewolf appeared a little later, she threw the handkerchief at the animal's jaws, as her boyfriend had advised. When she got home the girl noticed that her boyfriend had the fibres of the handkerchief between his teeth.
175552: Someone came into an inn in Bassily and said: "Give us three drinks", to which the landlady replied: "But there are only two of you". The man threw the third drink at the statue of Christ and shouted: "Now he has one too!" The next day that man fell into a brewer's vat.
175561: A man had gone to gather stones from the field on the Keienberg. The man sat at the top of the hill and threw the stones down when someone passed by. Because of this, that passer-by thought the place was haunted.
175563: A man could make white mice without tails appear in the house by tying a knife into a handkerchief. After the priest had baptised the man again, he had lost his magic power.
175576: On a farm there were three goats. When a sorceress had been with the goats and pulled a tuft of hair from one of them, the goats were bewitched. One day the farmer went with a hen to the white canons of Gent. The friars said to the man: "Go home, and when you get home all your animals will be in good health. On your way home you will meet a hen." And so it happened.
175581: A man had holy water bottles shaped like a statuette of Mary. Such bottles always had to be filled three-quarters full. A farmer was always visited at midday by a woman who came to bring the parish newsletter. Because the farmer was just eating then, he had no time to offer the woman a glass of water. One day the farmer held a bottle of holy water in front of him. After that the woman never came by again.
175601: In the Lobos a man's horse stood still because it could not go on. That must have been witchcraft.
175604: A man and a woman came across a pretty little cat on their way. They took the animal with them and put it under a manure tub. The next day the man said to his father: "I brought home a pretty cat and she was sitting in her shift under that tub." That cat was a witch.
175636: A man from Mijlbeek could catch rats. A farmer who did not want to pay for his services was told: "You'll end up paying five cents a rat!" A week later there were at least fifty rats running around the farm.
175682: In 1940 three girls who lived next door to each other died in Sint-Joris-Winge. People believed that someone had put the evil hand on those girls.
175687: Two men were transporting chickens with a cart pulled by one dog. When the men saw a dog along the way, they grabbed it and harnessed it to the cart. But the men's own dog became very frightened, so one of the men said: "Let that dog go again, for the animal is bewitched." The other followed this advice, after which the men's dog calmed down again.
175690: In Okselaar there once lived a witch who walked about at night with a pitchfork. There was also a wizard who could open the locked church door by throwing his cap against it.
175694: Witches could make people blind by touching their face.
175702: Every evening in Grimbergen a man met a finely dressed lady. One evening the man grabbed the lady by the neck. A moment later the man had the lady's head in his hands, but the rest of her body had vanished.
175708: In Onze-Lieve-Vrouw-Lombeek lived a woman suspected of being a sorceress. A man was bewitched after he had gone to work for her and she had given him a slice of bread. As a result the man could hardly see anything any more.
175741: Black cats were often seen near a woman from Vlezenbeek.
175746: In the past people believed it was best not to sleep with the shutters up. If one did, one could fall victim to the mare.
175749: In Wespelaar a woman had given birth. When her husband was walking home, he met a witch, who said: "It's already here." Yet that witch had not been in the house where the child was born.
175750: A farm in the Driesstraat in Brussegem used to be haunted. At night the ghosts rode around outside with a calf.
175769: People who were ridden by the mare had a bad dream. They tried to walk but made no progress, or tried to call out but no sound came.
175806: In Rodenem (Halle) lived a man who drank a lot. A woman from the village was always angry with that man. When the man had died, his hearse drove past that woman's house. Right at that spot the horses shied back and the hearse could not go on.
175811: A woman went on a pilgrimage to Korbeek-Dijle with a child from the village who had fallen ill through sorcery. On the way the woman met a witch, who gave the child a stern look. The pilgrimage did not help, for the child died.
175847: If you had been touched by a witch, you always had to strike higher to break her power.
175865: The Warande was haunted. The castle had been fired upon by the counts who lived at the castle of Rummen. Later the castle was demolished. At night a coach left the castle and drove to the village.
175874: On a castle farm worked a gardener who every evening heard stones being thrown against the gate. When people went to look, the noise stopped there, but stones started being thrown against the other gate. The matter was investigated, but nothing came of it. People came from far and wide to look at the haunted castle. However, after a family living in the castle moved out at Berchem fair, the castle was never haunted again. People therefore believed that that man had caused the haunting by means of electricity. In that way he had wanted to lower the value of the castle so that he could buy it cheaply.
175902: In Opwijk lived a witch who owned books. A farmer who was taking his cow to be bred had to pass that witch's house. Later that day, when the farmer had been home with his cow for two hours, the animal began to grow restless. The farmer sent for the vet, who said: "There is evil at work here." The farmer went to the fathers of Affligem, who gave him a medal and blessed bread. The farmer also had to do a nine-day penance. Less than three months later, the people who had done this to the farmer were struck by the same misfortune. They too went to the monastery and were given the same advice.
175905: A witch used to live in Molenbeek. During the First World War the Germans asked the witch whether she could move her wagon, which was standing on the road. The witch said the wagon was not allowed to stand anywhere else. The Germans wanted to move the wagon themselves, but however they tried, they could not.
175911: In church someone had placed a blessed candle under a witch's chair. Because of this the witch could not get out.
