175922: A witch from Sint-Lambrechts-Woluwe brought misfortune to many people. A farmer's wife's rabbits kept dying, until it was finally decided to have the farm exorcised. Some people who walked past the witch's house crossed their hands over their chest and said: "What is God's is kept by God."
175925:
A neighbour always came to visit at a farm. When the farmer's wife was churning butter, the neighbour said she would not be able to make butter. And so it was. The farmer's wife wanted to go and see whether other people nearby could churn butter, but the neighbour said: "No, the others have no butter either." That was true.
The farmer's wife always breastfed her little daughter. Because of this the child had got a red rash around her mouth. When the priest once met the mother and child, he saw the rash and said it was witchcraft. The clergyman also said that the witch would come to ask for something and that the farmer's wife must give her nothing. Some time later the witch did indeed come to ask for something. When the farmer's wife refused to give it, the witch thought to herself: 'Just wait, I'll get you yet.' After that the butter failed again.
The child, however, was cured and could be breastfed again.
175933: A black cat always sat on the doorstep of a house in Sint-Stevens-Woluwe. When the man chased the cat away one evening, the animal said: "You will regret that!" A few days later the man died.
175938: People who felt unwell or had a lot of misfortune said they were ridden by the mare. When people had misfortune in their stable, they believed they were bewitched. Some friars and priests went to sprinkle houses with holy water to protect the occupants against witchcraft.
175949: People who had made a promise and then died had to come back after their death to fulfil that promise.
175955: Some people who were going to cut fodder near the airfield met a witch on the way, who said: "But it is far too cold to cut fodder!" However hard the people tried, they could not cut any fodder.
175963: In the card game there was a man who always won. Another player bent down and saw that the fellow wore pointed shoes. At that same moment the man grew little horns. After the frightened player had said: "In the name of the Lord!", the man had vanished.
175981: In Sint-Pieters-Rode lived a witch who sometimes flew to a stable in the form of a crow and caused misfortune there. One morning a farmer managed to shoot down the crow. A few hours later the farmer saw a woman from the village whose arm was covered in blood.
176006: At the stroke of midnight the children in a house in the Biezenweide in Halle began to cry. The children saw a figure standing there that hit them, but the other people could see nothing. The children fell ill and two of them even died. When the fathers came to exorcise the children, they were drenched in sweat. One day a father said to the mother of one of the children: "The culprit is someone who often comes into this house." Some women often came to the woman's house to get plants. Those women would then stay for a cup of coffee. The father gave the mother a candle, which she had to crumble under the visitors' chair. The culprit would then be unable to stand up. The woman the mother suspected, however, was able to get up from her chair. The mother never again had the chance to unmask the witch, and she also felt there was little point any more, since she had already suffered so much misery.
176009: In Landen lived a witch who could give people lice or an eye disease. If you had been touched by that witch, you were bewitched. A man who had shot a poacher dead came to live next door to that witch. Within two days the man was covered in lice.
176010: In the old days it was a bad sign if thirteen people sat at table together.
176030:
A twenty-year-old young man always met a foal when he came back from visiting his girlfriend. One day the young man shot at the foal with his gun, and it then turned into a crow. When he got home, the young man went to the priest, who gave him a relic and advised him to pray and do penance. "The woman who comes to wash her hands in the tub here is the guilty one," the clergyman claimed. That is how the man discovered that his own maid was the witch. The maid was of course dismissed on the spot.
Later she was shot dead north of Tienen when she appeared in the form of a magpie. A farmer had shot the magpie there because the animal always sat in his trees and frightened his horses.
176037: A man had moved a boundary post to have a bigger piece of field. One day, while picking cherries, the man fell out of the tree and landed on the boundary post he had moved. He was killed instantly. From then on the man had to haunt that spot every night. The ghost pulled up the boundary post and called: "Where shall I carry it? Where shall I carry it?" After a drunkard answered one night: "Carry it back to the place where you got it!", the ghost appeared no more.
176042: A man who was ridden by the mare saw a black cat every evening. After he tied some medals with a cord around the leg of his bed, he was no longer troubled by the mare.
176053: A newly married couple saw a fat man in a cap approaching, walking backwards. The man had been bewitched and could therefore walk backwards as fast as forwards.
176077: Some boys who had been visiting their girlfriends in Neerlanden on a Sunday evening went for a chat in a café in Wezeren. At a certain moment the boys decided to go home. They had leaned their bicycles outside against the windowsill. When they came out, they found that the wheels of their bicycles were completely bent, so that they could no longer be ridden. After that incident the café landlady never had any customers again.
176080: On a farm there was a big ginger tomcat. Every month one of the animals on that farm died. Whenever a cow was due to calve, the calf always died. Finally the people went to an exorcist in Rillaar. Then they took the train to Leuven to fetch the brown friars. The friars knelt praying until they were drenched in sweat. One of the friars said: "I need a living creature to put the evil on." The friar put the evil on the ginger tomcat. An hour later the cat was completely emaciated. The cat then had to be buried alive. Shortly afterwards the farm burned down. The farmer and his wife then went to a healer from Rillaar, after which the witchcraft came to an end.
176083: Two sisters who had to go and fetch their uncle one evening saw a big light by the side of the road. The girls did not dare go on because they thought the light was a stallicht (will-o'-the-wisp). That was a lost child that had no soul. In reality the light was a candle their brother had lit to frighten his sisters.
176089:
In the past people often got lost on the unlit country lanes. A man who worked a lot in the woods in winter cycled home in the evenings. One evening the man saw a pedestrian taking a back road. That pedestrian did not reach his home until the next morning. The man had sat down behind a beet clamp to shelter from the wind, but he had not dared to knock at the farm to ask the way.
People who got lost believed they had been bewitched.
176116: A woman wanted to use her whistling kettle to make coffee. But the kettle began to smoke, whereupon a man said: "Look, there's evil in that. You must go to mass and be the last to stay sitting in the church. There you will see the person who bewitched the kettle. But you must stick the nail of an Easter candle under the steps. The witch will then be unable to leave the church."
176118: A farmer who had no barn to store his grain made a pact with the devil, who would build him a barn before the first cockcrow. But when the rooster crowed in the morning, there was still a hole in the barn, so the farmer could keep his soul.
176122:
At midnight a mass was said at a castle in Sint-Pieters-Rode. A horse-drawn coach could then be seen driving there. The people in the coach were going to the mass at the castle.
In the past it was the custom for the parish priest to go and say mass at the castle. It was believed that this priest was having an affair with the countess who lived at the castle.
176143: A woman who had been to the shop had put all her purchases in her apron. On the way she was hindered by a cat running under her feet. The woman kicked at the cat, which then leapt up at her. It was a witch who had turned herself into a cat. When the woman got home, she no longer saw the cat, and in her fright she dropped her purchases on the ground.
176144: A witch from Meusegem often turned herself into a cat that sat meowing. Witches could also take the shape of dogs.
176148: People whose eight-year-old son was ill put a nail from the Easter candle under the threshold. They suspected a neighbour of having bewitched their son.
176149: When children met a witch, they quickly made the sign of the cross to protect themselves against her magic. When the witch gave them strawberries, they did not eat them.
176167: A black cat could be a witch in animal shape.
176179: In Goetsenhoven lived a woman who was said to be a witch. People who were touched by that witch fell ill or met with misfortune.
176222: A woman came to visit a farm. A mother who worked on that farm was convinced that this woman had bewitched her child. That day the woman went into the kitchen, where a pot of red cabbage stood. The farmer's wife's daughter lifted the lid of the pot and said: "Mother, look how much water there is on that red cabbage!" The visitor said: "Ah, have you made red cabbage? That's tasty!" A moment later the pot was completely burnt black.
176225:
Stallichten (will-o'-the-wisps) or glow-worms appeared in the dark above a lake or a stinking pit. People believed they were will-o'-the-wisps. These were wandering souls from hell or purgatory. People also took a shooting star to be a wandering soul.
Usually stallichten were just vapours.
176269: A wizard's brother had fixed someone to the ground by magic. But because he no longer knew how to release his victim, the wizard himself had to come.
176315: A girl had met a boy at the fair in Landen. At midnight the boy said to the girl: "I have to leave, because I still have to walk home." On her way home the girl met a dog. She threw her handkerchief at the beast and was unharmed. When she saw her boyfriend again in a dance hall some time later, she noticed that he had the threads of the handkerchief between his teeth. The girl ended the relationship at once.
176317: On a farm in Halmaal there worked two farmhands who always played cards in the evening. One day one of them said: "If I die before you, you must go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel for me. If you die before me, I will go on pilgrimage for you." When one of the farmhands died, the other had already forgotten his promise. During his card evening the farmhand suddenly became so tired that he went home early. As soon as he lay in his bed in the horse stable, he saw a little light flying around. Frightened, he asked the light what it wanted. A voice rang out and said: "What I want is for you to keep your promise and go with me to Scherpenheuvel. As long as you have not done so, I must suffer." The next moment the light had vanished. The horses in the stable were extremely agitated. When the farmhand went on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel, he sweated as if he were carrying a load of a hundred kilos on his back. After making the promised pilgrimage, the farmhand entered a monastery.
176319: In Sint-Kwintens-Lennik lived a woman suspected of being a witch. A drunkard who met this woman at the annual fair challenged the witch by saying she could do nothing to him. The witch replied that he would not be laughing the next day. The next morning the man got up with a bad hangover. He wanted to eat, but could not. Because a week later the man still could not eat, he sent for the doctor. The doctor, however, could not help. The man went to the curate, who advised him to go to the fathers of Affligem. One of the fathers, who had special powers, said to the man: "Go home. On the way you will meet the witch, but she will not be able to do anything to you. Just keep riding." On his way home the man did indeed get past the witch's house without any trouble. After that the witch never bothered him again.
176332: On a farm that had been struck by the evil hand, a beautiful pheasant was seen one morning, which vanished a few moments later. After that the calves on the farm ran up against the walls in fear and then died. A sow carrying thirteen piglets died eight days before they were due to be born. The farmer consulted the parish priest, who had to ask the bishop's permission before he could come and exorcise the stable. Three days later the priest came in a white robe. He exorcised all the stables, sweating terribly as he did so. While the priest was at work, a female rag-picker walked past. The clergyman was able to free the farm from the evil hand.
176343: The devil with his long tail really existed. Whenever he did something, fire could be seen everywhere.
176347: In Wezembeek lived a witch who made all the chicks on a farm die. The people then had to send for a Passionist to exorcise the stable and break the witch's power.
176349: A woman often woke at night from a nightmare and then saw an alvermannetje (elf-like little man) walking on the linen cupboard and vanishing a moment later. The woman had already been on a pilgrimage, but it had not helped. One day the woman's husband went to the fathers of Averbode. The man had to pray a number of Hail Marys and Our Fathers and pay some chair money. Then he had to sit in a small booth. Behind him hung a closed curtain. A father had said to the man: "When that curtain opens, you will see someone pass by in the mirror in front of you. But on no account may you look round." When the curtain was opened, the man did indeed see someone he knew. After he had said the necessary prayers, his wife slept soundly from then on.
176367: Three of a woman's children died after a witch had said at their birth: "Oh, what a lovely baby!"
176372: A carter suddenly could not go on with his horses when a sorceress was standing on the road. After a passer-by had made the sign of the cross, the horses could suddenly go on again.
176381: A woman who was staying in Westerlo was always followed by a cartwheel when she walked through the woods.
176399: A woman coming back from the fair in Hoegaarden found a pretty cat in Nerm. She picked up the cat and carried it in her skirt. The animal, however, grew heavier and heavier. By the church in Sluizen the cat had turned into a fat dog.
176408: A farmer who had moved the boundary post of his land haunted at midnight after his death with a boundary post in his hand, calling: "Where must I take this boundary post?" One night a drunkard answered: "Put the boundary post where you got it!" Since then the haunting farmer has not been seen again.
176455: A man working somewhere got a pat on the shoulder from someone. After that the man lost his way. He kept ending up at the same place, so he decided to go and ask someone the way.
176464: In a house, sounds were heard at night as if chairs were being moved. In the morning people found that the chairs were indeed in a different place.
176468: A woman came peddling wool at the Halsput. Whenever that woman went outside, she always briefly stroked the cow's back. After a while the people who lived there could no longer make butter. They then sent for a father from Affligem to exorcise the house, after which they could churn butter again.
176473: A twenty-one-year-old man who had just become a father had to go and buy a cradle for his child. As the man walked home with the cradle on his head, he met a woman, who pulled at the cradle and said: "Well, have you had a child?" The man hurried home with the cradle and laid his child in it. But the child lay crying in the cradle all night. One day the father had a visit from a woman, to whom he told what had happened when he came home with the cradle. The woman fiddled briefly with the mattress in the cradle. After that the baby never cried in that cradle again.
176497: People who believed they had been bewitched by witches went to the fathers.
176506: One evening a whole lot of black cats were seen walking in the Heidestraat in Hamme. People believed those cats were witches.
176521: A woman suspected that someone who came to visit her was a witch. One day the woman simply left that visitor standing at the door. The visitor had been to England and was going to bring fabric for the woman. But the woman did not want to accept anything from her.
176527: In Kampenhout lived a woman who always carried a black cat with her. One day the black cat was burnt. Afterwards it was found that the woman herself also had burns.
176573: In Dworp lived a girl whose mother was a sorceress. That girl sat at the window for thirty or forty years because she could not walk. One day the girl went on pilgrimage to Lourdes. When she came back, she could walk. People believed the mother had bewitched the girl so she could not move.
176584: In Webbekom a woman is said to have been unmasked as a witch because she wore a bandage around her head after she had been wounded in the form of an animal.
176593: On a farm where the doors were always locked in the evening, every morning a figure was seen sitting above the fireplace. Those people had a lot of bad luck. Their horse cart would not move forward.
176608: Returning dead with a sheet over their heads appeared in the churchyard.
176621: If you had broken a mirror, misfortune would follow.
176655: A farmer sold his soul to the devil because he needed a barn to store his harvest. The barn had to be finished at six o'clock on Saturday evening. When there was still a hole in the barn, the farmer's wife ran outside and clapped her hands, so that the rooster began to crow. The farmer's wife cried: "Look, time is up. You will not get my husband's soul, because the barn is not finished!" The devils could no longer close the hole and had to leave.
176671:
A farm in the Ourystraat was haunted. Since the farm was zwart goed (confiscated church property), that was not surprising. At night a white spirit appeared. The doors would then fly open and the furniture changed places. The priest had advised the people to say: "If you are of the devil, disappear. If you are of God, speak."
Somehow the haunting stopped at a certain moment.
176683: Anyone out on the street late in the evening could sometimes feel a werewolf jump onto their neck. If you could strike the werewolf until it bled, he turned into a human.
176685: Along the Steenweg to Kester stood a house where the cow was sometimes tied to the manger. A farmer did not dare walk past it because there was a well there and he was afraid the witches would throw him into it.
176725: One evening a girl went for a walk with her boyfriend. At a certain moment the boyfriend said to her: "If you ever meet Klerre (a shape-shifting spectre), take off your apron and throw it over his head. Then Klerre won't be able to harm you." A little later the boy disappeared for a moment because he had to relieve himself. The girl had taken only a few steps when she met Klerre. She did as the boy had advised and took off her apron. Klerre tore the cloth into a thousand pieces. Further on the girl was overtaken by her boyfriend, who had the threads of her apron between his teeth. That is how the girl found out that she was in a relationship with Klerre.
176726: In marshy meadows will-o'-the-wisps were often seen floating about, making a squeaking sound. Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of unbaptised children. After a while the will-o'-the-wisp disappeared back into the ground it came from. The lights never harmed anyone.
176731: If people dropped something, they believed misfortune would follow. It was also dangerous to lay crossed knives on the table. Crossing a knife with a fork was not allowed either.
176735: In a house a child had been struck by the evil hand. After the house had been exorcised, the child recovered.
176779: A man coming back from the fair at Bekkevoort came to a little chapel on the Oude Tiensebaan and said to Our Lady: "You've stood here long enough with that crown on your neck. I'll carry it for a while". The next day the man could no longer speak or walk. He could only walk backwards while drooling.
176797:
A girl from Neerhespen had married a rich man from Overwinden. When the girl and her husband were walking in a carnival procession, she threw confetti at a woman from the village, who then said: "You didn't do that for nothing! It won't be long in coming!" Two weeks later the young couple's house was sold.
A man who was in a relationship with the daughter of that same witch always had a pale complexion. The man was killed in the war.
176835: The stalkaarsen (will-o'-the-wisps) sometimes seen along the rivers were the souls of children who had died unbaptised. If the lights asked to be baptised in the evening, you had to say: "I baptise you alone." Otherwise you were overwhelmed by lights that you could never baptise all of.
176846: In Heikruis near the Kattenbos in Bogaarden, the cats flew through the air. Those cats were witches.
176857: A woman who was home alone with her children because her husband had to work experienced strange things in her house. All the doors stood open, even in the attic. In the cellar the water was turned off. The lamps had also been turned off, so there was no light in the house. The woman never found out who was responsible for this teasing.
176862: On a farm there was joy over the birth of a calf. Some farmhands kept watch by the stable when they suddenly saw a bull standing right in front of them. Assuming it was a bull that had broken loose, the farmhands put the animal in the stable. The next day the bull had disappeared and the calf lay dead. It was a witch who had turned herself into a bull to get to the calf.
176871: The Russian general Orloff and a priest agreed that whichever of them died first would return after his death to tell what things were like in the hereafter. After the priest had died, the general was sitting in his drawing room one evening. Suddenly a dark cloud appeared and the general heard a voice call: "Orloff, Orloff, I am in hell. I am in hell."
176873: A woman had slaughtered a pig in a time of poverty. The woman gave a ham to a neighbour. Shortly afterwards the woman's baby began to cry. The woman went with her child to Kortenaken. There she was told: "The child has received something from someone and it will die." And the child really did die.
176874: A boy was always being beaten by a witch whom only he could see. The parents went to the white fathers of Ghent for the boy. The fathers came to exorcise the boy and gave the neighbours biscuits against the evil. The last time the witch came to beat the boy, she was flung back and forth between the chairs and sweated terribly. Then the boy saw the witch leave, fall into the water a little further on and drown. The boy died at the age of fifteen.
176886: A girl was peeling potatoes because her mother was ill in bed, when a woman came by and asked for a slice of bread. The girl gave her a slice and the woman said: "It's hard having someone ill in the house when you otherwise want for nothing. The eggs are there in the cupboard and the meat is hanging on the hook round the corner." The girl did not understand how the beggar woman could know that. After the beggar woman had left, the girl could hardly walk. Later that day a woman from Scherpenheuvel came asking for the leftovers from lunch. The girl said she had no potatoes left, but could give her some soup. When the woman had gone, the girl found that she had left behind a box of matches. The girl urged everyone not to use a single one of those matches. The following week the girl gave the woman her matches back. The woman replied: "You can keep them, I can't do anything with them anyway." But the girl insisted until the woman took the box. Who knows what would have happened if she had used the matches...
176907:
A miller and a farmer mocked a statue of Saint Rumoldus, who was depicted with a dog holding a mastel (a ring-shaped bread) in its mouth. Afterwards the miller saw dogs everywhere among his sacks of grain. Other people could not see those dogs. The miller, whose inn was completely ruined, was told by the priest that he would commit suicide. Later he did indeed hang himself in the town hall of Itterbeek.
The farmer who had mocked the statue could not get a single ridge tile onto his roof.
176928: A boy had to go to Schakkebroek for a woman, because he was not afraid of witches. For in Rummen lived a woman who could cover people in lice or make it so they could no longer walk properly.
176930: Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of unbaptised children who came to haunt.
176948: A woman worked as a maid for a professor in the Blijde-Inkomststraat. One day the maid's child fell seriously ill. Because the doctor could not help, the maid went to the parish priest, who advised her to go on a pilgrimage. The clergyman foretold that on the way the maid would meet someone who would want to give her a shawl for the child. On no account was she to accept that shawl. The maid went on the pilgrimage and followed the priest's advice. When the child recovered shortly afterwards, the maid sat with her baby on a bench along the Boulevard. Suddenly the woman she had met on her pilgrimage came walking up. The woman touched the child. That evening the child was ill again. The maid went back to the priest, but he said that this time he could not help her. Shortly afterwards the child died. At night the maid always heard music above her head, as if people were dancing in the attic. In the end the maid moved to Brussels, where she experienced nothing strange any more.
176971: A woman had a newborn baby that cried all night long. The doctor was called, but he could find nothing wrong. Four or five days later knocking was heard on the roof. The mother went to look in the street, but saw nothing. They consulted the fathers of Affligem, who said: "Listen, a woman regularly comes to your house to look at the child. You must keep that woman out of your house by putting a piece of blessed candle under the threshold." The people followed the father's advice. When the witch later passed by and they said: "Come on, come in and have a look at our baby," the witch replied: "I have no time today." The witch never came in again. The child's father had once called her a 'filthy redhead'. But the child never became fully healthy. It had been bewitched when the witch touched it on the head.
176986: An old farmer's wife from Hakendover stood next to a neighbour watching a house burn. The farmer's wife took the neighbour by the arm and said: "Oh, you're here too!" When she got home, the neighbour found that she was covered in lice.
176991: Black cats were incarnations of the devil.
177012: A man who always swore had to fetch his books at the small chapel, where two devils were waiting for him. But the man did not dare speak to the devils and hurried back home. The devils, however, had crept into his house and smashed everything there. Only when people had read the Gospel of Saint John did the devils leave.
177013:
In a house all sorts of things were thrown down from the walls at night. Because there was an evil book in that house, the priest was sent for. The clergyman threw the book into the stove to burn it. But when the priest was five kilometres away, the book was already back. The fathers of Sint-Truiden came to read over the book and then burn it.
A man who owned a similar book could make a carter's horses stand stock-still.
177014: In Leerbeek lived a witch. If you were touched by a witch, you had to strike higher immediately. If you had put a piece of the Easter candle under your threshold, no witches could come in. Many people put some holy water in their butter churn, because otherwise a witch could bewitch the butter.
177020: In Bogaarden lived a woman who was suspected of being a witch because she was often out at night and read bibles. People claimed that this woman's son had been bewitched. The boy had died when he was thirteen or fourteen. One evening someone had seen the witch performing rituals with holy water or herbs in front of the photograph of the dead boy. The stevenisten (members of a Catholic dissident sect) used to have similar rituals too.
177046: On a farm people were very afraid of a certain woman. After that woman had once come to visit, they had nothing but misfortune.
177067: One day Celeke drank a glass of beer in a café 'on tick'. Shortly afterwards the man died. One day the café owner, who did not yet know about Celeke's death, said: "Well, I don't see Celeke anymore. And he still owes me five cents here." The next moment a five-cent coin fell on the floor. That was Celeke coming to pay his debt.
177078: If people keeping watch in the evening in a sick person's house saw a black bird fly past, it was believed that the sick person would not live much longer.
177082: Some people were followed by a cat along the way. They could not catch the cat and believed the animal had something to do with evil.
177087: A man from Waanrode had fought a large dog. Because of this the dog had to take off its skin and reveal itself. He said to his attacker: "If you dare tell anyone about this, you're done for." When the man went to Diest one day, he met the werewolf, who said to him: "You told after all!" The man had said nothing at all, but the werewolf did not believe him and threw him into the Demer. The man drowned there.
177096:
A boy had learned to ride a bicycle so he could get to work faster. As the boy was cycling down a street behind a lorry, the witch who lived there came outside. The lorry had to brake and the boy ended up in the brook. The witch then said to the boy: "Lying in there, little man?" The boy answered angrily: "You can see that, filthy woman! It's your fault I'm lying here!"
When that witch had visited a baby, it often happened that the child afterwards had some defect or other.
177111: On a farm in the Middelstraat people were sitting talking by the stove one evening. Suddenly the farmer heard a noise. He went to look in the stable and to his great astonishment saw three cows standing there, while he had only one! When people went to look in the stable again the next morning, the two ghost cows had disappeared.
177114: A man who was digging at night saw a strange figure approaching. The werewolf jumped around and got on the man's nerves. Then the man said: "If you push against my spade once more, I'll knock your legs off!" A moment later the man struck out with his spade, after which the werewolf took on his human form. It turned out to be one of the man's neighbours.
177141: A man who was bewitched got a pain in his arm and in the end even died.
177146: In the devil's barn in Meise there was a hole that could not be closed. The farmer who had had the barn built had sold his soul to the devil.
177165: In Langdorp lived a man who could turn himself into a black dog.
177168:
Along the Steenweg to Ninove stood two houses in which a woman lived. In those houses the loom could be heard working at night, although the woman was asleep.
Because the neighbours were afraid, they went to the fathers of Affligem.
177220: In a house where wicked people lived and where there was always gossip, horses' legs suddenly began dancing up and down in a cooking pot on the stove.
177227: It was said that the house of a gravedigger was haunted. Because his little daughter was always thrown out of her bed at night, the priest was sent for. When the priest came in, the door fell on his head and he died.
177240: A man and a woman always heard footsteps coming up to their bed. A little lamp was also burning, which was often put out. At a certain moment there was knocking on the window and a voice said: "People, get up." Burning beams flew out of the hayloft. In the morning there was no trace of the fire. In front of the hearth, though, there was a lot of soot on the floor, and in the soot the paw prints of a dog could be seen. On their neighbours' advice the people had prayers read over their house. After that the haunting was over.
177247: If two people had died in a parish, a third death would soon follow.
177273: A father whose child was possessed by the devil had the fathers of Affligem read prayers over the child. The child was sprinkled with holy water and the father was also given a medal. On his way home the father saw five hundred people sitting in the field, pulling up lettuce and all saying: "I've seen you before." The man was afraid and protected his child with a gun. When the man got home and had laid the child in the cradle, he heard a buzzing at the window as if there were lots of bees outside. The man went outside and saw one bee. He shot at it with his gun, but the gun did not work. After the man had put a blessed candle on his gun, he did hit it, and the devil was gone. The child was cured as well.
177284: At midday some people secretly went gathering potatoes on the border of Kumtich, Tienen and Vissenaken, because they knew the policeman was away eating then. "Run, the policeman's there!" one of the women shouted. Another woman said calmly: "Let him come, he won't get far. Just fill your sack." The woman muttered something, after which the policeman stood still. When the people were back on the Tienen border, they put down their sacks. The woman said: "Now you can come, comrade." For there the policeman could no longer do anything to them. Later many books were burned in that woman's house. They were books such as 'De verborgenheden des volks' (The Secrets of the People). The priests came to exorcise that house.
177285:
In winter, on frosty nights by moonlight, the witches could be seen dancing in the meadow in the shape of cats. Laughter and singing could then be heard until morning. A farmhand driving his cart to the field in the morning came across a cat and struck the animal with his whip. The next morning a woman from the village had a red welt on her forehead. Around a tree a circle could be seen where the grass had been trampled.
A farmer who went to watch the witches' dance one night heard the laughter of a woman he knew well.
177286: In Tienen lived a beggar woman who was suspected of being a witch. That woman could make beautiful hats. One day she offered to make a hat for a neighbour. When the neighbour received the hat, she found that it was completely full of lice.
177287: A man had seen a horse that would at one moment become very big and then very small again. If you sat on that horse, you would sometimes fall off because it had suddenly become very small.
177288: A farmhand who worked on a farm threw his shoes at a big black cat on the way. The cat stayed sitting by the shoes, so the man was frightened and had to go back to that place the next day to fetch his shoes.
177295: A man always had to walk past a witch's house on his way to work. At that spot the man was always hindered by an animal that got under his feet. One day the parish priest gave the man a small object that he had to sew into his coat. After that the man was never hindered by that animal again.
177298: A man coming back in the evening from the rosary in Meerbeek met a big barking dog. At some moments the dog changed into a horse.
177318: A man from Vissenaken had to carry the werewolf in the Binkom fields.
177342: In the guardhouse in Kessel the haunting always began at a certain hour. People were thrown against the wall and the chairs were lifted up to the ceiling. One day the priest of Holsbeek came to keep watch in the house together with the sexton. Not even half a minute after the haunting had begun, the clergyman ran away in fright.
177358: A werewolf was a man who went out at night in a cowhide or horsehide to leap on passers-by and make them carry him. People who had to carry the werewolf usually ended up drenched in sweat. Only people who were not afraid were spared such tormenting.
177387:
A man who saw a woman walking who lived on the Malheide wanted to test whether that woman was a witch. When the man crossed the witch's footprints, the woman turned around and said: "I didn't know it was you following me so fast." That is how the man knew the woman was a witch.
The witches gathered at midnight on the square of the Boterham in Essenbeek.
177394: A man who had seen a strange cat somewhere went looking for it with his friends on Sunday during high mass. The men, however, could not catch the cat. The next Sunday they went back and saw the cat sitting under a culvert. The men shut the cat in so that it could not get away. Strangely enough, a little later they saw the cat coming out of a house through a tiny crack. The men shot at the animal but could not hit it.
177415: People who were ridden by the mare had a nasty dream.
177416: A ten-year-old girl had been struck by the evil hand. The girl fell ill and stopped growing. She also had an ugly face and ugly hair. Her hair became stiff and fell out. One day the fathers came to exorcise the child. The clergymen put a relic under the threshold and said: "Tonight a woman will come here." That evening a woman came by who could not manage to enter the house. The people would only let her in after she had promised to undo all the harm she had done. The woman had put a knotted rope in her bed. The more knots she untied, the plumper the child became. And so in the end the girl recovered.
177436: At a convent farm in Terbeek a gentleman dressed in black appeared at night. When a man went outside and grabbed at the gentleman with his hand, suddenly there was nothing to be seen. On that farm they also had much misfortune with the animals. In the end they put a holy relic under the door.
177440: A farmer who had a lot of work met a smart gentleman in the field one evening, who said: "Are you still working so late, good man?", to which the farmer replied: "Yes, I have to." The gentleman said to the farmer: "If you like, you can lead a quiet life from now on. The first thing you bind tomorrow you must give to me, and then your work will be done for you." The farmer agreed. That evening, however, he became uneasy and told his wife what he had done. Before the cock crowed the next morning, the farmer's wife got up and tied a horse's rein around a thick tree. The tree was torn out, roots and all, and dragged off by the devil. If the farmer's wife had not done that, she herself would have been the victim when she tied the strings of her apron.
177455: In Pepingen lived a woman from whom children were not allowed to accept anything. In the old days, when people went to fetch buttermilk from the farmers, they always had to pay five centimes. After all, if you accepted something for free, you could become bewitched. People who were possessed by evil could have a priest read prayers over them.
177458: A mother who had a six-month-old baby was visited by a woman. When the mother took the baby out of the cradle, the woman said: "Oh, you have a sweet, pretty baby! And she has such lovely rosy cheeks!" and pinched the child's cheek. After the woman left, the baby fell ill. The child vomited and grew weaker by the minute. The father's employer advised him to take his little daughter to the friars. When the man and the woman arrived with the child at the friars of Dendermonde, one of the friars asked: "Did you tell anyone you were coming here?" The mother answered: "Yes, my mother knows." The friar said: "You should not have done that. Now I cannot help you. Take that child and go outside." The parents went outside and walked around Dendermonde for a while. Then they went back to the friars. One of the friars read prayers over the child until he was drenched in sweat. Then he said: "Madam, she is saved. And it was high time. But you must not bear any hatred towards the person who did this to you." The clergyman also gave the people a medal to hang above the door.
177477: By wounding a werewolf, you could unmask him.
177483: A girl had stayed rather late at the inn where she had arranged to meet her boyfriend. The next day a sorceress from the neighbourhood knew when the girl had come home. Yet the girl had not seen the sorceress.
177521: People who were ridden by the mare in their sleep had a stoppage of the blood, which made them go completely stiff.
177524: A man was bewitched so that he could not move from a crossroads by someone he knew well.
177529: On a farm in West Flanders the labourers could not go to the kermis (village fair) because the harvest of a one-hectare field had to be bound. One man said he would do the work alone and still go to the fair. When the family had left, the man said: "Everyone bind his bundle!" and a little later: "Everyone stand his sheaf upright!" When the man then wanted to set off for the fair, he made a mistake in saying the magic formula and said he would fly 'through' hedges and bushes instead of 'over' hedges and bushes. When the man arrived at his destination, his clothes were completely torn.
177532: In Scherpenheuvel there stood an oak with a small chapel hanging on it. One day a shepherd wanted to take the statue of Mary out of the little chapel. But the shepherd stayed stuck to the tree until someone came to free him the next day and put the statue back in the chapel. The tree was already full of objects that pilgrims had left there. There was hardly a leaf or branch left on it because the pilgrims all wanted to take something away. In the end the tree was sawn down and statues of Mary were made from the wood.
177564: Two friends had agreed that whichever of them died first would come and tell the other what things were like in the hereafter. When one of the friends had died, the other saw a ghost appear in the Keustermansbaantje next to the railway. He asked: "Well, how is it up there?", to which the ghost replied: "Everything is reckoned precisely, and not a single oat grain is forgiven."
177581: In Hoegaarden lived an old woman who sometimes went to mass in the evening. On the way, the woman ran her hand along the wall of a large farm. Animals died very often on that farm, so the farmer decided to go to the priest. The clergyman said: "We will pray for that." Eventually the old woman died. After that, no more animals died on the farm.
177586: In the Beertstraat there was a house where the furniture danced and where noise was heard at night. The man who lived there had the priest come to read prayers over the house. After that the haunting came to an end.
177591: One night the grain mill in the attic of a house in Buken began to turn by itself.
177607: A girl worked as a maid for a judge. The girl was leaning out of the window when a woman passed by on her way from church. The woman said to the girl: "That my little friend." Because the woman was a sorceress, the girl did not dare respond.
177633: A boy worked as a farmhand in Vertrijk. On that farm the cow was always untied at night. It was probably a witch who did it.
177639: A man coming home at night saw an unknown dog at his door and was terrified.
177641: A farm in Neerlinter was haunted. At night a priest with a funeral procession and a coffin always came past.
177646: Bontegem was plagued by rats. In the evenings at least a hundred rats ran through the street. People said the rats had been sent by a witch.
177648: If one saw an owl, it was believed that someone would die before long.
177671: In the Predikherenstraat stood a haunted house that had once belonged to a monastery. In the attic lay a white stone with the inscription: "Forget me not". One day the woman living in the house had the blacksmith come to loosen the stone. The woman probably found a pot of money there, for afterwards the house stayed quiet.
177672: A maid who slept in the attic room always saw a white apparition at night. It looked like someone wrapped in a sheet. The parish priest advised the maid to go to confession and take communion. If the ghost still appeared, the maid had to say: "If you come from God, speak. If you do not come from God, leave." The maid also had to ask whether she could help the ghost. If she shook the ghost's hand, she had to make sure she had a handkerchief wrapped around her hand. When the maid asked the ghost the next night what it wanted, she was told: "I was supposed to do the procession of Sint-Pieter, and I did not do it. Now I must suffer. Will you do the procession in my place?" The ghost gave the maid its hand. The handprint was burned into the handkerchief. Afterwards the maid had to go to the church, where the priest was waiting for her. The maid knelt at the communion rail and heard three knocks. "That is normal," said the priest, "now she is released!"
177684: Some people who were working in the field sat down against a tree at midday to eat their sandwiches. When the people got up afterwards, the tree they had been sitting against vanished into thin air.
177693: Stallichten (will-o'-the-wisps) were the souls of unbaptised children. If on seeing such a light you said: "I baptise you in the name...", the light disappeared.
177694: People who were ridden by the mare always had bad luck and went on pilgrimage.
177699: An old woman with a basket often came to a farm in Honsem. Little bones lay in the manger of the cowshed. When the people asked the woman to remove the bones, she pretended to know nothing about it. The priest came to read prayers over the shed and the people placed a relic under the threshold. After that the old woman could no longer come in. So she was certainly a witch.
177701: Some men were out poaching by moonlight in the Bergstraat in Galmaarden. Suddenly it seemed as if the moon was darkened. The poachers heard beautiful music and laid their guns on the ground. When a hare came running up, the poachers believed it was a black cat. The moment they grabbed the animal by the tail, the music stopped. As soon as they let it go, they heard the lovely music again. A little further on they saw a stable, where there was a hellish noise and which was full of cats. A black cat was standing there the whole time turning the tail of another cat. At the stroke of twelve the whole scene had vanished. The black cat had changed into a little woman turning a cat's tail. She was a neighbour of the poachers. Frightened, the woman said to the men: "Tell no one that I come here, or they will burn me alive."
177717: In a house in Halle a witch walked up to the cradle of a two-year-old child. The witch touched the child and stayed to chat for a while. Then she left. From that day on the child was sad and cried day and night. The child also grew very thin. The child's father sought the advice of a witch exorcist from Nieuwenhoven. The witch exorcist said to the man: "I cannot help you. At home you must burn the cradle and all the child's bedding and then buy a new cradle. This child will die, but your next child will live."
177718: In Jette lived a farmer who was ridden by the mare. Friars from Affligem were brought to the farm to read prayers over the place. A friar put an Easter candle under the threshold.
177724: People who were in a bad mood or had a strange illness were said to have been ridden by the mare.
177725: A family from Ganshoren rented a two-family house from a woman suspected of being a sorceress. The owner herself lived in the front part of the house. To protect themselves, the people put a wardrobe against the door connecting the two parts of the house. At Christmas everyone in the house was ill except the daughter and the father. The father sent his daughter to the neighbour to fetch a glass of punch and a piece of gingerbread. At midnight the daughter, who had also drunk some of the punch, lay rigid in her bed. The father believed his daughter was dead and got up to fetch the doctor. When the owner saw the man leaving, she asked: "Where are you going?" The owner went with the man to the doctor. The two had barely got outside when the man fell down the stairs. When the doctor arrived, he said: "There is little I can do about that." The daughter nevertheless recovered.
177739:
People who were ridden by the mare were tormented in a dream as a result of something unpleasant during the day. They then felt a heavy weight pressing on them. Reading a bad book could also lead to being ridden by the mare. One could then have prayers read over oneself by a brown friar of Sint-Truiden, read the bad book again backwards and then burn it. If one had not first read the book backwards, it would not burn.
Whoever was ridden by the mare at night could put a flattened branch of the acacia tree under his bed.
177753: A boy who could not read or write went to work on a farm in Wallonia. His master gave the boy a book. The master had said: "Just have a look in that, then you can do anything." When the boy had done so, he could do all sorts of things that were not normal, such as making rats and mice. One day the boy went to Geldenaken with a man. The boy said to the man: "If you meet anyone, strike at that person's face with your handkerchief." A little later the man was approached by a big growling dog. The man struck at the dog's head with his handkerchief, whereupon the animal vanished. When the farmhand came back, he said: "Yes, my hour had come. By reading that book, I have become possessed by the devil." Some time later the farmhand was seriously ill. He could not die, and because the priest could not help him, he sent for the brown friars. After prayers had been read over the boy four times and he had sworn never to take up that book again, the boy could confess and receive communion, so that he could die in peace. While the book was being burned, the boy kept saying: "It feels as if I have four heavy stallions on top of me."
177766:
Witches could turn into a black cat.
If you kicked at a black cat in the evening, you could not hit the animal.
177779: Every time L.H. went from Sint-Truiden to Zoutleeuw past the marshy Ven, he saw the ghost of his dead father appear in the woods.
177795: One Sunday a long-haired man was playing cards in a café. When one of the players bent down to pick up a dropped card, he saw to his great dismay that instead of feet the long-haired man had legs with hooves. The player made the sign of the cross, at which the strange man disappeared.
177801: A poacher saw a hare in the woods during high mass. He tried to shoot the hare, but did not succeed. The next week the poacher went back, but this time too he could not catch the hare. On the third Sunday the poacher saw the hare sit up on its hind legs, clap its paws and say: "Another mass missed, another mass missed!" After that the poacher never again tried to catch that hare.
177824: A mother had four children, all bewitched by the same woman. In the evening the children lay crying for hours because they were afraid of the sorceress. A man who was bewitched had a swollen head and could hardly see anymore. The people went to the White Fathers, who advised them to do penance. On their way home the people had to read a text on a slip of paper, stating that the evil had no hold over them.
177827: A courting couple saw lots of little lights near the Netelzeep (?), which disappeared as soon as they came closer. Those lights were the souls of unbaptised children.
177831: A woman who was ridden by the mare made noise and could not move. To protect herself against the mare, the woman put her shoes under the bed with the heels towards it.
177855: Many animals died on a farm. Whenever a new animal was bought on that farm, a woman suspected of being a sorceress came to look at it.
177888: A strange coach always came to the witch Mieke D.M. Sometimes there were a few gentlemen in the coach, other times the coach was completely full of fire.
177891: A man could not sleep at night because he was thrown against the ceiling in his bed or flung against the walls. The man would then cry so loudly that the neighbours could hear. The room had been filled with straw so that the man would not be killed falling on the hard floor. Other people advised the man to go to Mass like everyone else. When the man did so, he was freed from the devil's torments.
177892: At a mill there worked a farmhand who was always noticeably tired during the day. The miller discovered that at night his farmhand roamed about as Kleudde (a werewolf-like spirit) with a wolf skin. One day the miller sent his farmhand to Baasrode with a sack of flour. When the farmhand was gone, the miller heated the oven and threw the skin into it. A moment later the farmhand was already standing by the oven to save his skin. As soon as the skin had burnt up, the farmhand said: "I am saved!"
177920: People coming back in the evening through the cornfields near woods and bushes from the inn or from visiting their girlfriend sometimes suddenly felt two paws on their back. That was the werewolf making itself carried. Later it was discovered that werewolves were in fact ordinary people. Sometimes people dressed up in a wolfskin to frighten late walkers out of their wits. The victims then ran home scared to death. The next day the wives would tell their neighbours that their husband had had to carry the werewolf a long way. Especially in the Flemish regions with many woods, much was told about the werewolf.
177940: A woman saw lights moving among the trees. They were the souls of unbaptised children. You were not allowed to point at such lights.
177941: A boy who was always ill could not be helped by the doctor. The mother took her son to the priest of Elingen, who read prayers over him. Then the clergyman said: "At Easter the boy will come to the procession and he will be cured. Someone will come to visit you to ask for something. You need not give anything, because you will not have what is asked for in the house." When the woman got home, she went to the pump to fetch two buckets of water. There she saw a woman from the neighbourhood approaching, who asked: "Don't you have any lime left for whitewashing?" The woman answered: "No, I don't."
177946: A carter whose horse would no longer go on sought advice from a man in the neighbourhood. When the man reached the carter, the horse started moving again. Because of this, people believed that man was a sorcerer.
178023: A woman sat down on a chair in an inn. The woman became uneasy because a cat had crept under her chair. It was, after all, a black cat.
178057: People ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) had a horrible dream. In the evening at bedtime you had to take a little bottle and urinate in it. Then you had to seal the bottle. If the maar then came in, she could not get out again and would beg to be let go.
178058: A mother with a baby was often visited by a neighbour who was said to be a witch. One day the mother was working when the neighbour came in, so she could not stop the woman from going to the child's cradle and saying: "What a sweet child!" From that day on the child hardly ate anything and cried all day. One day the grandmother said to the child's mother: "The baby surely has 'het vivelaine' (a bewitchment illness). He is bewitched. You should take him to Grivegnée in Liège. A shepherd lives there who can cure that illness." The mother went to Grivegnée, where prayers were read over the child. The healer advised the mother to fetch a relic from the Brown Friars in Sint-Truiden and put it under the threshold. Then the witch would no longer be able to come in. The woman did as she was advised. A few weeks after the visit to the healer in Grivegnée the child was cured. One day the mother heard her neighbour call out: "Someone is at your apples!" But the mother pretended not to hear properly and gestured to the neighbour to come in. The mother wanted to know whether the neighbour could still enter her house. When the neighbour tried to set her foot over the threshold, she could not. It was as if there was a wall that she kept bumping into. The neighbour then turned around and never visited the woman again.
178069: In a bewitched stable the cow always stood the wrong way round. When the people came back into the stable a little later, the cow had turned around again. Yet the people had heard nothing.
178070: Old people who did not go out much were sometimes said to have been ridden by the mare. When those people did go outside, everyone looked at them in surprise because they had not been seen for so long.
178106: A man had bought a castle where nobody wanted to live because it was haunted. Every night the man heard calling and groaning. One night, when the man was baking cakes, bones suddenly fell out of the chimney. A little later a skeleton stood in the corner of the cellar. Then the ground opened and the skeleton went to a secret cellar.
178122: In Wezemaal lived a sorceress who went out every night with a wheelbarrow on which she had placed a burning lantern. Wherever the sorceress went, people had misfortune. Once, when the witch had walked past a house where only unmarried young men and women lived, the occupants of that house went mad.
178153: According to the friars of Affligem, a little boy who cried all the time was bewitched. On their way home the people would meet someone, but they were not allowed to speak to that person, the friars had said. In the lane the parents did indeed meet someone, who asked: "Have you been out for a walk?" The parents did not answer and their child was cured.
178182: In Neerhespen lived a woman who went to do the washing at a large farm. One day, as that woman was coming back past the churchyard, she saw two big eyes in the hedge. Then the woman was leapt upon by something. The woman ran home quickly, crept into her bed and died.
178185: A boy going to the kermis (fair) met a witch on the way. When the boy arrived at the kermis, he found that his neck was full of lice. Strangely enough, when he got home the boy did not have a single louse left.
178220: A woman was coming back from a visit to her parents-in-law in Herfelingen. Because there were always sorcerers in the shape of cats on that road, a man had gone along with her. The man was approached by one of the cats and kept kicking at the animal. The woman said to the man: "What is the matter with you? That cat never comes to me. It always comes to you."
178246: A man had bet a bottle of jenever that he dared to go and cut a branch from a bush on the Warande between midnight and one o'clock. The man set off but never came back. The next morning his friends went to the Warande to see what had happened. The man lay dying beside the bush. He said to his friends: "A fiery horse-drawn coach appeared. The coachman struck me!"
178266: When people saw a cat in the evening, they said it was a witch.
178276: A woman had got de vlek (an eye disease) after giving a bouquet of roses to a witch. As the woman was praying to Our Lady, she suddenly heard a loud bang and then a voice that said: "Go to sleep in peace. The evil is gone."
178280: A man was coming back from Zichem with his wife and little daughter. On the way they were bothered by a cat that kept jumping against their legs. However hard the man tried, he could not chase the cat away. This convinced the man that the cat was a witch from the neighbourhood who untied the cows on some farms. When they got home, they tried to slip into their house without the cat coming in with them, but they did not succeed. There was no way to get the cat out of the house. Inside, the cat jumped up on everything.
178296: In the Koestraat people used to see will-o'-the-wisps moving back and forth. A farmer who had to fetch the midwife heard something when he reached the wood. Because the man saw a brilliant light in front of him, he said: "I baptise you in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit". Then more and more will-o'-the-wisps appeared, so the man had to keep baptising. A little later the midwife came by and said: "I baptise you all in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit". The next moment all the lights had vanished.
178305: Every Tuesday a woman came into a café to drink a glass of gin. Once, when the café owner had slaughtered a pig, the woman asked for some tripe, to which the man replied: "I slaughtered that pig for myself and not for anyone else." Then the woman said: "Your pigs will never get fat again." And indeed, after that the café owner was never again able to fatten a pig.
178315: In Hoegaarden lived a woman who had made a pact with the devil and could bewitch people by striking them. Anyone touched by that witch was sometimes no longer able to lift their arm.
178349:
People who dabbled in sorcery were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit). Such people sought help from priests and friars, who came to read prayers over them.
A man who had a pig that would not grow had a friar come to read prayers over his sty. While the clergyman was praying, drops of sweat rolled down his face because it cost him great effort to drive out the evil spirits. After the priest's intervention the man had no more trouble with his pigs. He believed he had fallen victim to the arts of a sorceress who had been to a public sale in the neighbourhood.
178367: A woman did not trust her aunt, because the aunt was suspected of being a witch. One day, when the woman was coming back from the tram, she was followed by a black cat. Two days earlier she had visited a sick person together with her aunt. The woman passed her aunt's house and saw the door open. Her aunt touched her, but the woman reacted quickly by striking higher. That woman would never have accepted a handful of cherries from her aunt.
178369: At the Klokkenborre in Lembeek bells are said to have sunk once during a storm or a war.
178370: A farmer had such luck with the harvest that his barn was too small to store all the grain. Around ten o'clock in the evening the farmer went for a walk to think about his problem. The farmer met a gentleman who offered to build him a barn that would be finished the next morning before the first cockcrow. In return the farmer had to give his most precious possession. The farmer had his best horse or his best cow in mind and did not realise that the gentleman was after his soul. The farmer went home and woke his wife to tell her that a barn would be built. The farmer and his wife could not get to sleep and saw that the devils had started work. The rooster usually began to crow around three o'clock. But around two o'clock the farmer's wife got up and banged on the henhouse, so that the rooster began to crow an hour early. The devils had to flee, although the barn was not yet finished. The hole in the barn could never be closed afterwards.
178384: A girl saw the ghost of her dead uncle Jef appear. The uncle said: "Josephine, you must marry that boy." The girl answered: "No, uncle, he is a redhead and I don't want a redhead."
178396: In Vissenaken lived a shoemaker who always knew when a witch had been in his house. Once, for example, the man was visited by a witch who said: "What beautiful flowers you have." When the witch touched the flowers, they immediately let their leaves and blossoms droop.
178411: An old man walking in the meadow with his wife kept seeing a white lady walking in front of his wife's feet. The woman said to the apparition: "I wouldn't want a dress like that, and get out of the way!" When the white lady then looked angry, the man said: "Go and seek your bread elsewhere, for we belong to God." Then the white and the black lady disappeared. (Apparently two figures had appeared.)
178416: A witch came into a house where there was a small child. "What a beautiful child!" said the witch, and she stroked the child's head. After that the child's head was turned back to front. When the father came home, he asked his wife who had visited. Then the man went to the witch's house with an axe in his hand and said to her: "I'll chop you to pieces like dung!" The witch went back with the father, touched the child again and said: "There's nothing wrong with that child! What you drag me here for!" After that the child's head was right again.
178417: On a corner in Halle a white rabbit sat every evening that no one could catch. The priest had already sprinkled that spot with holy water, but the rabbit still came there.
178427: In a house where bread was being baked, the dough would not rise after a sorceress had visited. A little pot of holy water was placed on the kneading trough. Shortly afterwards the dough did rise.
178437: A trader from Kampenhout saw a black cat in front of him along the Steenweg to Elewijt. When the man struck at the animal with his stick, two cats appeared. The more the man struck, the more cats he saw. In the end the man fell to the ground exhausted. The next day he was dead. People said he had been bewitched by a black cat.
178449: A sorceress was still sitting in the church because the priest had left his missal open. Then the sorceress walked up to the clergyman and asked whether he would like an apple or a pear.
178464: A woman who was bewitched was very fat one day and very thin the next. One evening the woman saw two white rats holding each other's front paws and dancing together. Her husband, however, did not see this strange apparition. Sometimes the woman also saw toads appear.
178480: If people saw two magpies, good news would come.
178488: In Beert lived an unmarried woman suspected of being a sorceress. When that woman sat in church in her hooded cloak, she coughed the whole time. One day the woman had gone to buy three cakes and a kilo of sugar loaf. She had laid it all on the roadside for when the children came by. But the children wanted nothing from her because they did not trust her.
178491: A house in Buken was haunted. The butter churn there always started working by itself.
178500: A man who was sawing called on the help of his dead mother-in-law because the saw kept getting stuck. After that the ghost of the mother-in-law made the sawing go much more smoothly.
178503: A woman had sold a calf. A little later, however, a dealer came by who offered more for the calf. The woman immediately sold the calf to that dealer. When the first buyer was on his way to collect his calf, the woman saw a spider crawling on the wall. That is how she knew the man was coming. It was an omen.
178504: A dead woman always came back to haunt at night. The woman would then sit upright in her bed, and her toes were tied together with straws.
178540: A woman who had bought a black stove invited someone to come and look at it. When the visitor came in, the stove had turned into a black pig. When the visitor had left again, the stove was back. It was a witch who had installed the stove.
178548: A man who had moved a boundary post during his life to have more land had to haunt after his death with the boundary post in his hands. The ghost kept calling: "Where shall I put it? Where shall I put it?" One day a drunkard answered: "Damn it, leave it where it is!" After that the ghost was not seen again.
178549: When a child was bewitched, people cut open the child's pillow and found lots of little copper pins in it.
178551: It was said of a vet from Kobbegem that he consorted with the devil. When that man heard someone approaching in the evening, he called out: "My friend, who is there?" If one did not answer, one had to stand still until the vet was home.
178567: When a child died somewhere, people believed the child had been bewitched. The priest would then come to bless the house and place a relic under the threshold, so that the witch could no longer come in. Werewolves disguised themselves and went to the witches.
178568: In the devil's barn in Oppem (Brussegem) there was a hole that could not be closed. The devils always came and threw the stones out.
178575:
If someone gave you a pat on the shoulder, you had to pray the Gospel to protect yourself against sorcery.
In Rotselaar lived a woman suspected of being a witch.
When an animal in a stable fell ill after an old woman had visited, people often believed that woman was a witch.
178586: A man was often visited by a woman who brought misfortune. After that woman had been by, no butter could be made. The man went to the friars of Tongerlo and received a relic to put under the butter churn. When the man churned, he found that the butter lay at the bottom of the churn instead of at the top.
178592: A farmer had sold his soul to the devil in exchange for a new barn, which had to be finished before the rooster crowed for the first time the next morning. But when the rooster crowed in the morning, there was still a hole in the barn.
178620: A man coming back at night with some friends from the music society's rehearsal met a miaowing cat. After one of the men had kicked at the animal, a little later there were a good ten cats. The men ran off scared to death.
178631: In Meerbeke stood a haunted house. Everyone who spent the night in the house was dead the next morning. At midnight four gentlemen appeared in the house and said: "Lift that stone". When people lifted that stone, they died. One day a brave soldier decided to put an end to the strange events. When the four gentlemen said: "Lift that stone", the soldier answered: "You took plenty in your lifetime. Do it yourselves!" When the gentlemen lifted the stone, three chests of money came to light. All the money had to be divided among the poor.
178637: In the past people were afraid of black cats because they believed these animals were witches. A farmer who was not ill but still lay in bed was visited every evening by a black cat that came and sat on his shoulder. That cat was a witch. Once the cat had been chased away, the farmer was soon able to leave his bed.
178646: When people had a lot of work, it could sometimes happen that they got more done in half an hour than they normally would in a whole day. The devil was helping them then.
178650: A girl went to help with sewing at a family where a baby lay in the cradle. The little boy, however, was bewitched, so that his head looked as if it were made of wood and he had a long beard. A woman who was having a dress made by these people had put the evil hand on the child. That woman regularly came to see whether her dress was ready yet. Once, when the priest was in the house, it came out that this woman had bewitched the child. The people chased the sorceress out and ran after her with the poker.
178659:
A hunchback had a pendelaar (dowser using a pendulum) come from Leuven because he wanted to be rid of his hump. The pendelaar dug a bone out of the ground.
The man had got his hump after a fall. However, he believed a witch from the neighbourhood had given him the hump.
178705: A woman who was plagued by ants got up before midnight to pray, after which the ants disappeared.
178714: A woman who went to cut clover for her animals saw a rabbit sitting in the field. The woman picked up the rabbit and carried it home in her apron. On the way, however, the animal grew heavier and heavier. When she got home, the woman found that the rabbit had turned into a big stone. She took the stone back to the clover field, where it turned back into a rabbit.
178716: A woman had said to a girl: "You're wearing a white little shirt". A little later the girl was completely covered in lice.
178738: A priest from the Netherlands was always robbed while he was saying mass. When his maid came to warn him one day that a thief was at work again, the clergyman fixed the thief to the ground by magic. On leaving the church, people saw the thief standing by the gate.
178744: Some people had bought a piece of land to farm. One night they saw a coach without a horse driving across that land. The people said: "Where a coach without a horse drives, the land will be laid out in streets, and that means misfortune." A short time later the people were indeed expropriated for next to nothing, and lost their livelihood. They had fallen victim to a rich and powerful man.
178746: In Dormaal there used to be a little white rabbit that no one could catch. People were a little afraid of that rabbit.
178754:
Near the castle of Winge there once stood a monastery that had been sold as confiscated church property. The nuns and friars who had lived there were extremely rich because they had swindled people out of all their possessions. Later the place was haunted. One night the farmhand N. saw two horses approaching in the castle lane, ridden by two headless nuns. N. nearly died of fright.
In the castle cellar a strange rumbling was always heard. When the cellar was opened, a friar was found there who crumbled to dust when touched. After that no more sounds were heard in the cellar.
178766: Between Kobbegem and Asse a returned dead man haunted with a post on his shoulders.
178771: Some brothers had to fetch a dance tent in Budingen with a horse cart. On the way the men saw something walking beside them the whole time that looked like a grandfather clock. The men began to pray, but the object did not disappear until they had reached the village.
178791: One Sunday evening a girl was coming back from Steven (1) together with her boyfriend. They were followed the whole way by a cat. When they began to pray the Gospel of Saint John, the cat suddenly vanished. It was a witch.
178805: During the First World War a woman sewed socks so she could afford some food. A farmer kept a pig in order to have some meat. The seamstress passed the farm every day and asked: "Well, how is your pig doing? I'll come and have a look!" After a while, however, the pig began to behave strangely. The animal ran into the walls and did not fatten. In the end the farmer even had to slaughter the pig. Afterwards the farmer bought another pig several times, but each time the same thing happened. One day the farmer and his wife decided to buy a new pig and say nothing about it to the seamstress. When the seamstress came by, she again asked: "How is the pig doing?" But the farmer's wife no longer invited the seamstress to come and look at the animal. And so that pig lived.
178824: In Wemmel lived a woman of whom the children were very afraid. That woman was said to have once bewitched people. The bewitched children started sweating and crying at night.
178825: A butcher had already lost three children to sorcery. One day a woman who was said to be a witch had been in the butcher's shop. When the child was put to bed that evening, it began to cry and had convulsions. Someone was sent for, who said: "The child is bewitched. Put a cross and a rosary on the stairs and have prayers read over the child." After this had been done, the child had no more convulsions.
178846: People who were ridden by the mare wanted to walk, but could not.
178861: A woman was always tormented by her mother-in-law, whom she suspected of witchcraft. When the woman's brother died in 1979, she went to the hospital. While the woman was sitting on a chair there, her mother-in-law came to stand beside her and, praying, laid a hand on her head. This suddenly made the woman feel very short of breath. For twenty-seven years the woman was tormented by her mother-in-law. Because of the witchcraft, the woman often suddenly could not breathe.
178862: When a strong wind blew in Aalst, people said it was a freemason coming back. A few days earlier a freemason had died in Aalst.
178904: The churchyard of Sint-Martens-Lennik is said to have been haunted in the past.
178929: People said of a farmer from Elingen whose daughter had died that he had been bewitched.
178941: A woman had refused to give three thousand francs to some Bohemians (travellers) who had called at her house. The next night the woman found that all the cows in her stable had been untied. One day the woman saw one of the Bohemian women kneeling in the stable, ranting to bewitch the animals.
178956: People who had misfortune often said they had been ridden by the mare.
178959:
On the Keiberg lived a girl of fifteen or sixteen who was said to be a witch. Whenever the girl's older sister had to go and cut grass, she always saw a hare leaping around her. One day the older sister was scratched in the face by the hare. People claimed the young girl had done it.
It was believed that if you crossed a witch's footprint after it had snowed, the witch would look back. A man on his way to Scherpenheuvel once tried this, and he saw that the witch really did look back.
178967: A schoolgirl could make a mouse or a rat appear by throwing a stone or a clod of earth. The girl was taken to Sint-Truiden to have prayers read over her. Children who had such special powers had not been baptised properly. That could sometimes happen when people did not understand the priest properly during the baptism and did not repeat his words correctly.
178973: A man had shot a snipe but could not find the animal anywhere. When the man went home after a while, he saw the snipe sitting waiting on his doorstep. The animal said: "Ah, there you are? I've been sitting here a long time!"
178996: A man fell off his bicycle in front of a sorceress's house. The man shouted: "Oh, you filthy sorceress!" At that moment the sorceress was standing outside at her door.
179009: A witch came into a cowshed in Molenbeek. She rubbed a cow on the back and said: "That's a fine beast". By evening the spot where the witch had laid her hand was full of lice.
179012: During catechism class a boy made mice by throwing a handful of earth on the ground. The other children told the priest. At first the clergyman did not believe them, but when he had seen it with his own eyes, he had to believe it. The priest took the boy into the sacristy, where prayers were read over him. After that the boy could no longer make mice.
179014: A man who wanted to make butter found that his churn was always full of dung. The man went to the monastery of Affligem, where prayers were read over him and he received holy water with salt. The friars said to him: "The first person who comes to you is the one who did it." Later that day the man saw a woman come running up, saying: "Oh dear, oh dear, now my butter has turned to dung!"
179048: A girl had taken over the magic arts of her grandmother or her aunt. For it was said that a witch could not die before she had passed on her magic arts to someone. A man whose trouser button had come off went to the witch to have the button sewn back on. When he got home, the man found that he was covered in lice. The man went back to the witch, thinking: "If I got them here, maybe I can get rid of them here". When the man left the witch, he had indeed lost his lice.
179053: People who were ridden by the mare tried to call out, but could not breathe. To protect oneself against the mare, one had to put one's clogs upside down next to the bed. Some people claimed the mare was a stoppage of the blood.
179059: In a house in Kattebeek there was a little son who was bewitched. Two friars came to read prayers over the boy. When the friars went home, they were drenched in sweat. The friars had to carry the burden of the witchcraft until they got home.
179083: A man out with a wagon suddenly could not go on because a witch had bewitched the wagon so it could not move.
179092: In the past it was believed that black cats were witches.
179116: The bridge over the Malebeek was haunted, so that some people could not get across it.
